Sports.title: How the death of Jayden Adams shook a community: ‘Being on the pitch was his happy place’
Sports.content:
For Jayden Adams, the South Africa midfielder who died this month at the age of 25, football was a “safe space”. Those words, used by Adams’s junior coach Steve Barker at his memorial service last Thursday, tell you everything you need to know about his life beyond the pitch.

Adams’s battles were bestowed on him almost from birth. Though he was born into newly democratic South Africa, by the early 2000s the revolution was well on its way to being betrayed. The vote was extended to all, but few could make full use of the freedoms available to them because socioeconomic circumstances in the country had barely changed. Stellenbosch, where the Adams family were based, is a perfect example.

Its facade is a tourist dream: a university town nestled among vineyards, Cape Dutch architecture and indie boutiques. Most visitors never venture beyond the town centre or into its suburbs, which are home to the far less privileged and are havens of neglect. Those areas are classic Apartheid hangovers, where the wealth has been preserved for a historically advantaged elite and those on the margins, working-class communities of people of colour, are all but invisible.

Ironically, that is how Adams is most often described. He moved in the shadows, both of society and the sport in which he excelled. “Jayden was a guy of very few words. He was quiet, very shy and the smallest among his teammates,” Brendine Johnson, an Adams family spokesperson, says. “Initially, a lot of people missed his football qualities because of his size, but he had a very good fighting spirit. It just wasn’t always on display.”

Adams, whose funeral took place on Saturday in Cape Town, loved the game dearly and his aunt Monica Thaoge recalled how, as a child, he would kick anything round – “even onions” she said at his memorial. His parents, Juanito and Candice, previously mentioned potatoes as their son’s football of choice. Nobody in the family talks about lacking in financial means because theirs was a community striving to make life better. But there were absences, especially early on.

View image in fullscreen Members of the Mamelodi Sundowns football club carry Jayden Adams’ coffin at the funeral service for the player on Saturday. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

“Everybody in areas like that is just trying to make ends meet,” says Roger Telemachus, the former South Africa cricketer who grew up on the same street as Adams’s father in Cloetesville. “For the kids, they may not have noticed so much because they were occupied, mostly with playing sport. Some fathers, like Juanito, really encouraged their kids and everyone used to play everything on the street: tennis, football, rugby, cricket. It was also the best way of staying out of trouble.”

Problems were there for everyone to see and, according to Telemachus, have got worse “in the last 20 years”. They include gangsterism, substance abuse and crimes that range from petty to serious. Adams was able to escape from that life when he moved to the slightly more affluent area of Ida’s Valley, but still he did not have a life of luxury. For a period, the family of six, which included four children, lived in a two-bedroom place. At other times, they were with his maternal grandmother, Marianna. “He basically grew up in her yard,” says Johnson.

Things started to change for Adams when he was picked for the Stellenbosch Academy Under-18 side at the age of 15. “The environment was tough, especially if you are not big or tall enough, but when physicality was no longer the most important thing, people saw that Jayden was technically very good,” says Johnson.

His coaches agree. Barker, the nephew of South Africa’s Afcon winning coach, Clive, and the current coach of Simba in Tanzania, gave an emotional assessment of Adams’s skills shortly after his death. “You get many good footballers but you get few great footballers. Jayden was great,” he told Newzroom Afrika.

“Jayden had three attributes that set him apart: an incredible first touch, his weight of pass – I’ve never seen anything like it – and he loved the game so much. Being on the pitch was his happy place. He didn’t pass the ball, he used to caress the ball. He was special and his football intelligence was just outstanding.”

View image in fullscreen Jayden Adams played in South Africa’s World Cup group game against Czechia despite the death of his grandmother the day before. Photograph: Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire/Getty Images

It was under Barker that Adams blossomed. He became the first player from the Stellenbosch Academy to play in South Africa’s top flight, the Premier Soccer League. Five years and an international call up later, the country’s richest club, Mamelodi Sundowns, came calling. This year, at the start of his second season with them, Adams shaved his head, in what he joked was a sign of maturity and called himself a “grootman” (big man). The nickname stuck.

Adams never said it, but he may also have realised how much he had grown up. By then, he had been picked, played for and dropped from the national side after arriving late at a training camp and irking the head coach, Hugo Broos. He had also lost two of his academy teammates, including a close friend.

In February 2023, Oshwin Andries, who was 19, died from stabbing injuries he sustained in Paarl, which is 16km north of Stellenbosch. Three years later, Jeandre Gaffoor, 20, drowned in the Krom River.

When Sundowns won the CAF Champions League in May, Adams dedicated his medal to Andries. To lose so much has weighed on the town, but through Adams they have had reason to celebrate.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Fortnightly Sign up to The Hotspot A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Members of Adams’s family, including his father, Juanito (centre left), and mother, Candice (centre right), at his memorial service last week. Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty Images

His role in Sundowns’ continental victory and a call-up to the World Cup squad suggested Adams’s career trajectory was rising. After a first season at Sundowns where he was often playing off the bench and his place in the side was questioned, he had become integral to the team. At Adams’s memorial, the Sundowns senior coach, Steve Komphela, called him “the heart of our team and the heartbeat of our playing style” who “understood the game like a coach and played it as a player”.

In the past year, Adams was playing to the potential people who knew him well had seen years ago and surprising others with his courage and drive to succeed. South Africa’s captain, Ronwen Williams, recalled an incident at this year’s Africa Cup of Nations when the tiny Adams took on a tall Mali opponent with some choice local words. Williams asked Adams if he knew the size of the player he was sledging, but Adams shrugged it off and replied that the Malian wouldn’t understand anyway.

“That was the character he had,” Williams said at the memorial, smiling through his tears as he bade farewell to the teammate he called “my ma se kind” (my mother’s child, a term of endearment used in South Africa).

As his star rose, Adams was careful not to advertise his achievements. “Jayden knew what he had, but he never wanted to voice it. He was very competitive, but he would never brag,” says Johnson. “You get people who are very good verbally on social media. Jayden was not like that. And he wanted to give back. After every game, he would be giving away shirts and boots to kids who asked.”

He also concentrated on providing for his family because he “always promised them he would change their financial situation”.

View image in fullscreen Jayden Adams signs a South Africa shirt for a young Mexican fan who arrived at the team’s World Cup hotel. ‘He wanted to give back.’ Photograph: SAFA

At the World Cup, Adams played for them, even through immense pain. His grandmother Marianna died the day before South Africa’s match against Czechia and Adams opted to remain with the squad. He played that match and appeared in good spirits afterwards and called the 1-1 draw positive, even if he was feeling the opposite way.

He also played the next game against South Korea, which South Africa won to reach the knockouts for the first time. Post-game footage showed him sitting on his own while the rest of the squad celebrated with a signature song and dance.

At the memorial, Komphela offered the Adams family a Bible verse as a comfort, but it may as well be a summary. Psalm 23:4: “Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.”

They will know Adams took that walk many times over his short life and he did not fear. He leaves behind his parents, three siblings, a partner, two children and a community who have gone through what no neighbourhood should. In all that, he has gone from not wanting to be known to spending a week in the footballing world’s spotlight. A minute’s silence was observed at several World Cup games in Adams’s memory. That is not the way his family would have pictured him coming to global attention, but it has shown them that, in football, he was always far more valued than anyone thought.

“I don’t think the community knew how big he was and how people enjoyed his football,” says Johnson. “It’s a huge shock.”

Sports.title: From Haaland love to Mexico’s Merlin: 26 memories from the 2026 World Cup
Sports.content:
Curaçao’s historic first goal

“I played with him on my PlayStation, and now I’ve scored against him,” Livano Comenencia said after converting Curaçao’s first World Cup goal past Manuel Neuer in their opening match against Germany. The smallest nation ever to qualify for the World Cup went on to lose 7-1 but that goal – their only one of the tournament – will go down in history.

‘Cablegate’

Should Jude Bellingham’s first goal against Norway have been ruled out? Perhaps so given the ball appeared to hit an overhead cable in the buildup. Fifa insisted there had been no such intervention; Norway’s manager, Ståle Solbakken, was sure there had been. “Many on the bench reacted immediately … the ball fell down straight in front of us,” he said, furiously.

Marsch’s musings

“I’d rather be us than them,” said Jesse Marsch after Canada were comprehensively beaten by Morocco in the last 16. “It takes some nerve to say that when you lose 3-0,” said Morocco’s head coach, Mohamed Ouahbi, in response. Marsch also somewhat hilariously overestimated the capacity of BC Place after his side’s 6–0 win over Qatar, saying: “There’ll be 60 million people that said they were here.”

Glittering Golden Boot race

Between 1978 and 2018, only the original Ronaldo had scored more than six goals at a single World Cup (eight in 2002). Lionel Messi and Kylian Mbappé had matched the Brazilian’s tally by the semi-finals this time around, with Mbappé winning the Golden Boot after scoring two goals against England in the third-place playoff.

Scotland fans take over Boston

Scottish supporters marked their return to football’s biggest stage in 28 years by taking over Boston, filling Fenway Park with songs and drinking their pubs dry. With the Tartan Army crowning some of the city’s most recognisable statues with bright orange traffic cones, the “Boston cone” was greeted by Boston’s mayor, Michelle Wu, upon its arrival from Glasgow last week. Scotland’s players may have made little impact in the US this summer, but their fans no doubt left a legacy.

Ronaldo scores … and then goes out with a whimper

‘CR7’ finally ended his knockout goal drought against Croatia as Portugal squeezed into the last 16. However, joy soon turned to despair when Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the next round. Ronaldo struggled to have any impact on proceedings, managing only 19 touches in what was his final World Cup match. “I gave it all, I gave it my best,” he said afterwards.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo scored against Croatia but could not prevent Portugal going out against Spain. Photograph: Marcel van Dorst/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

Embolo’s mistaken identity

The mistaken identity rule was updated for this World Cup to cover situations where a player was booked but the offence was committed by the other team and well and truly took effect during Argentina and Switzerland’s quarter-final in Kansas City. The referee, João Pinheiro, initially issued Argentina’s Leandro Paredes a yellow card for his challenge on Switzerland’s Breel Embolo before the VAR called him to the monitor. Embolo was then ruled to have dived and was punished with a yellow card himself – it was the forward’s second of the game and he was duly sent off. “This rule destroyed the game today,” said Switzerland’s head coach, Murat Yakin, after his side’s 3-1 loss.

Iran’s unprecedented tournament

Competing against the backdrop of their country’s conflict with the US, Iran’s players faced incredible difficulties before a ball was kicked. With their training base abruptly switched from Arizona to Mexico before the tournament, the team were then only allowed to enter the US the day before their first two matches and had to leave immediately after. Despite that, they only narrowly missed out on the knockout rounds after Austria and Algeria drew 3-3 in the final round of the group stage to send them home on goal difference. “What these players have done should be written in history because the host country treated us very unfairly,” Iran’s head coach, Amir Ghalenoei, said.

Erling Haaland: internet phenomenon

Snapchat stories. Stuffed raccoons. Doing next to nothing against Brazil for 79 minutes and then scoring twice in 11 minutes. It’s fair to say Erling Haaland made his mark at the World Cup. “When someone asks me what my biggest fear is but I can’t say being charged at by Haaland at full speed so I just say spiders,” reads a video that has racked up millions of views on Instagram, a reference to how Haaland chased down Iraq’s goalkeeper, Jalal Hassan, for his second goal of the tournament.

Turkey are definitely not dark horses

Turkey were tipped to go far but, in the end, didn’t even make it out of the group stage. Indeed, they were the second country eliminated from the tournament following back-to-back losses to Australia and 10-man Paraguay. “We should have won these games … everybody’s sad, everybody’s crying,” said Arda Guler, Turkey’s wonderkid after his country’s less-than-wonderful showing.

View image in fullscreen Arda Guler (right) grimaces during Turkey’s defeat by Australia. Photograph: Lee Smith/Reuters

Egypt outrage after controversial exit

“I’m going home and won’t be watching any more games from the tournament,” said Egypt’s head coach, Hossam Hassan, after his side’s loss to Argentina in the last 16. “What happened to us wasn’t fair. We should have had a penalty, a goal was disallowed and I don’t know why.” Hassan was not alone in thinking crucial decisions had favoured the world champions in what was arguably the game of the tournament in Atlanta.

The wonder of Wonderwall

It started off as a standard submission for the World Cup’s official track list but was quickly adopted by England’s travelling support as the theme song of their tournament run, Oasis’s 1995 classic creating a genuinely uplifting bond between plays and fans. Harry Kane went as far as describing the post-match ritual of standing alongside his teammates, arms around each other’s shoulders, and facing a wall of happy, singing English faces as one of his “favourite ever moments in an England shirt”.

Lamine Yamal’s brother becomes a star

Lamine Yamal had a great World Cup but not as great as his three-year-old brother, Keyne, who captured hearts worldwide with his wide-eyed, big-grinned expressions of delight whenever his older sibling shone at the tournament. A young star was born on the back of another young star and both look here to stay.

Mexico’s unofficial mascot

Merlin the duck became a sensation after being spotted at Mexico’s post-game celebrations following their opening World Cup win over South Africa. Indeed, Merlin became so famous that he was granted a meeting with Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum. “We feel very honoured to be here with the president, it is an honour for us to stand before you and for the whole world to see the beautiful side of Mexico.” said Karla Gómez, Merlin’s owner. Sadly, Merlin was unable to watch Mexico in the flesh due to Fifa regulations.

Death, taxes and Merino’s late winners

Messi, Mbappé, Haaland, Harry Kane … this has been a World Cup of goalscoring superstars well and truly coming to the fore, and then there has been Mikel Merino. The Spain midfielder came off the bench to score crucial winning goals against Portugal and Belgium in back-to-back knockout games. It was some contribution from the Arsenal player to his country’s World Cup triumph.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Merino races away after a late goal against Belgium. Photograph: Ringo Chiu/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

Aguirre meets Gordon

“Gordon!” shouted Javier Aguirre at England’s left-sided forward during the first-half hydration break of an epic last-16 encounter at the Azteca, followed by something indistinguishable when Anthony Gordon turned back to look. Keen-eyed internet users later deciphered it as a very cheerful “fuck you!” from Mexico’s manager, with both men subsequently laughing with delight. “I’d just run the full-back down the line,” Gordon said after England’s 3-2 win. “So I took it as a bit of a compliment from him.”

Vozinha’s star power

After being named player of the match in Cape Verde’s opening goalless draw with Spain, Vozinha teared up. “My mum didn’t manage to be here because of the visa,” said the 40-year-old goalkeeper. Two days later the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, announced that arrangements had been made to waive the cost of Ana Évora’s visa; she was subsequently in attendance as her son played in a 2-2 draw with Uruguay and became one of the stars of the tournament.

Penalty drama between Netherlands and Morocco

Neil El Aynaoui struck the crossbar. Justin Kluivert’s effort ricocheted off a post. Bart Verbruggen almost saved Soufiane Rahimi’s strike but helplessly watched it squirm under him and into the back of the net. At 2-2, Quinten Timber put his shot well wide, handing Morocco the advantage only for Achraf Hakimi to do the exact same thing. Standing bolt upright, Yassine Bounou saved from Crysencio Summerville before Ismael Saibari put an end to the rollercoaster of a truly remarkable last-32 penalty shootout.

Tuchel hits out at photographers

“I’m begging Fifa to change the position of the photographers in the national anthem, because I could not see my team,” Thomas Tuchel said after England’s opening win against Croatia. “It was a very special moment, and I was standing in front of a wall of 50 photographers and I could not see one single player.” It wasn’t the first time at the tournament that England’s head coach made his frustrations clear.

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel is not ready for his closeup. Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty Images

Opener smashes red-card record

Mexico’s 2-0 win over South Africa kicked off the World Cup and simultaneously almost equalled the 2022 tournament’s tally of red cards in a single match. Yaya Sithole capped off a terrible second half for South Africa by getting sent off just after the break before his teammate Themba Zwane and Mexican defender César Montes were shown red cards within eight minutes of each other.

“Overturn this”

With the vast majority of the football world rooting for them, Belgium reacted to the suspension of Folarin Balogun’s ban for the USA’s last-16 encounter with the Red Devils in Seattle with a ruthlessly commanding performance. They beat the co-hosts 4-1 and marked the victory with a string of celebrations that made clear what they thought of the controversy surrounding’s Balogun’s presence on the pitch, including an imitation of Donald Trump’s dance moves in the dressing room afterwards and a gleeful tweet from the team’s official account that simply read: “Overturn this.”

Paraguay go from heroes to villains

There was widespread delight when Paraguay eliminated Germany in the last 32 with a show of togetherness and defiance but their popularity diminished during their subsequent defeat by France on the back of a brutal display of the dark arts. Joe Hart brandished the South Americans an “absolute disgrace” while his fellow BBC pundit Micah Richards thought that the approach was wholly unnecessary, saying: “Paraguay are better than that. Defensively they were so good and they didn’t need to get into these antics.” The Uzbek referee, Ilgiz Tantashev, also faced intense criticism after inexplicably failing to book any Paraguay players.

France players embrace Deschamps

After Kylian Mbappé scored the first of his two goals against Sweden, he and his teammates ran over to Didier Deschamps and hugged their head coach. The gesture was a response to Deschamps’ return to the touchline following the death of his mother. When asked about the embrace, Mbappé said: “That’s the DNA of this group. The coach has been through certain circumstances, and we’re all with him and will continue to support him.”

View image in fullscreen Didier Deschamps is embraced by Kylian Mbappé as France take on Sweden. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

Referee stops play – with an injury

In a bizarre twist, the USA’s 2-0 victory over Australia in the group stages had to be stopped for, and not by, the referee, Felix Zwayer, after he collapsed with cramp in the dying minutes of the contest in Seattle. Australia’s midfielder Aiden O’Neill and the USA’s Balogun helped Zwayer stretch out the cramp amid ironic cheers from the crowd.

Croatia goal disallowed by a hair

Croatia had seemingly rescued their World Cup campaign from the jaws of defeat after Josko Gvardiol tapped in at the back post in the final stages of their last-32 encounter with Portugal in Toronto. But then VAR got involved and the goal was ruled out after Fifa’s sensor technology discovered that the cross to Gvardiol had taken the faintest touch off the head of Igor Matanovic. “It was very bad refereeing,” said Croatia’s manager, Zlatko Dalic. “I’m not saying that sometimes VAR can’t be of help, but it kills the emotions, it kills everything.”

Jayden Adams tributes

Jayden Adams, who featured in all three of South Africa’s group games, passed away just days after returning home from North America. “Today, South African football mourn the loss of a talented player whose passion, dedication, and love for the beautiful game inspired many,” read a national team tribute. A minute’s silence was observed before all quarter-final matches, alongside an outpouring of touching tributes to the 25-year-old midfielder.

Sports.title: Liverpool start Iraola era in style to beat Sunderland but Gomez injury deepens defensive worries
Sports.content:
The Andoni Iraola era at Liverpool opened with a victory over Sunderland in Nashville – and a deepening of concerns over the defensive options at his disposal. The sight of Joe Gomez hobbling off after 10 minutes of the new head coach’s first game and two teenagers forming a raw central defence partnership in his absence intensified the spotlight on a department in need of work.

Liverpool had few issues at the other end of the pitch against Regis Le Bris’s side, resplendent in pink in Tennessee, where second half finishes from Dominik Szoboszlai, Federico Chiesa and Lewis Koumas delivered an ultimately comfortable win.

“Probably the worst news has been straight away the injury of Joe,” admitted Iraola, who will have been impressed by lively displays from Calum Scanlon, Kieran Morrison and Koumas.

“We were happy because we were going through training without losing any players and unluckily for us we’ve lost Joe straight away.”

View image in fullscreen Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola speaks with Federico Chiesa on Saturday. Photograph: Andrew J Clark/ISI Photos/Getty Images

Geodis Park paid tribute to the late Kevin Keegan before kick-off on Saturday with both sets of supporters applauding the Liverpool, Hamburg and Newcastle great prior to observing an impeccable period of silence in his memory. The crowd itself was sparse, with plenty of empty seats around the 30,000 capacity stadium, although the official attendance was given as 24,897. Charging from $129 to $392 (£96 to £292) for tickets to a pre-season friendly missing its contingent of World Cup players perhaps explains why.

Sunderland were without Granit Xhaka, Brian Brobbey and summer signing Thomas Meunier. Liverpool’s absentee list included World Cup finalists Alexis Mac Allister and Victor Munoz, Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch, who will join the tour next week, and Virgil van Dijk, Cody Gakpo and Alisson, who also resume pre-season training next week but back on Merseyside.

Liverpool also had a summer signing missing. Jeremy Jacquet, acquired for an initial £55m from Rennes, was left out as a precaution but is expected to feature before the tour concludes against Leeds in Chicago next Sunday.

“With Jeremy we decided to take it easy with him,” Iraola explained. “He’s had a lot of months without playing, he’s been training very well, but we’re going to take it easy with him. He will play probably in the last game of this US tour, he will have time to have minutes.”

View image in fullscreen Joe Gomez is helped by trainers after going down early with an injury. Photograph: George Walker IV/AP

Having expressed worry over his “very thin” defensive options earlier in the week, Iraola’s resources were stretched further when Gomez went down injured early on. The luckless Gomez was unable to continue after treatment and his departure meant Liverpool’s central defence comprised two 18-year-olds recruited in January, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe. Kostas Tsimikas took the captain’s armband from Gomez, then passed it on to Szoboszlai when he was replaced at the interval.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Talla Ndiaye, a £1m signing from Amitie in Senegal, and Ndukwe, a £2.5m transfer from Austria Vienna who only teamed up with Liverpool this summer, reflect Liverpool’s policy of recruiting central defenders for the future. The here and now must also be addressed. With Ibrahima Konate exiting to Real Madrid, Giovanni Leoni yet to resume full training after his ACL injury, Gomez injury prone and Jacquet untested in the Premier League, though rated extremely highly, the responsibility on Van Dijk will be considerable next season. As it was last season.

The answer to the future quiz question of who scored the first goal of the Iraola era at Liverpool is Kieran Morrison. The 19-year-old winger started on the right, also known as the chasm left by Mohamed Salah, and slid a fine finish into the far corner of Melker Ellborg’s goal when released inside the area by Harvey Elliott, another player desperate to impress the new Liverpool head coach following a wasted season at Aston Villa.

View image in fullscreen Jaydon Jones and Timur Tutierov combined for a Sunderland goal. Photograph: Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images

Sunderland equalised in style when Enzo Le Fée broke from midfield and swept a superb shot into Giorgi Mamardashvili’s top corner from 25 yards. Le Bris made 10 changes at half-time, Iraola five, and Sunderland soon took the lead when Jaydon Jones picked out Timur Tutierov inside the area and the striker slotted beyond the Liverpool goalkeeper from 12 yards.

Szoboszlai gave the majority of the crowd what they had paid good money to see when controlling a loose Sunderland clearance 22 yards out and beating Ellborg with a convincing finish. Chiesa steered a clever shot inside the near post from Calvin Ramsay’s pass behind the Sunderland defence before Koumas, released by Szoboszlai, sealed the win.

Sports.title: Arsenal make shock approach to sign Vinícius Júnior from Real Madrid
Sports.content:
Arsenal are exploring a shock deal to sign Vinícius Júnior from Real Madrid. Arsenal have inquired about the Brazil international, who has one year remaining on his contract at the Bernabéu.

It is believed any move for Vinícius – who scored 22 goals for Real last season and four for Brazil at the World Cup – is at a formative stage as Mikel Arteta seeks a marquee signing to build on the club’s first Premier League title in more than two decades.

The 26-year-old Vinícius fits that bill, with Atlético Madrid’s Julián Álvarez, RB Leipzig’s Yan Diomande and Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain also on their radar.

Arsenal bolstered their attacking options with the £34m signing of Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge this week. Morgan Rogers had also been identified as a target, but it is believed Arsenal were not prepared to pay more than £80m for the England international, who has joined Chelsea in a £117m deal – a British record fee.

Vinícius’s future at Real is uncertain after José Mourinho’s return and the club could cash in on the player, rather than risk losing him for nothing in a year’s time.

Mourinho, who has signed a three-year deal at the Bernabéu, was criticised for comments he made after Vinícius accused Benfica’s Gianluca Prestianni of racially abusing him during a Champions League tie in February. Mourinho, Benfica manager at the time, said “something happens, always” in matches where Vinícius plays. Prestianni was banned for six matches after he admitted to using homophobic language towards Vinicius.

Tzolis followed Piero Hincapié – who turned his temporary deal into a full-time switch – and the goalkeeper Illan Meslier, who was out of contract at Leeds, as Arsenal’s third addition.

Bruno Guimarães could also move to the Emirates with Arsenal keen on signing the Brazil international. After Newcastle’s 1-1 pre-season draw at Gateshead on Saturday, Eddie Howe said: “We don’t want to lose our best players. I’ve spoken to him [Guimarães] as I would do. Bruno is just a fantastic person. We’ve had some really good conversations, both before the World Cup, during the World Cup and after the World Cup.

“I don’t know what’s going to happen with Bruno’s future. That’s for other people to speculate about.”

Sports.title: Japan football great ‘King Kazu’ Miura, 59, scores first competitive goal in four years
Sports.content:
Japanese football icon Kazuyoshi Miura scored his first competitive goal ⁠in nearly four years on Saturday, finding the net at the age of ⁠59 as ⁠Fukushima ​United thrashed Iwaki Furukawa 7-0 to advance in the Emperor’s Cup.

Miura, affectionately known ⁠as “King Kazu”, struck in the 52nd minute to put Fukushima 5-0 ahead, capping a trademark ⁠run into the box by meeting a teammate’s ​cutback with a first-time ‌finish at 59 ‌years and 149 days.

The goal sparked celebrations among teammates ‌on the pitch and the bench before the veteran forward was substituted three minutes later.

It was Miura’s first competitive goal since November 2022, when he scored for Suzuka PG, now Atletico Suzuka, in ‌a Japan Football League defeat by FC Osaka.

The former Japan international is preparing for ​a remarkable 42nd season as a professional after extending his loan spell with third-tier Fukushima United until June 2027.

Miura joined the club from Yokohama FC in ⁠December and will remain with Fukushima after making six ​appearances ​during a shortened 2026 ​campaign.

With Japan’s professional leagues set to switch ​from a ‌spring-to-autumn schedule to ​an ​autumn-to-spring calendar, Miura will enter his 60s still playing professionally, adding another chapter to one of football’s most enduring careers.

Sports.title: Defoe’s shock Woking exit came after ‘growing concerns’, says club
Sports.content:
Jermain Defoe’s departure from Woking came after “growing concerns” at the club with Jody Brown, the National League side’s director of football, claiming the former Tottenham striker failed to turn up for training.

Defoe’s contract at the National League club was mutually terminated on Thursday after four months in charge. In is first managerial job, the 43-year-old oversaw two wins and one defeat in six matches. The former England forward had said it was “impossible for me to continue” and described his time at the club as an “eye-opening” experience.

But the club responded strongly on Saturday. “The recommendation to appoint Jermain as manager was mine, and I take full responsibility for it,” Brown said. “After meeting with him on several occasions, I believed he was the right person to lead the club into an exciting new era.”

But he went on: “However, in recent weeks there had been feedback from across the club, including players, staff and other departments, regarding growing concerns.

“To better understand the situation, I asked Jermain and Paul [Bracewell, the assistant manager] for a brief report outlining the squad’s current depth, recruitment targets and any operational challenges, so we could provide the support required and accelerate preparations for the season. That report was requested on more than one occasion but was never received.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“A meeting was subsequently scheduled involving the directors, manager, assistant manager and head of operations to review preparations for the season. Neither Jermain nor his assistant attended that meeting or that day’s training session. Throughout his tenure, Jermain had never communicated any serious concerns directly to me, so I am not going to speculate on his reasons.”



Defoe has not publicly responded to Woking’s claims.

Sports.title: Premier League: club-by-club guide to transfer business so far – and what they still need
Sports.content:
Arsenal

For once, Mikel Arteta is not spending his summer looking for a No 9. Instead the champions have moved to strengthen out wide after the departure of Leandro Trossard with Christos Tzolis arriving for £34m having scored 33 league goals in his last two seasons from Club Brugge’s left wing. After missing out on Morgan Rogers to Chelsea, they will not want to be beaten to Alex Scott’s signature. Defensive cover will probably be necessary after the injury to William Saliba at the World Cup. Billy Munday

Major ins Piero Hincapié (Bayer Leverkusen, £45m, after loan), Christos Tzolis (Club Brugge, £34m) Major outs Leandro Trossard (Besiktas, £15.3m), Jakub Kiwior (Porto, £14.5m)

Aston Villa

It is a very busy summer of comings and goings at Villa Park. Alejandro Garnacho is primed to swap places with Morgan Rogers and there is still scope for Emiliano Martínez to leave, forcing their hand in goal, and Arsenal’s interest in Ezri Konsa is not going away. Striker is another position without guarantees, with Nicolas Jackson one option, especially if Fenerbahce’s interest in Ollie Watkins becomes something more concrete. A left-back to replace the departing Lucas Digne is a must, while Leon Bailey is available for transfer and could head to Hull. Will Unwin

Major ins Johan Manzambi (Freiburg, £51m), João Gomes (Wolves, £34m) Major outs Morgan Rogers (Chelsea, £117m), Youri Tielemans (Manchester United, £35m), Donyell Malen (Roma, £21.6m)

Bournemouth

Plenty will depend on Alex Scott and whether he stays or goes, with interest in the midfielder, who has turned down a new contract, from Chelsea, Manchester United and Arsenal. Regardless of that, Benfica’s António Silva is lined up to replace Marcos Senesi, while the search is continuing for a right-back. With a first season in the Europa League ahead, planning accordingly to ensure the squad is sufficiently robust to cope with a more hectic schedule than usual is paramount. WU

Major ins Álvaro Rodríguez (Elche, £21.4m) Major outs Luis Sinisterra (Cruzeiro, £5.2m), Marcos Senesi (Tottenham, free)

Brentford

Usually a big sale pushes the Bees into action but not this summer. Experience has been on the agenda, with Jaidon Anthony and Callum Wilson acquired, while the arrival of the young centre-back Jannik Schuster could mean the end of Ethan Pinnock’s time with the club. They are, as always, likely to look at bringing in players with potential. The Manchester United teenager Noah Ajayi falls into this category but whether a deal progresses remains to be seen. WU

Major ins Jaidon Anthony (Burnley, £15m), Jannik Schuster (Red Bull Salzburg, £14m), Callum Wilson (West Ham, free)

Brighton

Investing in the defence early has freed up time to do other critical business, with a central midfield refresh potentially in the offing, while there is a desire to bolster the winger bullpen. Evan Ferguson is back at the club after a loan spell at Roma but whether he has a future at the club remains to be seen. If not, finding suitable support for the 35-year-old Danny Welbeck will be part of the strategy with the a Conference League campaign awaiting. Bart Verbruggen has attracted interest in Europe and a departure would call for a new No 1 to be found. WU

Major ins Luka Vuskovic (Tottenham, £46m), Zadok Yohanna (AIK, £21.5m), Pascal Struijk (Leeds United, £18m), Costinha (Olympiakos, 11m) Major outs Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham, £52m), Diego Coppola (Paris FC, £15.3m), James Milner (retired), Solly March (released)

Chelsea

Marc Cucurella’s sale has left a hole to fill at left-back. Options there include a return for Newcastle’s Lewis Hall or a move for Rayo Vallecano’s Pep Chavarría. The midfield is also looking light with Andrey Santos out the door and Enzo Fernández linked with a move away. The reluctance to sign a goalkeeper suggests 20-year-old Mike Penders is not far from competing for the No 1 spot. The capture of Morgan Rogers will excite supporters, but they still crave a top centre-back and striker. BM

Major ins Morgan Rogers (Aston Villa, £117m), Marco Palestra (Atalanta, £47m), Geovany Quenda (Sporting, £40m), Emmanuel Emegha (Strasbourg, £21.6m) Major outs Marc Cucurella (Real Madrid, £52m), Andrey Santos (Manchester United, £50m), Tyrique George (Everton, £18m)

View image in fullscreen England attacker Morgan Rogers is an exciting signing for Chelsea. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

Coventry

Without putting too fine a point on it, quality across the board is required. The club are still working on bringing the Brighton goalkeeper Carl Rushworth back after a successful loan in the Championship but price and competition for his signature will complicate matters. Finding strikers capable of converting chances will be integral to their chances of survival for Frank Lampard’s side. Norman Bassette has returned to Belgium after spending last season out of loan. WU

Major ins Loum Tchaouna (Burnley, £20m), Aurèle Amenda (Eintracht Frankfurt, £15.4m), Frank Onyeka (Brentford, undisclosed fee)

Crystal Palace

Making sure Maxence Lacroix, Jean-Philippe Mateta and Adam Wharton are still at the club come kick-off is imperative. Chelsea’s interest in Lacroix and Wharton will cause the most concern, while extending Mateta’s deal beyond the end of the season will need to be addressed. The starting lineup is strong but greater depth, with another European campaign in the offing, is imperative for the club. Óscar Mingueza was a sensible signing on a free, especially after not replacing Marc Guéhi in January. Walter Benítez may leave in search of first-team football, which would leave a gap in the goalkeeping department. WU

Major ins Óscar Mingueza (Celta Vigo, free)

Everton

Young, developing potential has been recruited so far in the form of Hayden Hackney – player of the season in the Championship with Middlesbrough in 2025-26 – Tyrique George and Merlin Röhl, the last two after loan spells with David Moyes’s side last season. But established players are still required to fill several weak spots, especially at right-back, a position that has needed strengthening for far too long now, and centre-forward. Left-back, central midfield and another wide player – the return of Jack Grealish possibly – would also be on the wishlist. Andy Hunter

Major ins Tyrique George (Chelsea, £18m), Merlin Röhl (Freiburg, £17.3m), Hayden Hackney (Middlesbrough, £16.5m) Major outs Séamus Coleman (released)

Fulham

It is a new era at Craven Cottage under Álvaro Arbeloa and there is much work to be done. The loss of Raúl Jiménez and, more important, the player of the season, Harry Wilson, means there are holes to fill. Like a year ago, it’s been a slow start to the window and things will need to speed up if they are to find a new striker, winger and a centre-back. Real Madrid’s Franco Mastantuono and Gonzalo García are under consideration, having previously worked with Arbeloa. WU

Major ins Jonah Kusi-Asare (Bayern Munich, £5.2m) Major outs Issa Diop (Ipswich, £8.5m), Harry Wilson (Leeds, free), Raúl Jiménez (Wolves, free)

View image in fullscreen Leeds signing Harry Wilson excelled last season for Fulham. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

Hull

After avoiding an expected six-point deduction for breaching spending rules by selling the goalkeeper Ivor Pandur and the midfielder Aidon Shehu to Rangers and Panathinaikos respectively for a combined £8.5m at the end of June, the playoff winners aim to make 10-12 new signings before September. Reinforcements are required all over the pitch, with central defence, central midfield and attack particular priorities. “Think about us like a volcano,” says Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Yet as much as the manager, Sergej Jakirovic, needs new faces he will be anxious to retain last season’s exceptionally powerful team spirit. Inspired loans and free transfer imports could prove crucial. Louise Taylor

Major ins Jack Butland (Rangers, £3.5m) Major outs Ivor Pandur (Rangers, £6m)

Ipswich

Promotion brings enough problems but doing so with a new manager brings added complexity as Gary O’Neil seeks to shape his squad. The aim is to be better prepared for the Premier League than last time by signing those with the physicality to compete in the top flight, preferably having done so before, hence the signing of Issa Diop. Inroads have been made but the spine of the team needs strengthening, especially in midfield and at centre-forward. WU

Major ins Emersonn (Toulouse, £24m), Abdul Fatawu (Leicester, £20m), Issa Diop (Fulham, £8.5m), Chuba Akpom (Ajax, £7m) Major outs Arijanet Muric (Sassuolo, £6m)

Leeds

Daniel Farke has traditionally preferred to operate with a small, closely bonded, first-team squad but acknowledges a little expansion is required. As the defender Joe Rodon recently put it: “We want to make our squad bigger and better.” So far, though, the goalkeeping department has shrunk appreciably, with Karl Darlow and Illan Meslier having left while Lucas Perri is coveted by Torino. If new keepers currently top Farke’s shopping list – and Manchester City’s and England’s James Trafford in particular – the Southampton central midfielder Shea Charles is not far behind. Leeds seem determined to acquire the 22-year-old but the Champonship club are reluctant sellers who will demand top dollar. With Harry Wilson and Tarik Muharemovic having already arrived to reinforce attack and central defence respectively, considerable focus is on midfield where Julian Brandt, a free agent after leaving Borussia Dortmund, is also coveted. LT

Major ins Tarik Muharemovic (Sassuolo, £34.1m), Harry Wilson (Fulham, free) Major outs Pascal Struijk (Brighton, £18m), Karl Darlow (Manchester United, free)

Liverpool

Arne Slot wanted two new wingers and a right-back before he was sacked in May and the change of head coach has not changed Liverpool’s priorities. Victor Muñoz has been signed as a versatile forward but not as an immediate starter under Andoni Iraola, and the pursuit of top wide talent continues. Bradley Barcola and Yan Diomande are of interest, although Paris Saint-Germain may determine both their futures. Iraola is concerned at the thinness of his defensive options and, while in an ideal world he would consider Conor Bradley to be Liverpool’s first-choice right back, the Northern Irishman’s recovery from a serious knee injury is likely to force another transfer move. AH. AH

Major ins Jérémy Jacquet (Rennes, £55m), Víctor Muñoz (Osasuna, £34.5m) Major outs Mohamed Salah (released), Ibrahima Konaté (Real Madrid, free), Andy Robertson (Tottenham, free)

View image in fullscreen England midfielder Elliot Anderson has completed his move to Manchester City. Photograph: Nathan Ray Seebeck/Imagn Images/Reuters

Manchester City

Elliot Anderson may already have joined for a British record transfer fee but City are still in the market for another midfielder, with the 18-year-old Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi being targeted for about £85m. Enzo Maresca also has Malo Gusto, one of his right-backs when he was Chelsea head coach, on the radar. A striker will be on the list, too, if Omar Marmoush leaves. And with Real Madrid retaining an interest, will Rodri sign on again? Spain’s World Cup-winning captain has a year left on his contract and his stock has rocketed. The incomings mean several players could leave, with Kalvin Phillips, Jack Grealish, Tijjani Reijnders, Nico González, Savinho and James Trafford among them. Jamie Jackson

Major ins Elliot Anderson (Nottingham Forest, £116m), Mathys Detourbet (Troyes, £21.6m), Jeremy Monga (Leicester, £12.5m) Major outs Nathan Aké (Fenerbahce, £7m), Bernardo Silva (Real Madrid, free), John Stones (free agent)

Manchester United

Michael Carrick is keen to add a third new midfielder after the arrivals of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, with Real Madrid’s Eduardo Camavinga, Bournemouth’s Alex Scott, Roma’s Manu Koné and Fulham’s Sander Berge on the list. He is also considering a move for a left-back: Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and Fulham’s Antonee Robinson are being monitored. There will be outgoings too. At 28 Marcus Rashford is in his prime and available, surely for a fee in the same region as the £26m Barcelona balked at. Player and club want an exit yet at the moment he will start the new season at United. For the right deal this will change. JJ

Major ins Andrey Santos (Chelsea, £50m), Youri Tielemans (Aston Villa, £35m) Major outs Rasmus Højlund (Napoli, £43.2m)

Newcastle

Much hinges on whether Bruno Guimarães stays or departs for Arsenal during a summer already featuring a significant changing of the St James’ Park guard. The adjustment to life after Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali could be eased if Eddie Howe is able to attract a higher calibre central midfielder – Monaco’s Aladji Bamba has joined for £34m – and goalkeeper – Parma’s Zion Suzuki is one possibility. Most signings will be expected to conform to Newcastle’s new transfer policy of recruiting players aged 24 and under, with a valuation broadly between £20m and £40m. Meanwhile Nick Pope, Joe Willock and Jacob Murphy could depart. The club are operating under a three-year Uefa settlement agreement after breaching European spending rules but Howe’s overriding current priority is keeping Guimarães. LT

Major ins Bazoumana Touré (Hoffenheim, £43m), Ewen Jaouen (Reims, £21.6m), Sean Steur (Ajax, £20m), Aladji Bamba (Monaco, £34m) Major outs Sandro Tonali (Tottenham, £92.5m), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona, £69.3m), Kieran Trippier (Wolves, free)

Nottingham Forest

Spending the money made from the Elliot Anderson sale is a top priority. Lucas Bergvall leads the list of replacements and the midfielder has told Tottenham his preference is to move to the City Ground but a deal needs to be agreed. If not, Monaco’s Lamine Camara could become part of the thinking. A new right-wingback and striker are also being plotted, with Sporting’s Ousmane Diomande a target in central defence. There is no requirement to sell any key players but the futures of some on the fringes are up in the air. WU

Major outs Elliot Anderson (Manchester City, £116m)

Sunderland

Régis Le Bris says he is hoping to add “six or seven” new players this summer. Sunderland’s manager wants to ensure the squad is sufficiently robust to cope with the twin demands of Premier League and Europa League campaigns but has been bolstered by Granit Xhaka’s decision to recommit to the club amid interest in the captain from Chelsea. If recruiting holding midfield cover for Xhaka is one transfer priority, so too is providing Brian Brobbey with high-calibre attacking competition while also fortifying the right-winger and left-back positions. Le Bris is under no pressure to sell, so any attempts to acquire his increasingly influential attacking midfielder Enzo Le Fée will be strongly resisted. LT

Major ins Thomas Meunier (Lille, free) Major outs Eliezer Mayenda (Rennes, £17.1m)

Tottenham

Despite acquiring a new central midfield and a new central defence, Roberto De Zerbi said Spurs are “not finished yet” in the transfer market. An upgrade on Richarlison up front should be a priority, while Marcus Rashford could be a blockbuster arrival out wide. As for outgoings, Cristian Romero and Lucas Bergvall could follow Luka Vuskovic and Will Lankshear through the door. Interest in Pedro Porro will be high after his outstanding World Cup and there is still uncertainty over Guglielmo Vicario’s future in goal. BM

Major ins Sandro Tonali (Newcastle, £92.5m), Mateus Fernandes (West Ham, £85m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Brighton, £52m), Andy Robertson (Liverpool, free), Marcos Senesi (Bournemouth, free), Martin Dubravka (Burnley, free) Major outs Luka Vuskovic (Brighton, £46m), Radu Dragusin (Fiorentina, loan)

Sports.title: Missing a major football tournament? Fear not, Wafcon 2026 is about to start
Sports.content:
The men’s World Cup may have finished but do not worry, the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) is ready to pick up where Spain and Argentina left off. The 34-match event will take place between 26 July and 16 August, which sandwiches it between football’s global showpiece and the start of the league season in Europe. Here’s your guide to one of the most underrated but interesting events on the sporting calendar.

Why is it being played now?

The tournament was scheduled to take place in three Moroccan cities – Rabat, Casablanca and Fes – between 17 March and 3 April. However, only 12 days before it was due to start it was postponed for what the Confederation of African Football called “unforeseen circumstances”. Strangely, the conflict in the Middle East, which affected several travel routes, was never cited as one of them. Caf’s communications director, Luxolo September, said Morocco requested new dates “for a number of reasons”, none of which were disclosed.

South Africa appeared to offer to host the tournament, before Morocco was reconfirmed and a new window was announced. A revised match list, which included only two of the three original host cities, Rabat and Casablanca, was revealed on 25 June. The draw remained the same.

Several teams, including South Africa and Nigeria, expressed frustration at the late change, especially as they had already been playing warm-up matches in preparation for the tournament. Also, the change meant that, for many players, they will be out of season.

What is the setup?

This is the first time the tournament will be played with 16 teams – up from 12 in the past two editions – but the inclusion of the final four sides was unsatisfactory. They were added to the tournament only after the qualification process, which ran from February to October 2025, had been completed. The four sides – Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Mali and Egypt – were picked on rankings.

While the Egypt midfielder Nadine Ghazi admitted that the team’s qualification was “different, if I can put it like that”, they hope to take inspiration from their men’s side, who reached the World Cup last 16 before losing to Argentina.

Another team that will be looking to their male counterparts’ performances for motivation is Cape Verde, who are one of two tournament debutants. Malawi are the other first-timers.

The teams are divided into four groups of four. The top two sides from each group will progress to the quarter-finals. All matches kick off at 6pm or later local time, unlike the 2025 edition, when some teams played at 3pm in extreme mid-summer heat.

Who are the favourites?

The competition’s most successful competitors, Nigeria, achieved “Mission X” and won their 10th Wafcon title in 2025, and it is difficult to look past them this time. They have retained the core of that squad, captained by Rasheedat Ajibade, but will be without the defender Ashleigh Plumptre because of a foot injury. The striker Asisat Oshoala and the goalkeeper Chiamaka Nnadozie headline their squad.

View image in fullscreen Nigeria, who defeated Morocco in last year’s final, are aiming for a record-extending 11th Wafcon title. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images

Morocco have been the runners-up in the past two editions and will be looking to go one better, especially as this could be the last in their trio of home tournaments. The 2028 Wafcon is set to be held elsewhere.

Other strong candidates are the 2022 champions, South Africa, who have an experienced squad, and Zambia, who were bronze medallists in 2022 and quarter-finalists in 2025.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Who are the biggest stars?

Malawi will make their first Wafcon appearance, with many eyes on sisters Tabitha and Temwa Chawinga. Tabitha, who will captain the side, plays at European powerhouse OL Lyonnes, while Temwa is at Kansas City Current, where she has been voted the NWSL’s MVP for two successive seasons. She was also the highest-ranked African player on the Guardian’s 100 best female footballers in the world last year in sixth place.

Local fans will get behind the Morocco captain, Ghizlane Chebbak, who has won the Golden Boot at the past two Wafcons, scoring eight times across those tournaments. At 35 years old, this may be her last major tournament and she will not want to move on without a trophy.

View image in fullscreen Malawi’s Tabitha Chawinga (left) and her sister Temwa will be making their Wafcon debuts.

Zambia’s NWSL heavyweights Barbra Banda and Racheal Kundananji scored three goals each at the last tournament but could not take the team past the quarter-finals. Given their reputations the pair will be hoping to ensure Zambia can continue to enhance their reputation as serious continental challengers.

Ghana were the most improved side last year, when they lost to Morocco on penalties in the semi-final. Their forward Princess Marfo, who recently signed for PSV Eindhoven, and Evelyn Badu, fresh off a hat-trick for Montreal Roses, are two to keep an eye on.

What’s at stake?

In short: money and major tournament qualification. Prize money at the last Wafcon increased by 45% in total, with each team earning at least $125,000 (£94,000) and the winners, Nigeria, pocketing $1m. This time there is something else at stake too: the four semi-finalists will qualify for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil, while the four losing quarter-finalists will play off to decide which two teams advance to the inter-confederation deciders.

Sports.title: 'F*** you and them': Jermaine Jenas hits back at his critics in bizarre pancake video after former BBC star's car-crash Good Morning Britain interview
Sports.content:
'F*** you and them': Jermaine Jenas hits back at his critics in bizarre pancake video after former BBC star's car-crash Good Morning Britain interview

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jermaine Jenas has unequivocally hit back at his critics in bizarre fashion after uploading a topless video of himself dancing in his kitchen.

Former England and Spurs star Jenas, 43, was one of the BBC's rising stars before he was axed from his role on Match of the Day in August 2024 following the discovery of inappropriate messages sent to two women.

Jenas had served as a regular presenter on The One Show and 5Live before his wife, Ellie Penfold, confirmed she had split from the former footballer in the wake of the scandal - having been together for 16 years.

He is now in a relationship with Parisien estate agent Anne Leplaideur, 31, with the pair spotted holidaying together this summer.

He spoke at length about how he had 'lost everything' during his 'tough two-year period' in a car-crash appearance on ITV's Good Morning Britain last month, in which he was grilled by presenters Kate Garraway and Ranvir Singh.

Jenas took issue with Singh's 'line of questioning' and later claimed the presenters had 'a thirst for blood', with the former footballer accused of 'skirting around the issue' of his behaviour and responding to questions in a defensive manner.

Jermaine Jenas has hit back at his critics in a defiant Instagram message on Saturday

But taking to Instagram on Saturday, Jenas posted a defiant message while dancing and spinning a plate of white chocolate pancakes.

'I no longer care how the story gets told,' the caption read. 'F*** you and them… Respectfully.'

Rio Ferdinand responded to the post by saying: 'Okaaaaay… these tunes don't fit the caption ffs.'

The ITV interview saw Garraway ask Jenas what he had 'learned'. Jenas replied: 'To say I was happy in the industry I was in is an overstatement. When it comes to what I've learnt, it's a very specific thing to put my finger on.

'It's probably a little bit of an unfair question to find that one thing. You go through life, you make mistakes and there were things happening on the outside of work also affecting my behaviour.'

Singh then accused him of 'skirting around what you've learnt', but Jenas responded: 'I'm not skirting around anything, Ranvir.

'I'm more than happy to have the conversation, which is why I'm here. I'm not here to be defending myself in any way, shape or form.

The 43-year-old ex-footballer was grilled during a car-crash interview on GMB last month

He was accused of 'skirting around the issue' of his BBC sacking in August 2024

'I know what I did was wrong and I accept those punishments. Nobody is skirting around the responsibility of what I did. I know what I did and I know what I did was wrong. So I don't understand where that line of questioning is coming from.'

Singh then asked him for his 'advice to other men who are in positions of power in any industry and who think they are just flirting with women at work who… what is your advice to other people then who might be learning from your mistakes?'

Jenas replied: 'I think they can look at what happened to me and make their own assumptions about what they have to do with their own lives.

'I'm not here to preach to other people about what they should do with their lives. I'm here to explain to people my own experiences of what I've been through and what I've done and the impact that it's had on everybody in my life.

'I'm not here to dictate to people in terms of what they want to do. I understand why you have to come at me with this line of questioning and it's completely fine and if you feel like I have not been punished enough then go ahead and keep going.'

Singh said she was 'not saying that', adding that Jenas had spoken about 'what's been taken away from me' – but 'people might say you put yourself in that position, you risked it all by doing what you did'.

Jenas replied: 'Oh, 100 per cent. I did put myself in that position and I'm not sat here begging and pleading for my job back.

'I'm fully accepting of what has been taken away from me. I put myself in that position and that's where the learning comes from – and that's where I have to now look forward to what is coming next. That's where the post comes from.

Jenas, 43, split from wife Ellie Penfold after inappropriate messages sent to two women were discovered

'It's impossible to not learn about yourself when you are put into the position that I was put into, that I put myself into. You have to take stock, look around yourself, look at your own behaviour and realise that things have to change.

'I've done that over a period of time where it's been very tricky – granted I put myself in that position.'

Jenas deflected throughout his ten-minute interview, pleading for forgiveness because everyone 'makes mistakes'.

The 43-year-old learnt of his sacking from the BBC while live on radio.

He added: 'The learning from it doesn't always have to be negative. We are so obsessed in this industry with "oh, he's been cancelled" – everything has to be negative.

'Hang on a minute, I'm a person who has learnt a lot from my mistakes and spent ten to 12 years in this industry and had a brilliant career and really enjoyed my time on television. There's a lot for me to give back.

'I'm not saying on television, it could be on any different platform where I know a lot of people feel how I feel.

'I'm a human being. We make mistakes. You two [Singh and Garraway] can't sit in front of me and say you've never made a mistake in your life. We all make mistakes, we live in the public eye.

'Every mistake I made was made public and I had to handle that as a man. That's exactly what I did. The thing now is about moving forward and what I'm about to do next. Currently, I'm not sure.'

Sports.title: World Cup hero Vozinha, 40 - who gained 29MILLION followers after denying Lionel Messi - set to join iconic South American club despite links to David Beckham's Inter Miami
Sports.content:
World Cup cult hero Vozinha is set to complete a move to famous Chilean side Colo Colo despite links to David Beckham's Inter Miami.

The 40-year-old was one of the heroes of Cape Verde's surprise run to the last-32 stage before they were beaten 3-2 by Argentina after extra-time.

As well as keeping a clean sheet against Spain and Saudi Arabia, Vozinha made 18 saves across the tournament and outperformed his xG against by 0.9.

His standout performances were among the highlights of Cape Verde's debut appearance at the World Cup.

At the start of the Spain match in Cape Verde's World Cup opener, he only had 50,000 followers on Instagram, but after making a memorable seven saves, that number dramatically increased, with Vozinha now having 28.6million followers.

FIFA announced last week that Vozinha had been named in the World Cup's team of the tournament.

Vozinha is expected to join Chilean side Colo Colo despite links to David Beckham's Inter Miami

The keeper was one of the stars of Cape Verde's run to the last-32 stage of the World Cup

Vozinha had been without a club heading into the tournament after leaving Portuguese second division team Chaves at the end of last season.

His availability led to speculation over a possible move to join Messi at Inter Miami, with Vozinha asked about the possibility in a television appearance after the tournament.

'I love football to still be here at 40 years old is because I truly have this passion,' Vozinha said.

'I want to play for at least another one or two years, depending on how my body feels and reacts.

'We never know what tomorrow brings, but I want to keep playing.

'I just hope I can find a club that truly wants me as a footballer, not for marketing purposes.'

Vozinha is now expected to complete a move to Chile's most successful club Colo Colo, who have won a record 34 league titles.

Anibal Mosa, president of Blanco y Negro, the company that manages the Chilean club revealed Vozinha is due to fly to Santiago in the coming days to complete the move.

'Vozinha is going to be a Colo Colo player,' Mosa said.

'In the next few days, he will travel to Chile, undergo the necessary medical examinations, and then be presented here at the Estadio Monumental.'

Colo Colo are currently 12 points clear at the top of Chile's Liga de Primera.

Vozinha has had a nomadic career, playing for clubs in his homeland, Moldova, Slovakia, Cyprus and Portugal's second tier and he has won 94 caps for Cape Verde.

Sports.title: Simon Jordan airs Anthony Joshua conspiracy theory after boxer knocked out rival despite hitting the canvas TWICE to set up money-spinning Tyson Fury fight: 'Something not quite right'
Sports.content:
Simon Jordan airs Anthony Joshua conspiracy theory after boxer knocked out rival despite hitting the canvas TWICE to set up money-spinning Tyson Fury fight: 'Something not quite right'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Simon Jordan has questioned the nature of Anthony Joshua's victory over Kristian Prenga as he recovered from two knockdowns to set up a lucrative showdown with Tyson Fury.

Joshua, who had been returning to the ring after seven months of inactivity, appeared on the brink of defeat in the opening round against Prenga.

The Albanian heavyweight knocked Joshua down just 20 seconds into the contest with an uppercut.

Joshua then survived another knockdown later in the round, with fans fearing the long-awaited showdown with Fury was at risk.

The second round proved dramatically different as Joshua unleashed a series of heavy blows to force Prenga towards the ropes, before delivering a knockout blow.

Joshua's stunning turnaround, coupled with Fury's victory over Mariusz Wach just 24 hours earlier, cleared the path for the two British heavyweights to finally meet in one of the most lucrative fights in boxing.

Anthony Joshua survived two knock downs in the first round against Kristian Prenga

Joshua responded in the second by delivering a second round knockout of the Albanian

Simon Jordan questioned the nature of Joshua's victory given the difference between the two rounds

talkSPORT presenter Simon Jordan controversially questioned the dramatic difference in the rounds between Joshua and Prenga.

Jordan declared 'something not quite right' as he appeared to reference the sums on offer for Joshua's fight with Fury.

'Not having that… #anthonyjoshua fight,' Jordan posted.

'Dropped twice and sets the tempo, how's that ? … Prenga totally different in 2nd

'Something not quite right, all designed to rinse maximum amount of money…'

Punch stats for the fight revealed the stunning difference between the two rounds, with Joshua landing just five of his 22 attempted punches in the first, while Prenga connected with 15 of his 32.

The second round swung with Joshua landing with 13 of his 46 punches, as Prenga dramatically dropped off by landing three of 17 attempted.

Despite Jordan's comments on social media, Joshua insisted that 'champions rise' in a post-fight interview after coming through the test.

Prenga had stunned Joshua in the opening round and landed 13 of his 32 attempted punches

He landed just three of 17 punches in the second round as Joshua became the aggressor

Prenga was sent to the canvas by a brutal blow from Joshua, who later declared 'champions rise' when asked about the dramatic turnaround

'He [Prenga] gave me a good test but this is what champions do, we rise,' Joshua said.

'We get knocked down and stand up. That is life, that is life's motto.

'I want to give a massive thank you to Prenga and his team for putting up a good fight. It means a lot to them and it means a lot to me and that is why you see what you see in the ring.

'I want to give thanks to God. It was more than me in that situation, it can't just be me in them type of situations. There is a higher power that is calling.

'He's a strong guy and I think Eddie [Hearn] wants to sign him now! He is going to do well and he has a bright future.

'Maybe with a bit more experience, he [Prenga] will be up there with the rest of us. He is strong and durable.'

Looking ahead to the showdown with Fury, with contracts having already been signed, Joshua said in the ring: 'Have we got Tyson Fury in the room? Is he here or not?

'I am the meanest, most vicious champion. Nobody can stop me. He is no Oleksandr [Usyk].

'All jokes aside, there are two sides. One is the fighter and the other is respect. I respect everything he has done and everything that he has achieved, but as a fighting person, we're here now.

'I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat.'

Joshua had paid tribute to his two close friends, who were killed in a car crash in December.

Joshua will finally face Tyson Fury in a money-spinning contest with his rival having beaten Mariussz Wach a day earlier

Joshua paid tribute to his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, who died in a car crash in December

Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele died while the car they were travelling in struck a truck on a road near Lagos in December. The pair were on holiday with Joshua after he beat Jake Paul in Miami.

The heavyweight boxer, who was also in the vehicle, was taken to hospital before being discharged and flying home to the UK - where he attended the funerals of his strength and conditioning coach Ghami and Ayodele, one of his trainers.

Fighting in honour of Ghami and Ayodele, Joshua paid tribute to his friends by having their names printed on his military camouflage trunks.

He also walked to the ring wearing a military-style jacket to match his camo shorts. The jacket featured a medal bar displaying the IBF, IBO, WBA, and WBO titles - which he previously held - alongside pennants bearing Ghami and Ayodele's names.

Meanwhile, ‘Latz x Sina, My Brother's Keeper, MBK’ was printed on the canvas in his corner.

Asked about how he has been coping after beating Prenga, Joshua said: 'It's been tough,' before becoming emotional. 'That's my brothers. I don't want to talk about that.'

Speaking on DAZN, Matchroom Boxing chief Eddie Hearn admitted he feared the heavyweight had returned to the ring too soon after witnessing his struggles in the opening round.

'Nobody can imagine what he's been through in that last seven months. In that first round, I thought we'd come back too soon,' Hearn said.

'Boxing got him through. To even be in the ring tonight is astonishing. You don't know what he's been through. He had to go to the depths one more time to get up, like he has done the last seven months.'

In February, Joshua memorialised Ghami and Ayodele by having their names tattooed on his arm.

Sports.title: 'Hurt' Adam Ramsay-Peaty breaks down in tears after surprise Commonwealth Games bronze: Star reveals family feud has taken its toll and admits he 'doesn't know what went wrong'
Sports.content:
'Hurt' Adam Ramsay-Peaty breaks down in tears after surprise Commonwealth Games bronze: Star reveals family feud has taken its toll and admits he 'doesn't know what went wrong'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

First came an apology. 'Sorry guys,' said Adam Ramsay-Peaty, as his voice began to tremble. He wiped away a tear from his face and stared at the Tollcross floor to find his words.

The bronze medal around his neck felt like a heavy weight. 'It's hard because I know how hard I've worked. I know the s**t I've been through, which is no fault of my own. It does take a toll.'

After standing upon the podium, the 31-year-old walked around the pool and stopped for selfies with his adoring fans. An Englishman has not received a reception like this in Glasgow for a long time.

He stopped to hug his pregnant wife, Holly – the daughter of celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay – before kissing her pregnant stomach. They are expecting a daughter in December and, as the swimmer confessed, family life has changed his priorities.

'She's always super proud of me,' he said. 'As a father, it doesn't matter if you come home with the gold, as long as you come home with the teddy, which I did. That's what matters.

'As you can tell, the emotion is always something that I'm going to carry. I'm never going to be afraid to show weakness because it's so important for making stronger people, making stronger men, stronger fathers, stronger husbands.

'I think 'S**t, how have I worked so hard at this age?' - then you get a result like that. I'm better than that. Maybe it's because I've had two years out, but it does hurt. There's a lot going on in my head right now.'

Adam Ramsay-Peaty was brought to tears as he reflected 'I'm never going to be afraid to show weakness' after securing bronze at the Commonwealth games

Adam Ramsay-Peaty stopped to hug his pregnant wife, Holly - the daughter of celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay - before kissing her pregnant stomach

The pair wed on December 27 last year at Bath Abbey

Ramsay-Peaty was chasing from the start. He was not the leader of the pack. Perhaps he will fare better over 50 metres but here, over two lengths, he finished almost three seconds off his world record.

Australian Sam Williamson won gold and 18-year-old Filip Nowacki, of Jersey, claimed a brilliant silver that bodes well for the future of British swimming.

'I'm not crying because it's a bronze instead of a gold,' said Peaty, choking up throughout. 'I'm crying because I know that swim could have been better. I don't really know what went wrong in these last two weeks but something isn't hitting right, whether it's pace or focus.

'I feel like I couldn't have put more in, so you ask, 'What's the point of all the 5.30ams. What's the point of all the metres every day? What's the point of feeling exhausted all the time? What's the point of saying, 'No' to all the family events because of training?' It's because you want excellence and that isn't excellence for me.

'I enjoy a scrap but I lost that scrap in the last 25 metres. That's sport. Most of the time I've won the scrap. For some reason, the Commonwealths is that humble reminder.'

The wedding stories, the family feud and the social media abuse have taken their toll. The pool should be his place of escape but he swam with the world on his shoulders.

'People who comment and read headlines have got to look themselves in the mirror. Ignoring that comes at a cost. That hasn't played a part in that result here but it has to stop. Do better. I don't want young Filip to go through that.'

Join the discussion Has obsession with gold medals made us forget the human cost athletes pay for success?

Ramsay-Peaty was overcome with emotion in the mixed zone reflecting on his bronze medal

Throughout his decorated career, Ramsay-Peaty has been so far ahead of the field that he has had to look in the mirror to find competition. He has broken 14 world records, asserting a similar dominance to Sweden's serial pole vault champion Armand Duplantis. Untouchables. Now people will ask if time is finally catching up with Britain's greatest swimmer.

Nowacki is still waiting for his A Level results but the schoolboy from Millfield has already beaten his idol's teenage records. In 2012, Jason Kenny beat Chris Hoy to become the top dog of cycling. Lamine Yamal overcame Lionel Messi in last week's World Cup final. Swimming insiders believe it is a matter of time until Nowacki pulls a similar stunt.

'For me, he's got a very bright future ahead of him,' said Ramsay-Peaty, whose gold earrings caught the light of the cameras. 'He's my favourite for the 200m. He's definitely got the speed and he's about 25kgs less! He's got many many miles ahead of him, whereas my miles are probably coming to an end. I guess two years isn't that long to try and find that in me.'

Side by side, they look like David and Goliath. Nowacki is five inches shorter and does not have the same popping biceps. Ramsay-Peaty changed the game with his powerful upper body stroke but Nowacki's strength is in his kick. He keeps his hips high and moves more gracefully than his senior, who forces his way through the water.

Nowacki will discover his maths, economics and physics exam results during next month's European Championships. Then he plans to enrol at Loughborough University, where he can master his craft in time for the LA 2028 Olympics. Major medals are in his sights, although Ramsay-Peaty is not ready to stand aside just yet.

'To be racing one of the best in the world – arguably the greatest breaststroker of all time – is very special to me,' said Nowacki, who won the world junior championships last year in a time of 2:07.32, which would have medalled in every senior Olympics, bar one

Ramsay-Peaty knows a promising swimmer when he sees one. He has already signed up Nowacki to his own agency and will continue to mentor his prodigy.

'If I compare myself to 2014, 12 years ago, it's very exciting where Filip and his career can go,' he said. 'It's sport, it's beautiful, but f**k me, it can hurt.'
