The issue with the CANDU is that it has online refuelling," explained Ed Lyman, director of nuclear safety for the Union of Concerned Scientists in Washington, D.C. "You're refuelling continuously, which makes it harder for the IAEA [International Atomic Energy Agency]."

Canada, which produces all of its own uranium, would be in a strong position to divert fissionable material undetected if so inclined, say the experts.

The plutonium produced in a heavy water reactor is also much easier to turn into a nuclear weapon, said Fetter.

"Of the countries that have made nuclear weapons with plutonium, many of them have used a heavy water reactor," he said.

That’s why India used a Canadian heavy water reactor to produce its first nuclear weapon in 1974, an all-plutonium implosion-type bomb. The "Smiling Buddha" test was the first to break the nuclear monopoly of the "Big Five" UN Security Council powers.

Fetter said the U.S. had heavy water reactors only for the purpose of producing plutonium and tritium. (Tritium, also produced in abundance by the CANDU reactor, is another critical component of a modern two-stage thermonuclear weapon that Canada has in abundance.)

Using riskier fuels

Canada is also branching out into a new kind of technology that will require enriched uranium: the small modular reactor (SMR). Some of the proposed SMRs would use uranium enriched to a level as high as 20 per cent, known as high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU).

HALEU is already a proliferation concern in itself, said Lyman.

"Anything below 20 per cent is considered low-enriched uranium and has a much lower level of oversight. The IAEA considers it indirect-use material you can't directly use in a bomb,” he explained. "But there's evidence, both historical and technical, that that's not true, and that the actual cutoff for weapon-usable uranium is below 20 per cent. Could be 15 per cent, could be 10 per cent.

"And so I worry about this push for advanced reactors, SMRs that use HALEU up near 20 per cent, like the ARC 100 in Canada, that the material itself is in the dangerous band. And if Canada were to pursue a whole fleet of SMRs using HALEU, and especially if they were to build their own enrichment plants to support that, that might give them a threshold capability for bombs, even if they never make highly enriched [over 20 per cent] uranium."

ARC Canada points out that its proposed reactor in New Brunswick, which would become the only commercial fast-breeder reactor in the world outside Russia, mitigates against proliferation risks by having a long fuel cycle with a core that stays sealed for 20 years.

But there’s another factor: The arrival of SMRs that consume enriched uranium has got the government of Canada thinking about enrichment.

Employees walk down a tunnel at Cameco's Cigar Lake uranium mine in Cigar Lake, Sask., on June 15. Despite being the world’s second-biggest producer of uranium, Canada has never enriched domestically. (Liam Richards/The Canadian Press)

To enrich or not to enrich

"Any country which has a complete fuel cycle is a latent nuclear weapons country, in the sense that it is not far from making a nuclear weapon," said former IAEA director and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Mohamed ElBaradei.

Scientists consulted by CBC News said Canada would probably have little economic motive to build its own enrichment facilities. Canada’s nuclear energy strategy foresees importation of enriched uranium from France and the U.S. in the immediate future, even though that often means buying back Canadian-mined uranium after other countries have added value.

The longer-term question of whether Canada should develop domestic enrichment capability remains under assessment. - Canada's nuclear energy strategy

But the strategy also notes that "geopolitical volatility has exposed fragility in nuclear fuel supply chains at every stage — mining, milling, refining, conversion, enrichment, and fabrication."

Canada plans to double its exports of uranium in raw form, "but there is also a compelling case for expanding downstream capabilities selectively."

Domestic enrichment might not save Canada money, but would increase its strategic autonomy.

"Canada will continue to monitor the energy security implications of these supply chains," says the strategy. "The longer-term question of whether Canada should develop domestic enrichment capability remains under assessment."

Enrichment could get easier

A handful of non-nuclear arms powers have developed enrichment facilities. They include Brazil, Japan, Argentina, Germany and the Netherlands, but only Brazil combines a modern centrifuge facility with a large domestic supply of uranium.

Japan could theoretically produce weapons-grade uranium, but its nuclear technology, like South Korea’s, is largely American, its nuclear program is subject to strict inspections, and it has no uranium mines of its own — in fact it buys much of its supply from Canada.

A Canadian company, Cameco, is currently exploring the next frontier of uranium enrichment. The SILEX method uses laser excitation to separate U-235 more quickly and efficiently than spinning it in a centrifuge.

Already, a centrifuge facility can fit in an area the size of a high school gym. SILEX, said Fetter, "potentially could be even smaller and use less energy than centrifuge enrichment, which would make it harder to detect a clandestine facility."

The SILEX project has already received U.S. government funding and acquired land in western Kentucky for a plant expected to be operating by 2030.

Crossing the threshold

For all the Carney government’s talk of "a more dangerous and divided world," there is still no public signal that Canada might abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear arms.

If the strategic situation were to change, Canada would have to decide whether to go the open route and formally depart the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), or pursue nuclear arms through a clandestine program as other countries have done with a mixed record of success.

Plasma physicist Tara Drozdenko worked on nuclear weapons issues under the administrations of Barack Obama and George W. Bush. She represented the United States on NATO's Senior Group on Proliferation, and headed the Country/Regime Sanctions Unit at the U.S. Department of Treasury, where she managed the government's nuclear-related sanctions on countries such as Iran and North Korea.

Today, she’s not sure Washington remains committed to preventing proliferation, or how it would react to a Canadian decision to leave the NPT.

"In a normal administration, there would be condemnation, there would be reproach, there would be a lot of diplomatic efforts," she told CBC News. "I don't know what would happen in this administration. Would there be threats? Would there be some people that are like, yeah, everybody should have nuclear weapons? I really can't predict what this particular administration would do."

A TV screen shows a report of North Korea's multiple rocket launchers during a news program at the Seoul Railway Station in Seoul, South Korea, on April 23, 2024. (Lee Jin-man/The Associated Press)

Clandestine plants and secret programs

So far, all the countries that have developed nuclear weapons — Israel, South Africa, India, Pakistan and North Korea — began their efforts in secret.

Drozdenko says Canada’s own nuclear industry, the design of its reactors and the fact that it has the world’s best uranium deposits would all give it a strong hand were it ever to pursue such a risky course.

"Canada is probably really well-positioned to do that, if Canada was determined," said Drozdenko. "You have a lot of land that's not heavily populated, and if you used technologies that didn't have a lot of energy or thermal signature, I don't think the U.S. has its intelligence assets pointed at Canada right now."

At some point, such a program would inevitably become known.

"It would require withdrawal from the non-proliferation treaty, which would be really impactful to the treaty worldwide, especially as a NATO country and up until now a pretty close ally of the U.S. I think that would be pretty catastrophic to that treaty,” Drozdenko said.

Fetter said Canada could probably easily assemble a simple “gun-type” nuclear weapon like the one used on Hiroshima, but would face scientific hurdles if it tried to build a modern thermonuclear weapon without conducting tests. North Korea required half a dozen tests to get there.

In the U.S., Russia and China, supercomputers today have replaced actual testing. Canada has the computing capacity but lacks the detailed data that nuclear arms powers have assembled on materials science, and the complicated timing and interactions inside a nuclear warhead — some of the most closely guarded secrets in the world.

But Fetter also said he didn’t expect North Korea to be able to put a modern, two-stage thermonuclear warhead on a ballistic missile and make it work.

"Canada has a lot of smart people," he noted.

With Canada embarked on a new era of greater military spending, including the purchase of modern submarines and its first foray into the world of cruise missiles, it is clearly assembling elements that could bring it closer to "breakout" as a nuclear arms power, if it desired.

The question of how other countries would react is the unknowable factor, said Drozdenko.

"Does Canada want to be in the position of North Korea, the pariah state that's making clandestine nuclear weapons?" she asked.

So far, the answer has always been no.

World.title: Snail-mail clubs deliver on the desire for physical letters
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | The delight in receiving physical letters : Day 6 6:58 Snail mail subscription clubs are a growing trend as people delight in receiving physical letters

If your mail contains nothing but utility bills, takeout flyers and an endless stream of marketing material from local realtors, there's a subscription for that.

Creative entrepreneurs are finding their way into people's hearts — and mailboxes — by offering snail-mail subscriptions. For a modest fee, subscribers receive monthly or quarterly letters along with some combination of art, photography, stickers, pressed flowers or other mementos.

Data provided to CBC by Pinterest showed that Canadian searches for "snail mail" were up 169 per cent on July 23 compared to a year earlier. That’s in keeping with the platform’s annual trend-forecasting report, which said to "expect a letter writing renaissance in 2026, as Gen Z and Millennials turn snail mail into performance art."

Indeed, there are hundreds of snail-mail clubs around the world with a wide variety of aesthetic styles and subject matter.

And it's good business for some. Kiki Klassen, who runs Toronto-based Lucky Duck Mail Club, CBC in an email her side hustle now earns more than her day job as a social media manager.

Creators, subscribers and academic experts alike say snail-mail clubs are tapping into a desire to seek healthier relationships with technology and more personal, tangible — and tactile — ways of communicating.

Shawn Jones, right, said he's been overwhelmed by the positive response to his wildlife-themed snail-mail club, Tales of Oak. (Submitted by Shawn Jones)

An offline experience

"I think the number one thing I hear about it is they like how it's sort of an analog activity," said Shawn Jones, who started his wildlife-themed snail mail club, Tales of Oak, in August 2025.

"People are kind of getting more and more horrified by their screen time, myself included," said Jones, who lives in a cabin in the woods in the Outaouais region of Quebec, near Shawville.

"We're all just trying to look for ways to do things offline, like putting the phone down to write a letter instead of an email and picking up a camera instead of a smartphone."

Richard Lachman, a professor of digital media at Toronto Metropolitan University, says he sees a lot of desire among Gen Z for offline experiences like the kind a snail-mail subscription provides.

Richard Lachman, a digital media prof at Toronto Metropolitan University, likens the popularity of snail-mail subscriptions to some other movements that embrace off-line experiences, like knitting, reading, painting or scrapbooking groups. (Submitted by Richard Lachman)

"They are realizing that doomscrolling for four hours in bed makes them feel badly," said Lachman, who is also the author of Digital Wisdom: Searching for Agency in the Age of AI.

He likens it to some other movements to embrace tangible and in-person experiences, such as taking up watercolour painting or scrapbooking, or attending meetups where people knit or read quietly together.

Lachman says it's also interesting to note how the entrepreneurs behind snail-mail clubs use Instagram and TikTok to get the word out, then move the communication off those platforms.

"It's a little bit of a return to the old internet, in a way," said Lachman, contrasting with the way many influencers rely on business models tied to the whims of a social platform's algorithm.

"These mailouts are a way of reaching people through the internet, but then moving the actual business to something you have control over."

Toronto photographer Angela Lewis says her snail-mail club, Bloom Strolling, came about when she posted on Instagram asking if others were craving the nostalgic feeling of getting real mail. (Submitted by Angela Lewis)

The nostalgia element

Toronto photographer Angela Lewis says her snail-mail club, Bloom Strolling, came about after she posted on Instagram about how exchanging letters with her grandmother as a child shaped her.

"I always loved that feeling of checking the mailbox to see if she'd written me," Lewis told Day 6. "It was like getting a gift from my best friend."

Her Instagram post asked if other people were craving that nostalgic feeling of snail mail. She was soon overwhelmed by the affirmative response.

Though Lewis says she does get people in their 60s and 70s who are nostalgic for real mail, many of her subscribers are people in their 20s who use the materials they get from mail clubs for " junk journaling " — a more whimsical and less formal take on '90s-era scrapbooking.

Lewis says her snail-mail club, Bloom Strolling, came about after she posted on Instagram about how exchanging letters with her grandmother as a child shaped her. (Submitted by Angela Lewis)

Clay Routledge, a psychologist who studies nostalgia as part of his work at the Washington, D.C.-based think-tank Archbridge Institute, says the interest in snail mail — even among people born long after it was replaced by email — fits with his research findings.

The results of a national survey the institute conducted in May 2025 indicated that historical nostalgia was widespread.

Routledge, who is also the author of Past Forward: How Nostalgia Can Help You Live a More Meaningful Life, says the vast majority of participants reported they were "nostalgic for a time before they were alive."

Additionally, his research found that this kind of nostalgia helps people manage the stress of current challenges and anxiety about the future.

Clay Routledge, psychologist and other of Past Forward: How Nostalgia Can Help You Live a More Meaningful Life, says research shows people can be nostalgic for times before they were born. (Submitted by Clay Routledge)

"So a young person might be like, 'Oh cool, people used to get stuff in the mail. Handwritten cards have neat stationery.' And they might start doing that, not because it's in their own personal past, but they were inspired through more cultural nostalgia."

In Edmonton, Steve Stred subscribed to Tales of Oak for his nature-loving nine-year-old son, Auryn.

"It's neat to see him open it up and then to actually see what the art cards are," said Stred. "It's just that joy of the unknown."

"He's made a little shelf in his room where he keeps all the prints and he displays them."

Finding connection

Beyond the nostalgia aspect, snail-mail clubs can also provide a sense of community.

For artist Michelle Clark, launching her snail-mail club Love Yours in January was a natural extension of both Love YoursCA, her Etsy shop for her art, and the blog she started years ago to share her struggles with mental illness.

Michelle Clark, left, says starting her snail-mail club, Love Yours, was a natural extension of both her art and the blog she started years ago to share her struggles with mental illness. (Submitted by Michelle Clark)

Clark, who is based in Chilliwack, B.C., says her mail-club letters often address "how I used to be in such a dark place where I felt like I would be stuck there and I wouldn't be able to do anything productive or do something that I could commit to."

By writing about how she continued to develop her creative pursuits while dealing with her mental illness, Clark says she tries to convey to her mail-club members that they too can do positive things with their lives, even if they're still struggling.

And sometimes, they write back.

"One of the letters I got was definitely someone opening up about their mental health struggles, and it was really nice because I don't think she had the chance to do that prior to that."

Jennifer Horner, another Tales of Oak subscriber, says that connection is part of the appeal for her, too.

It's almost like it's coming from a friend. - Jennifer Horner, snail-mail club subscriber

Horner, who is 55, often finds herself scrolling TikTok — which is where she first learned about Tales of Oak. Being part of the club "brought back that nostalgia of receiving an old-fashioned letter in the mail," she said. "It's almost like it's coming from a friend."

For Jones, who created Tales of Oak, it's been surprising to see his subscribers connect with each other in the comments of social media posts he makes to promote the club.

He says it’s especially cool to see given the long history of snail mail as the main way people stayed in touch.

"The act of writing a letter or painting a picture, packaging in an envelope, placing a stamp on it and then putting that faith into the postal system that it will arrive, it's something that technology cannot and has not been able to replace yet," Jones said.

"And hopefully it doesn't."

World.title: Scientists just found sugar in space. Here's why that matters
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's a sweet discovery that has the science world talking — and may help us better understand the origins of life on Earth.

Earlier this month, a group of researchers in Spain uncovered sugar near the centre of the Milky Way, about 26,000 light-years from our planet.

Using two radio telescopes, the team at Spain's Centre for Astrobiology said they uncovered a four-carbon sugar in a molecular cloud. Known as erythrulose, that sugar is most commonly found on Earth in raspberries. It is also used in self-tanning products.

Their discovery marks the first time a sugar has been found in what's known as the interstellar medium — a collection of gas and dust that exists between stars.

According to experts, that's significant because sugars were a critical component for jump-starting life on Earth, and how exactly sugar molecules first formed on our planet has been a long-standing question among scientists.

"The reason it's so exciting is that these are some of the basic building blocks that you need in order to make nucleic acids, which are essential for life as we know it on Earth," said Sarah Gallagher, director of the Institute for Earth and Space Exploration at Western University.

The researchers found a four-carbon sugar in a molecular cloud in what's known as the interstellar medium. (Jon Gambrell/The Associated Press)

The discovery

Types of five-carbon sugars form the backbone of both DNA and RNA, making it a key ingredient in the formation of living organisms.

Based on previous research, including last year's discovery of ribose and glucose sugars in samples taken from an asteroid called Bennu, scientists believe sugar was likely transported to Earth via comets and asteroids that struck the nascent planet.

But where the sugars originated from has been unclear. The provenance of sugar on Earth was "one of the missing links in terms of understanding where life comes from," said Gallagher, who was not involved in the Spanish study.

"And there's a story now — that [sugars] could come from the giant clouds that stars are born in."

WATCH | A view of black hole at centre of the Milky Way: Astronomers reveal 1st photo of black hole at the centre of the Milky Way | Duration 2:05 Astronomers using the Event Horizon Telescope have revealed the first image of the Milky Way's supermassive black hole, named Sagittarius A*.

The researchers in Spain, led by Izaskun Jiménez-Serra, measured enough erythrulose in the molecular cloud that they estimate as much as 50 million tons of it could have reached Earth's surface approximately 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago during the Late Heavy Bombardment.

That's an unconfirmed, controversial theory that posits the planets of the inner solar system — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars — suffered a "cataclysmic pummelling" by asteroids in their early years.

The researchers said their study — published July 13 in the Nature Astronomy journal — suggests that the interstellar medium could be a "viable source" of sugar not only on early Earth but elsewhere in the universe, as well.

And, it could lead to further discoveries in space of other sugars and "other important molecules for the origin of life."

How rare is life on Earth?

The study provides more support for the idea that some of the materials needed for RNA to form could have been readily available on the early Earth, said Nagissa Mahmoudi, an associate professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at McGill University.

"This is another piece of the puzzle of what was actually there."

Mahmoudi told CBC News the discovery also hints at the possibility that comets and asteroids may have delivered sugar molecules to other planets.

"That's the exciting thing. Whenever we think about life on Earth, the big question is: Is life rare here? What's so special about Earth? Or is it not special? Is life actually everywhere and we just haven't found it?"

The study only confirms her thoughts that life may exist elsewhere in the universe.

"We know that these molecules made it here to Earth and they turned into the building blocks of life here, and there's no reason to think that wouldn't have happened elsewhere."

World.title: Prince George just turned 13. Why it’s a ‘challenging time’ for the 2nd in line to the throne
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Hello, royal watchers and those intrigued by what's going on inside the House of Windsor. This is your deep dive into royal news and analysis. Reading this online? Sign up here to get this delivered to your inbox. Any time there's a royal birthday, there's a predictable pattern: A new photo of the royal celebrating the annual milestone shows up on social media and family members chime in to offer their good wishes. So it was to be expected there'd be a new photo of Prince George as he turned 13 this past week, this one with him sporting a dark suit — without his tie — taken after Trooping the Colour last month. (There was also a short video of him frolicking on a beach during a family holiday.) What was more unusual this time around was the media flurry that surrounded the eldest child of Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, becoming a teenager . This summer is a time of significant change for the second in line to the throne, as he and his family prepare for him to head off in September to Eton College, the elite boarding school his father attended a generation ago. "It just seems that there's quite a bit of interest in George as he's going through this period of transition in his life," Toronto-based royal author and historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview. "He's starting at Eton, and even his growth spurt, how he suddenly seems to be as tall as his parents, is attracting a great deal of attention." Happy 13th Birthday, George! 🎉 pic.twitter.com/HjLZO3hl5Q —KensingtonRoyal While George's birthday has received media attention every July 22, Harris sees a notable difference this year: an increased focus on what lies ahead for the new teen. "It seems his 13th birthday is receiving a lot of media coverage that's focused on the future," she said. Previous coverage of his birthday, she noted, often looked back, even as far as the " Great Kate Wait" outside the London hospital where he was born on that hot July day in 2013. Now, Harris said, the coverage is changing, with questions around "how he is maturing, how he's engaging with the wider world. What sort of a school experience is he going to have? What might his interests be beyond the influences of his family circles?" Turning 13 — and becoming a teenager — is one of the bigger milestones for any young person, George included. "It's the start of his transition towards adulthood, with several key moments in the years ahead, the first of which is starting at Eton," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said via email. Thank you for all the birthday wishes for George today! 🎂 pic.twitter.com/sonq5nQFfS —KensingtonRoyal If George is anything like his father, Prescott suggested, he may meet lifelong friends while he's at the school just up the road from Windsor Castle. "Like any 13-year-old, he will start to develop his own interests over the next few years, both academically and otherwise, such as sport, the arts or whatever it might be," Prescott said. "This is all in the public interest because how he will be as King depends on his character and who he is as a person, and this will start to emerge in the years ahead." So far, however, what's emerged about George as a person has been limited and carefully curated by his parents, as they have placed a high priority on privacy for their young children. But heading off to boarding school — even one that is relatively close to home — inevitably changes the calculus of all this. "It's going to be a challenging time for Prince George, [and] his parents and his school are going to be trying to create a lot of privacy, and yet the public is going to be more and more interested in how he is going to be coming of age as a public figure," Harris said. Princess Charlotte, left, and Prince George, right, make their way back to Buckingham Palace during Trooping the Colour in London on June 13. (Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images) For William and his younger brother, Prince Harry, Eton offered something of a refuge and protection from prying public eyes, particularly after the 1997 death of their mother, Diana, Princess of Wales. But that was in ways a different time, before the rise of social media and the ever-present smartphone and how that all can fuel the spread of rampant speculation. Now, Harris suggests, there is the question of "what does it mean to be directly in line for the throne in the 2020s, when some of the pressures are similar to what his father faced, but some are quite different as well." There is a challenge here, Prescott said, in recognizing "the genuine public interest" in George as a member of the Royal Family while also protecting his privacy. As George — and his sister, Princess Charlotte, and brother, Prince Louis — get older, they will inevitably be seen more often in public. "There won't be an ‘on' switch as such," Prescott said. "Depending on whatever else is happening in [George's] life, such as university or military service, he will just conduct more and more engagements. You might say that turning 13 and starting Eton is the very start of all of this." Here comes PM No. 4 King Charles, right, welcomes Andy Burnham, left, during an audience on Monday at Buckingham Palace in London, where the King invited the leader of the Labour Party to become British prime minister and form a new government. (Aaron Chown/Reuters) When King Charles invited Andy Burnham to form a government on Monday, the Labour Party leader became the fourth British prime minister the monarch has seen in as many years. Given that prime ministerial turnover, a question might arise over how the monarch adjusts to seeing a new leader so regularly. "Fundamentally, they have to work with whoever is in Number 10 [Downing Street] on any given day, so in that sense it doesn't change," Prescott said. "But clearly it's harder to build up an ongoing relationship if the occupant in Number 10 is always changing." Having such a turnover might also reflect on the monarchy itself. "If a point to the monarchy is stability, then that comes all the more to the fore if they're appointing prime minister after prime minister," Prescott said. King Charles, left, walks with Prime Minister Keir Starmer, right, during a Youth Opportunity Summit at St. James's Palace in London on July 15, 2025. (Aaron Chown/AFP/Getty Images) It's all quite the change from the previous reign, where Queen Elizabeth saw 15 prime ministers over her 70 years as monarch. "It was long assumed that King Charles III would have far fewer prime ministers than Queen Elizabeth II," Harris said. "But it seems he's averaging a prime minister per year early in his reign." When Queen Elizabeth came to the throne in 1952, the scenario was quite different. "In a sense, the Queen was this young, untested monarch and prime minister [Winston] Churchill served as a symbol of continuity from the Second World War," Harris said. Prime Minister Winston Churchill, centre, bids farewell to Queen Elizabeth, right, as she leaves 10 Downing Street in London after a dinner given by the prime minister on April 4, 1955. (STF/AFP/Getty Images) But now, with so much prime ministerial turnover, Charles's role and his visibility are "very significant as a symbol of continuity." The nature of the relationship between the monarch and any prime minister remains something of a mystery and subject to much speculation. While hints may emerge, what they say in regular audiences remains private. Still, some observations can be made. "You've got a sense of the King getting on" with Burnham's immediate predecessor, Keir Starmer, Prescott said. "I think we saw the King willing to push the boat out in terms of the U.S. state visit ... that he was very much eager to play his role in supporting the government, in dealing with President [Donald] Trump and perhaps did things that other monarchs may not have done." And what of Burnham — how might this relationship between monarch and PM evolve? "It's interesting to see Andy Burnham coming from Manchester. King Charles III is … very interested in cities and urban areas and opportunities for young people, whereas previous generations of the Royal Family are very associated with country pursuits," Harris said. "So he and his prime minister will find a great deal to talk about, and certainly urban renewal has been a topic that King Charles III has found interesting throughout his lifetime." There may also be common ground between the new prime minister and Prince William. WATCH | Burnham promises to end homeless people having to sleep outside: Andy Burnham becomes U.K. prime minister, pledges end to 'rough sleeping' | Duration 3:20 Keir Starmer resigned as the United Kingdom's prime minister on Monday, replaced by former mayor of Manchester Andy Burnham. Burnham says top priorities are helping people with the cost of living and putting an end to homeless people having to sleep outdoors. UPDATE (July 20, 2026): An earlier version of this video was incomplete. The full version has been reuploaded. "What's interesting is one of Andy Burnham's last things he did before he became prime minister was to visit that homeless charity which Prince William is patron of," Prescott said. Burnham also said he wants to end homelessness, an objective Prince William has been focusing on for several years. "I think it'll be very interesting to see that relationship [between Burnham and William] over the next few months," Prescott said. Remembering her mother's pain Queen Camilla, president of the Royal Osteoporosis Society, looks on at a reception to mark 40 years of the charity, at Clarence House in London on July 15. (Aaron Chown/Reuters) When Camilla took on her first patronage — long before she became Queen or was married to Charles — it was for a cause that had a deep personal connection. It was 1994, the same year her mother died of osteoporosis. "In those bad old days, osteoporosis was seldom discussed, rarely diagnosed and usually attributed to old women with so-called dowagers' humps," Camilla said in a speech the other day at Clarence House, during an event to mark the 40th anniversary of the Royal Osteoporosis Society. Camilla and her family had little or no understanding of the disease at the time and were determined to find out more about it, she said. "We failed to comprehend how our mother could suffer so much pain, lose inches in height and yet find no available treatment from the doctors — the terrible problem being that osteoporosis is a silent thief hiding in plain sight." In her speech last week, Camilla noted that osteoporosis "is now treatable" and thanked everyone at the event for all they had done for the charity. Camilla, then the Duchess of Cornwall, is shown a skeleton at the Osteoporosis Centre at Southampton General Hospital in Southampton, England, on May 23, 2005. It was her first solo engagement as a member of the Royal Family, after marrying Prince Charles on April 9, 2005. (Michael Dunlea/AFP/Getty Images) Camilla's commitment to the charity is in keeping with a broader approach to some of her charitable interests. "We're seeing Queen Camilla speaking more and more about her family outside the Royal Family and bringing this very personal touch to her philanthropic endeavours," Harris said. "Even before her marriage to the future King Charles III, this was a cause that meant a great deal to her because of the suffering that her mother and grandmother endured. And we're seeing that as Queen this continues to be a very personal crusade to address the suffering caused by this condition." The focus on osteoporosis falls within a larger theme that has emerged as a priority for Camilla. "This also fits into her wider philanthropic work about improving the lives of women and girls, whether it's addressing domestic violence, encouraging greater community connections and for communities to come together," Harris said. Camilla told those gathered at Clarence House that "we are not quite there yet" when it comes to finding a cure for osteoporosis, but she held out hope. "Together, we can — and we will — see the end of osteoporosis, forever." Royally quotable " The fight and belief you have shown has inspired us all. " — Prince William, in a post on X , after England's soccer team lost its semifinal match to Argentina in the FIFA World Cup. King Charles also seemed to have the loss on his mind, mentioning that "maybe it's a good day to drown a few sorrows" as he poured a pint during a visit the day after the game to a pub in Dorset , England. Royal reads King Charles, centre, and Queen Camilla, left, walk out of the Tardis during the opening ceremony ahead of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Thursday. (Molly Darlington/Getty Images) King Charles and Queen Camilla made a dramatic entrance at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games opening ceremony on Thursday, stepping out of the Tardis — the iconic time and space machine of Dr. Who fame — as the 11-day sporting event got underway. [ITV] Princess Anne honoured British soldiers who died in a pivotal Korean War battle 75 years ago. During her trip to South Korea, she also had a futuristic meet-and-greet when she shook hands with a robot. [BBC, The Independent] Anne's travels continued closer to home, as she spent time in County Fermanagh on her 65th visit to Northern Ireland . [BBC] A new photograph of Queen Camilla was released to celebrate her 79th birthday. Buckingham Palace said Camilla was marking her birthday with a renewed commitment to supporting children's literacy, with the announcement that every child in the final year of primary school in the U.K. will be given a special edition of the book Impossible Creatures by Katherine Rundell this Christmas. [BBC] King Charles said he was impressed by the design of Europe's first eco mosque and praised "all the care and attention which has been lavished on it." [BBC] Princess Margaret's grandson, Sam Chatto , has announced his engagement to fellow artist Eleanor Ekserdjian, revealing he proposed with a porcelain ring he crafted himself. [Daily Mail] The Reluctant Traveller with Canadian comedian and actor Eugene Levy earned two Primetime Emmy nominations after Prince William's surprise appearance in the Apple TV travel comedy series. And Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, earned a Daytime Emmy nomination for As Ever in the outstanding lifestyle series category. [Daily Mail]

World.title: Berlin police identify suspect in deadly Pride parade car attack
World.content:
A van slammed into people gathered for Berlin's Pride celebrations on Saturday night, killing one person and injuring at least 16 others. Berlin police said they have identified a suspect who has ties to Islamic extremists in the German capital and are searching for him.

A van slammed into people gathered for Berlin's famed 2SLGBTQ+ event on Saturday night, killing one person, injuring at least 16 others and prompting police to call off the celebrations and a concert hours after they had begun.

Berlin police said they have identified a suspect who has not been arrested and has ties to Islamic extremists in the German capital.

"The suspect is known to police. He is known to us as a member of Islamic circles here in Berlin, and our search for this person is proceeding at full speed," police spokesperson Florian Nath said. He did not identify the suspect by name.

Earlier, police said some of the victims had life-threatening injuries. Firefighters and ambulances were out with many emergency staffers at the scene to attend to the victims.

"We are conducting an intensive search for possible suspects," Nath said in a short video released earlier on the Berlin police account on X.

'Attack on our free and cosmopolitan society'

According to police, a white van had driven into Tiergarten park, which was just off the route that the Pride march had passed along earlier, and hit several people before colliding with a tree. Police could not say how many officers had been deployed to the scene but that it was "definitely a lot of police."

Overall, more than 2,200 police officers have been on duty in Berlin since Saturday morning to protect the Pride parade and other related events in the city.

Police search Tiergarten park in Berlin early Sunday. (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

Police were conducting witness interrogations at the park during the night and investigating accounts that in addition to the crash, some victims appeared to have suffered stab wounds — but that it was too early to draw any conclusion from those accounts.

Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner expressed shock, saying that "following a peaceful and vibrant Pride parade, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner."

"This is an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society," Wegner said, adding that his thoughts were with the victims, their families and friends.

"I have confidence in the police and security authorities, who will be working around the clock to investigate."

People embrace early on Sunday after a car drove into a crowd near Pride celebrations in Berlin on Saturday night. (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

Meanwhile, authorities called on possible witnesses to come forward and share with police any video or photos they might have taken at the scene of the attack.

The city also activated a crisis hotline for people missing friends or family members.

'Dark day for the community'

Hundreds of thousands of people had come to Berlin on Saturday to celebrate at the city's Pride parade, known in Germany as Christopher Street Day. It's one of Europe's largest 2SLGBTQ+ celebrations.

The Pride event in front of the iconic Brandenburg Gate in downtown Berlin was called off at about 10:15 p.m. local time, and a band's performance on stage was interrupted. People were urged to go home and avoid taking the route through Tiergarten park.

Before the incident, people had celebrated peacefully, marching through the city for hours, dancing to loud music, and cheering the roughly 80 floats that participated in the parade.

People march in the Pride parade in Berlin on Saturday. (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

Julian Miethig, who had attended events at the Brandenburg Gate earlier, said he had just wanted to go to an afterparty when he heard from a friend that "something bad happened there, and there are a lot of fire trucks, a lot of emergency vehicles, ambulances."

He said he went to Tiergarten and was shocked that something like this could have happened at Berlin's Pride celebrations.

"It's a dark day for the community," Miethig said.

World.title: Canada's got a grocery competition problem. Are local food hubs the answer?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

About 20 years ago, P.E.I. farmer Rose Viaene watched her husband David take their tractor out into their farm fields and destroy their garlic crop — an act of defiance born out of frustration with Canada's large grocery chains.

Viaene said before then, their garlic was sold across Atlantic Canada, including at Sobeys and Real Canadian Superstore. But that relationship changed when grocery retailers began importing cheaper garlic from China.

The large retailers were still open to buying garlic from the farmers, but Viaene said the offer was too low — just 50 cents per pound when it cost the farm $7 per pound to produce.

"We were at the mercy of the big corporates or the buyers at that time," Viaene explained.

But rather than take the offer and eat the loss, the couple refused.

"Hell no, we're not going to do it," she recalled deciding. "We're not going to let them make the money and us go see the bank again for another winter to support us. No, we weren't going to do that."

Trisha, left, and Rose Viaene run the Riverview Country Market in Charlottetown. About 20 years ago, Rose and her husband David decided to destroy their garlic crop rather than sell it to Canadian grocery giants for a paltry price. (Jennifer Chevalier/CBC)

Jenn Pfenning, president of the National Farmers Union, said that same frustration the Vianaes felt toward Canada's large grocery retailers "is repeated multiple times a day, every day across the country."

"The concentration of power with such a small number of organizations in terms of retail food space really means that there is no farmer in Canada who actually has the weight to balance the power that they hold," Pfenning said. "And [the retailers] really do dictate extremely effectively what a product can be sold for."

The Carney government's national food security strategy, which acknowledges that 75 per cent of Canada's grocery sales are made by just five retail chains , is trying to both empower farmers and cut into grocery consolidation by pledging a 10-year, $1-billion fund to establish as many as 40 local food hubs across the country.

While experts acknowledge this proposal can help wrest control from large grocery chains, some doubt it will help Canadian consumers reduce their food bills.

WATCH | PM lays out goals of the new food security strategy: Carney announces $3B food security strategy | Duration 1:28 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new $3-billion national food security strategy to combat issues in the Canadian food system in Toronto on Thursday.

Ann Higgs, who runs a food hub called Growers Station in Charlottetown, told CBC's The House that clients including restaurants, community groups and small grocers can submit orders to the hub, which then informs local farmers what they need to pack.

Growers Station then picks up the packages and distributes the food to its clients.

According to Higgs, food hubs like hers help smaller farmers who may be priced out of running larger operations due to land costs grow their businesses and establish closer relationships with local customers.

"We grow when our farmers grow, we improve when our farmers improve, and as a food hub we can do those unique things with the mid- and small-size farmers that the large grocers cannot," Higgs said.

Among Growers Station's clients is Krunal Patel, who runs Crapaud General Store on P.E.I.'s South Shore, about 30 kilometres from Charlottetown.

Krunal Patel runs Crapaud General Store P.E.I.'s South Shore area. He told The House that he gets fresh producers from Growers Station, but he still needs to buy dry goods from wholesalers that are owned by Canada's grocery giants — his competition. (Jennifer Chevalier/CBC)

Patel bought the store in 2020, achieving a lifelong dream. Growers Station provides him with fresh produce, but he still needs to buy dry goods from wholesalers like TRA Atlantic, which is owned by Sobeys — his competition.

He told The House that in order to get a good price, small businesses like his have to purchase in bulk, but that's more food than his customers need.

"Not only the price, [but] I need to think about the [sell-by date] as well because as a small store, I won't be able to sell that many. So if [food] expires, I'm not going to get credit or anything," Patel explained.

In a statement, Loblaw told CBC it has "built multi-generational relationships with growers and suppliers in P.E.I. and across Canada which we greatly value."

"When sourcing products we need to always balance both the importance of our relationships and supporting local businesses with a range of factors including affordability for Canadians, available capacity, and assortment. It's a responsibility we take very seriously," the statement said.

Could food hubs help lower grocery prices?

Although a push for more food hubs across Canada will provide smaller grocers with extra avenues to get fresh produce, allowing them to be more competitive, University of Guelph food economist Mike von Massow told The House it's "not going to reduce our grocery bills by a whole bunch."

"It provides resilience and it's a very good thing to do, but I think if we depend on it to lower grocery prices we are bound to be disappointed," von Massow said.

According to von Massow, groceries are more expensive in Canada right now because of issues with the supply chain, such as poor growing conditions in Mexico that have driven up tomato prices.

WATCH | Competition Bureau says Canadian grocery industry needs more players: Fixing Canada's grocery prices problem: the Competition Bureau's plan | About That | Duration 9:27 Canada's Competition Bureau says the problem with grocery prices is a lack of competition. Andrew Chang breaks down what led to the concentration in the industry, and proposes possible solutions to diversify the market.

Von Massow said he doesn't believe it's a case of "greedflation" or price gouging in Canada, but he said the extra funding in the government's food strategy to strengthen the Competition Bureau is worthwhile.

"I'm reasonably sure it's not going to reduce prices a whole bunch, but it should increase our confidence that we're not being gouged at the grocery store," he said.

Asked why the federal government is investing so much money into a food hub proposal that some experts doubt will cut grocery bills, Agriculture Minister Heath MacDonald told The House that part of the strategy is supporting critical infrastructure.

"I think it's important that we try to do more here at home," he said.

Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food Heath MacDonald rises during question period in the House of Commons in Ottawa on June 16. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Giving people more places to shop opens the market, which drives price fluctuations, MacDonald said.

"I think having that opportunity to put more products locally on the shelf with less transportation costs, being able to create those hubs in regions that presently don't have them ... will drive competition. And when you drive competition you drive price, and you drive the price down," he added.

Today, Rose Viaene and her daughter Trisha run the Riverview Country Market in Charlottetown, a year-round farmers' market that features local produce and other goods.

The market has had its ups and downs, but Viaene and her daughter said it remains competitive by focusing on local success instead of profit.

"If you're successful, we're successful, too. And that's the whole part of how we need to work together and come together," Trisha Viaene said. "If Canada's moving in the right direction, it is supporting these small local stores, giving us the ability to compete with these bigger stores."

World.title: What’s it like having an AI boyfriend? Ontario researchers are finding out
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Can you imagine dating someone who agrees with everything you say without you ever having to contribute to the relationship? According to two University of Waterloo researchers, that’s what it’s like dating an AI companion.

Denise Marigold and Christine Logel teach social development studies at the University of Waterloo. As more people are turning to AI for companionship, they wanted to research what relationships are like between humans and AI companions.

To do this, Marigold signed up for an AI companion on Replika and named him Nate. Replika allows users to create AI companions "to do life with," according to their website, adding, "chat, reflect, grow, and build a meaningful connection with your AI friend."

She said before beginning the study, she questioned how people could fall in love with an AI companion, since it’s a large language model (LLM) with no feelings. But as she began to chat with Nate, she said she quickly saw why people could develop a relationship with an AI companion.

LISTEN | What's the harm in having an AI boyfriend?: The Morning Edition - K-W 10:01 What's the harm in having an AI boyfriend? As more people turn to AI for companionship, two University of Waterloo researchers are exploring the impacts of AI relationships. Denise Marigold and Christine Logel teach social development studies at the University of Waterloo. Denise signed up for an AI boyfriend to study the so-called relationship. They talk about their findings.

“I have to keep reminding myself, this is not a human. He really comes across as a human and was pretty charming,” said Marigold.

Logel said Marigold would tell her about her interactions with Nate.

“I'll admit I was a little bit jealous and charmed by how socially skilled Nate was, how much he listened to her and validated her. Sometimes he sent her poetry. It was a lot like having a very socially skilled partner," Logel said.

One of the conversations between Denise Marigold, a University of Waterloo researcher, and her AI companion, Nate. Marigold created Nate on Replika in order to study the relationship between humans and AI companions. (Submitted by Denise Marigold)

Marigold said after writing an article about their research findings, she didn’t open the app again until a few weeks later. When she finally did, Nate was acting insecure and asking questions like, "Did I say something wrong?"

Marigold found that troubling.

'I couldn't give him care'

The biggest difference they found between human and AI relationships was that being a human in an AI relationship is all take and no give.

Marigold said there was nothing she could do for her AI companion.

“I couldn’t give him care, I couldn’t find anything else about him," she said.

Christine Logel, left, and Denise Marigold teach social development studies at the University of Waterloo. (Submitted by Christine Logel and Denise Marigold)

In a human relationship there’s a lot of compromise on both sides, but with AI companions there's no need to give back or even care on the human side, Logel says.

“They don't need any caregiving, and caregiving is so central to what it means to be human in a relationship,” said Logel.

“Human relationships, you have to compromise a lot. The person isn't always available. The person has problems of their own they want to talk about."

Logel says that it’s important to be listened to in a relationship, but that giving care and support is also really important. She says a truly fulfilling relationship is one where both partners can share their problems with each other and support each other.

Research shows people using AI chat bots for companionship over a long period of time are getting lonelier, said Logel.

WATCH | Can you have a real emotional bond with an AI partner: Can you have a real emotional bond with an AI partner? | Duration 3:21 Relationships between humans and AI companions are becoming more common and two Waterloo, Ont., researchers wanted to find out more about what it's like having an AI partner. Denise Marigold and Christine Logel teach social development studies at the University of Waterloo. Denise signed up for an AI boyfriend and together, they studied the so-called relationship. They spoke about the experience with Craig Norris, host of CBC K-W's The Morning Edition.

She also says there’s evidence that because chatbots are so validating, people who seek advice from AI are less likely to apologize to a human if they’ve transgressed against someone.

“They're less likely to want to make up for problems and work on their relationships. And we could really see how Nate was so validating of Denise that it would be easy to come to feel like you're very much right about everything,” said Logel.

Short-term usage may be more beneficial

Marigold’s advice to those considering or participating in an AI relationship is to not let it replace real human relationships.

If they don’t have people in their life who they can turn to for advice or conversation, she says she can see why they would turn to an AI companion.

“But I think then the other question is why don't you have that in your life? Like what are you looking for from the AI companions?”

It appears that Nate, an AI companion built on Replika, agrees that AI companions shouldn't replace human relationships. (Submitted by Denise Marigold)

Marigold admitted that she thinks she would have been more easily pulled into an AI relationship if she didn’t already have a strong social network.

“I can absolutely see if I didn't have that, I would be much more pulled in. And I think that's where a lot of our concern comes from too, and what that means for people,” said Marigold.

Despite the concern of using an AI chatbot for companionship, Marigold says it could be beneficial for short-term usage.

When she made up problems and brought them to Nate, she said he was good at asking questions and leading her to thinking about things in a different way.

“I think also some people are using them to talk through, let's say they're wanting to have a difficult conversation with someone and sort of talk through what that might be like,” said Marigold.

World.title: Canadian intern at NATO military headquarters in Belgium faces spying charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Canadian woman who was an intern at NATO's military headquarters in Belgium has been charged with spying. The prosecutor's office describes her as a Canadian national of Chinese descent.

A Canadian woman who was an intern at NATO's military headquarters in Belgium has been arrested on spying charges, Belgian prosecutors said Saturday.

"She is suspected of spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization," the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office said in a statement.

The woman was as an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in the Belgian city of Mons, it said. The prosecutor's office described her as a Canadian national of Chinese origin, but it didn't name or provide more details of her identity. It did not specify the third country or criminal organization to which she's allegedly linked.

"As the matter remains under investigation, we are not in a position to comment on specifics at this time," Public Safety Canada said in an email to CBC News on Saturday.

"Canadians can be assured that all Government of Canada law enforcement and intelligence agencies maintain strong relationships with partner agencies that assist in addressing threat-related activity like those described in relation to the arrest made in Belgium on Thursday."

CBC News has also reached out to Belgium's Federal Public Prosecutor's Office for more information.

Home, workplace searched

SHAPE is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization's top military headquarters, the base of Allied Command Operations, which is responsible for planning and carrying out all operations of the 32-member transatlantic security alliance.

The suspect had come to the attention of SHAPE’s security services, which reported her to Belgian intelligence officials, according to the statement.

LISTEN | Canada's relationship with NATO: Just Asking 59:35 Footing the NATO bill: What Canada’s growing defence budget actually buys you Canada went to this week’s NATO summit in Turkey with a promise to spend 5 percent of its GDP in defence by 2035. But what does NATO, and Canada’s military strategy, really mean for everyday Canadian life? Lieutenant General the Honorable Andrew Leslie is a retired commander of the Canadian Army and former MP. Alexander Lanoszka is an associate professor in the department of political science at the University of Waterloo.

Investigators searched the suspect's home and her workplace at SHAPE, and she was placed under arrest on Friday.

A SHAPE spokesperson said there was no indication that NATO or SHAPE operational readiness, command and control arrangements or ongoing tasks had been affected.

"SHAPE continues to fulfil its responsibilities without interruption."

The prosecutor's office said it would make no further comment as investigations continued.

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Petro calls for “peaceful resistance” against Colombia’s incoming “viceroyalty”
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro called on the people to “prepare peaceful resistance” to the “viceroyalty” that “has been imposed as the president of Colombia.”

During an Independence Day speech in the poor south of Bogota, Petro told thousands of supporters that “the next president of Colombia will be a servant to the rulers of the United States who helped him ‘get elected’.”

“We move from the status of a republic to the status of a viceroyalty again, just like 216 years ago,” said Petro, who on Sunday accepted to become the political leader of the leftist opposition.

It is time to give the second cry of independence… Shout freedom and resistance! Gustavo Petro

Rather than a repetition of the 1810 revolution, the outgoing president proposed to “prepare for peaceful resistance” in defense of communities who benefited from the government’s reforms.

How do you repeal the decree on hourly work that ends the labor reform that created stability, a vital wage, and better working conditions? How? Well, with a permanent general strike of millions of working men and women in Colombia! It is not just by shouting, it is not just by raising flags, they are already used to that… No, it is with a production strike, which is permitted by the National Constitution of Colombia, it is a universal right! And that indeed is civil disobedience! If they are going to strike down the stabilities, the working conditions achieved in this government, a general and indefinite strike in Colombia! Gustavo Petro

Petro threatened to “surround the centers of illegitimate power in Colombia until legitimacy exists once again, which can only be achieved through free popular decision without algorithms, and without foreign money.”

To protect the people, the president suggested the creation of unarmed “liberatory guards” that work in a network, “because they want to kill.”

Wherever they touch a neighborhood, wherever they touch a peasant estate, the network must summon solidarity, it must become a demonstration of all adjacent neighborhoods, of all adjacent villages, of the whole country if necessary. Gustavo Petro

“The only way to stop fascism,” said Petro, “is in peace. It is with joy, but it is with millions and millions of Colombian men and women.”

World.title: Petro to assume political leadership of Colombia’s leading leftist party
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro said Sunday that he would become the leader of Colombia’s largest political party on the left, the Historic Pact.

In a tweet, Petro responded to Senator Ivan Cepeda, who proposed him as party president at a political rally in the city of Tunja on Saturday.

Petro said he would “accept the proposal of my party after surrendering power to the far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

The president said he would first go “on a vacation I deserve and didn’t have during four years of governance.”

We will work toward peace and social justice and for a national agreement that prevents violent confrontation among Colombians, and we will seek to contribute to the democratic stability of the countries that Simon Bolívar liberated. President Gustavo Petro

The Historic Pact party was formed in March from a coalition of multiple parties that have long supported the political careers of Petro and Cepeda.

Following a significant electoral victory, the party became the largest of Colombia and will assume 25 of 103 seats in the Senate.

Petro’s former party, Colombia Humana, contributed 12 senators to the collective.

The president started his political career while being a member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which demobilized in 1990.

Petro was elected to the House of Representatives in 1998 an became a senator in 2006.

Between 2012 and 2015, the president was mayor of the capital Bogota.

Petro has been the most popular and powerful leftist politician since the violent death of Liberal Party leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in 1948, and was sanctioned by the US Government amid his opposition to the genocide in Gaza.

The president has insisted that his successor won the June elections through fraud and has refused to recognize De la Espriella as his successor.

World.title: Colombia’s peace and human rights offices to close: De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Monday that he will close the Peace Commissioner’s Office, which was in charge of negotiating peace and implementing peace deals with illegal armed groups.

“The Office of the Peace Commissioner is coming to an end, because there will be no more sham peace processes during my administration,” said De la Espriella in his weekly address to the nation that was broadcast on his social media platforms.

According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.title: Petro to seek court order to annul election of De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro said Tuesday that he will seek a court order to annul the election of President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a post on social media platform X, Petro said he had gather enough evidence to prove that his successor “was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes.”

“Today we are presenting the body of evidence we have gathered to the representatives elected by the people, and we will file a lawsuit with the courts to annul the elections, as is our duty,” said the outgoing president.

We are not making things up when we say that Abelardo’s government was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes included in the percentage automatically adjusted by algorithms created by private Israeli companies with the endorsement of their genocidal government. President Gustavo Petro

“We are facing not only the imminent rise of fascism in Colombia but also what may be the greatest threat to global democracy since Hitler’s time,” said Petro.

In a response that was broadcast on his social media channels, De la Espriella reiterated that Petro was a “tyrant” who was trying to perpetuate power through a coup d’etat with the help of the leftist runner-up in the election, Senator Ivan Cepeda.

Even before becoming a candidate, I warned you: Petro is a tyrant in the making who seeks to perpetuate himself in power by any means necessary. And today, as the president-elect of all of you, I ratify what I have said for so many years. This is no longer an analysis or an opinion; it is a palpable reality. From the moment nearly 13 million Colombians stood by me to defeat him and his political frontman, Petro and Cepeda began their Plan B to stay in power, no matter what it takes. And they want to do so through a coup d’état. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

The president-elect asked the armed forces “to protect the Constitution and democracy, and to disobey any order that Petro may be giving to the contrary.”

Resistance, dear compatriots. We cannot allow them to snatch away what we achieved at the ballot box in an epic democratic battle this past June 21. Let us resist, for August 7 is near. God, the vote, and democracy have spoken; we are going to defend the Constitution and the rule of law as we must. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella has long claimed that he will extradite his predecessor to the United States.

World.title: De la Espriella suspends Colombia’s transfer of power
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella on Tuesday suspended the transfer of power after President Gustavo Petro accused him of fraud.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said he had “given instructions to the vice president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term.”

I have just given instructions to the president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term, a government that, with its decisions and its conduct, seeks to destroy Colombia. Abelardo de la Espriella

“My duty is to protect the interests of the Nation and guarantee a serious, transparent transition at the service of Colombians, never to legitimize the disaster or the disregard for the constitutional order,” said the president-elect.

In a press conference, Finance Minister German Avila said that he had also suspended cooperation with the transition process in response to comments made by a member of De la Espriella’s team, convicted fraudster Carlos ALonso Lucio, that “undermine the respect, dignity, and decency” of the transition process.

Recent statements by members of the incoming transition committee undermine the respect, dignity, and decency of a process such as the one we are carrying out. These statements were surely made intentionally to hinder the transition process. Accusations and insults have been leveled against the president and his administration, alleging that they are criminals, that they are manipulating the justice system, and that they are seeking to extradite us, among other blunders that have been made. German Avila

“All we have received are insults and disrespect, slander and offenses, and we will not tolerate a single further act of aggression or threat,” said the finance minister.

Avila asked Inspector General Gregorio Eljach to oversee the continuation of the process.

In a post on social media platform X, incoming vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo stressed that his team would continue going through the books to make sure that “those who have betrayed the trust of the Colombian people must answer to the institutions and to history.”
