The High-Andean Jewels of Chile’s Wetlands

The Salar de Surire in the Arica y Parinacota region sits at roughly 4,300 metres above sea level and hosts three of the world’s four flamingo species in a single location. Declared a Natural Monument and Ramsar Site, its white salt crusts and turquoise lagoons framed by snow-capped volcanoes make it one of the most photographed high-altitude landscapes in South America.

Further south, the Soncor Hydrological System inside the Salar de Atacama basin forms part of the Los Flamencos National Reserve and serves as the principal global breeding centre for the Andean flamingo. This same basin holds over 90% of Chile’s lithium reserves, placing it at the centre of a growing tension between conservation and the global energy transition.

The recently created Salar del Huasco National Park in the Tarapacá region protects another high-altitude salt flat where all three Chilean flamingo species coexist alongside vicuñas and alpacas. Its new park status signals a governmental push to safeguard these fragile ecosystems, though enforcement capacity remains limited.

Coastal Wetlands: Accessible and Under Siege

The El Yali wetland in the Valparaíso Region lies less than two hours from Santiago and hosts over 130 bird species, functioning as a critical stopover for migratory birds travelling between hemispheres. Its marked trails and visitor infrastructure make it one of the most accessible sites for travellers wanting to experience Chile’s wetlands firsthand.

Laguna Conchalí near Los Vilos in the Coquimbo Region remains one of the last intact coastal wetlands in the area, with more than 100 bird species recorded and a Nature Sanctuary designation dating back to 1996. The Batuco wetland, roughly 40 kilometres from Santiago, protects about 300 hectares and harbours 150-plus bird species including threatened ones like the reed cormorant.

A multi-scale vulnerability assessment found that 42.6% of evaluated coastal wetlands in Chile have high or very high vulnerability. The most exposed sites cluster in central Chile, where urban expansion, real-estate pressure, and reduced rainfall from climate change converge most intensely.

The Southern Riverine and Urban Wetland Networks

The Carlos Anwandter Nature Sanctuary on the Cruces River near Valdivia was Chile’s first Ramsar Site, designated in 1981, and remains the country’s most iconic riverine wetland. It is the principal habitat for the black-necked swan, an emblematic bird of southern Chile, and draws photographers and naturalists year-round.

The Rocuant-Andalién system in Concepción spans roughly 11 square miles and was designated a global Important Bird and Biodiversity Area by BirdLife International in 2021. Despite its international recognition, the complex has already been drastically reduced by industrial expansion and urban development, making it a emblematic case of an urban wetland system at risk.

Around Valdivia, the Angachilla and Llancahue wetlands form part of a network of Nature Sanctuaries that combine palustrine wetlands, flooded swamp forests, and remnants of ancient Valdivian temperate rainforest. Community-led conservation efforts in these peri-urban zones offer a model for balancing city growth with ecosystem protection.

Patagonian Peatlands and the Carbon Sink Factor

Patagonia’s vast peat bog complexes in the Aysén and Magallanes regions function as major carbon sinks, storing immense quantities of greenhouse gases in layers of partially decomposed vegetation. A new national law now explicitly recognises their role in climate mitigation, though poor extraction practices for “pompón” moss used in horticulture remain a serious threat.

Bahía Lomas in Tierra del Fuego is one of Chile’s most important coastal wetlands for migratory shorebirds, hosting large populations of Red Knot and other species that depend on its vast tidal flats. Its Ramsar designation underscores its hemispheric relevance, yet its extreme southern location means monitoring and enforcement are logistically challenging.

Chiloé Island alone concentrates roughly 29,500 hectares of wetlands embedded in a landscape of channels, estuaries, and peat bogs with strong cultural ties to local communities. The island’s wetland mosaic supports both traditional livelihoods and significant birdlife, including migratory shorebirds and waterfowl.

Lithium, Drought, and the Wetlands at Risk of Disappearing

The Salar de Atacama basin exemplifies the direct conflict between mineral extraction and wetland survival, with large-scale lithium operations drawing on the same groundwater that sustains flamingo breeding habitats. Regional analyses show that Andean wetlands across Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia face serious risk from expanding lithium and mineral extraction driven by global electric-vehicle demand.

Laguna Santa Rosa in the Atacama Region has already experienced documented environmental degradation and shrinking linked to mining and geothermal activities. The Limarí River wetland, designated a Ramsar Site in 2020, sits in a climate-change hotspot where severe drought and advancing desertification threaten to collapse its riverine ecosystem.

Arid coastal wetlands in northern Chile—including those at the mouths of the Lluta, Camarones, Loa, and Copiapó rivers—exist in zones of extreme water deficit and serve as crucial stopovers for migratory birds along the Pacific flyway. Many of these small sites go unnoticed in policy discussions despite facing threats from urbanisation, pollution, and water abstraction.

The Institutional Risk: When Wetlands Vanish from the Map

Civil society organisations recently reported that 539 wetlands were removed from Chile’s official biodiversity information system, shrinking the national register from 2,461 to 1,922 ecosystems. This cartographic erasure does not mean the wetlands have physically disappeared, but it strips them of legal recognition and leaves them more exposed to extractive or urban projects.

Only about 2% of Chile’s mapped wetlands have any formal protection status, whether as Ramsar sites, nature sanctuaries, or national park units. Restoration initiatives led by local communities and NGOs have recovered over 11,000 hectares across the country in recent years, demonstrating that degradation can be reversed when resources and political will align.

For investors and expats, the wetland protection gap represents both a regulatory risk and an emerging opportunity. Projects near vulnerable wetlands face growing scrutiny from communities and courts, while conservation finance and sustainable tourism ventures around iconic sites like El Yali or Carlos Anwandter are attracting increased attention.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Chilean wetlands are easiest to visit from Santiago?

The Batuco wetland lies roughly 40 kilometres from the capital and hosts over 150 bird species with growing visitor infrastructure. El Yali in the Valparaíso Region is less than two hours away and offers marked trails, making it the most developed wetland tourism destination near Santiago.

Why are Chile’s high-altitude wetlands threatened by lithium mining?

The Salar de Atacama basin holds over 90% of Chile’s lithium reserves, and extraction operations pump brine from the same groundwater that sustains flamingo breeding habitats and high-Andean lagoons. Cumulative impacts on water balance threaten the entire hydrological system, with regional studies warning that Andean wetlands across Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia face serious risk from expanding mineral operations.

What does the removal of 539 wetlands from Chile’s official register mean?

The removal from the SIMBIO biodiversity information system does not indicate physical disappearance but rather a loss of official recognition in state maps. This cartographic erasure leaves affected wetlands legally unrecognised and more vulnerable to extractive or urban development projects, as they no longer appear in the inventories used for environmental impact assessments.

A Historic Venue at the Centre of Cartagena’s January Revival

The Teatro Adolfo Mejía, known widely by its initials TAM, sits inside Cartagena’s walled city and is described by the Mayor’s Office as “one of the most important cultural settings in the country.” Its 2026 programme launches during the city’s peak cultural month, when international visitors fill hotels and restaurants across the historic centre.

The Instituto de Patrimonio y Cultura de Cartagena (IPCC) manages the theatre’s year-round cultural programming and agenda from January through April, a window that now anchors the city’s high season for cultural tourism. For property owners and hospitality investors, the January festival surge provides a reliable spike in footfall and premium room rates inside the walled city.

The Cartagena Festival de Música: Twenty Years of Programming Power

The 2026 edition marks two decades for the Cartagena International Music Festival, which runs from 4 to 12 January. Twenty-seven concerts are scheduled, with Teatro Adolfo Mejía serving as the principal night-time venue for the symphonic and chamber music programme.

The festival’s 2026 theme translates as “The Soul and the Body: Musical Universalism and National Schools.” It examines how composers across centuries have balanced a shared musical language with distinct national voices, a framing that resonates in a city where European heritage architecture meets Afro-Caribbean rhythms daily.

The Franz Liszt Chamber Orchestra returns as the resident ensemble, anchoring a programme that draws soloists and conductors from Europe, Latin America, and beyond. Ticket prices and exact schedules are published on the festival’s official channels closer to the opening date.

Where Gaitas Fit into Cartagena’s Broader Cultural Landscape

Traditional gaita music, played on long indigenous flutes and accompanied by drums, is deeply woven into the identity of Cartagena and the surrounding Bolívar department. The region hosts dedicated gaita festivals, including the Festival Nacional Autóctono de Gaitas in San Jacinto and the Festival de Gaitas, Cantos y Tambores in the El Socorro neighbourhood.

At previous editions of the Cartagena International Music Festival, groups such as Gaiteros de San Jacinto have appeared in workshops and crossover concerts, creating a dialogue between classical forms and traditional Caribbean sounds. While the formal 2026 season opening at TAM is a classical music event, gaitas remain a living presence in Cartagena’s streets, plazas, and community festivals throughout the year.

For expats and long-stay visitors, this dual musical identity is part of the city’s appeal: a morning of symphonic rehearsal inside a restored 19th-century theatre can be followed by an evening of gaita and bullerengue in a neighbourhood square.

What Follows: Hay Festival, FICCI, and a Packed First Quarter

The IPCC’s published calendar shows that Teatro Adolfo Mejía’s season does not pause after January. The Hay Festival Cartagena, a major literary and ideas gathering that draws international speakers and audiences, occupies the theatre in late January or early February.

The Cartagena International Film Festival (FICCI), the oldest film festival in Latin America, follows in March, using TAM for premieres and gala screenings. Jazz nights, choral performances, and theatre productions fill the gaps, making the theatre a year-round engine for the city’s creative economy.

The Read-Through for Investors and Expats

A well-programmed cultural season at Teatro Adolfo Mejía 2026 signals more than entertainment. It indicates that Cartagena’s public and private sectors continue to invest in heritage infrastructure and international programming, which supports property values inside the walled city and in adjacent neighbourhoods like Getsemaní.

For expats considering Cartagena as a base, the density of high-quality cultural events from January through April reduces the sense of seasonal isolation that can affect smaller Caribbean cities. The presence of a resident orchestra and a reliable festival calendar also creates demand for short-term rentals, hospitality services, and bilingual professional staff.

Colombia’s broader push to grow cultural tourism as a share of GDP, supported by ProColombia and local mayoral offices, means venues like TAM are likely to see continued public funding and international partnership. The 2026 season opening is a concrete data point in that longer trend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the Teatro Adolfo Mejía 2026 cultural season begin?

The season opens on 4 January 2026 with the inaugural concert of the 20th Cartagena International Music Festival. The festival runs through 12 January, with Teatro Adolfo Mejía hosting the main nightly symphonic and chamber music performances.

Does the 2026 season opening feature traditional Colombian gaita music?

The formal season opening is a classical music programme led by the Franz Liszt Chamber Orchestra. Gaita music is central to Cartagena’s cultural identity and appears in dedicated festivals such as the Festival Nacional Autóctono de Gaitas in San Jacinto, as well as in community events and occasional crossover workshops at the music festival.

What other events does Teatro Adolfo Mejía host in early 2026?

After the January music festival, the theatre hosts the Hay Festival Cartagena, a major literary and ideas event, followed by the Cartagena International Film Festival (FICCI) in March. Jazz, theatre, and choral performances continue through April and beyond under the management of the IPCC.

World.title: Anitta’s ‘Equilibrium 2’ Fuses Funk, Samba and Afro-Brazilian Faith
World.content:
Music & Culture

Key Facts —Album scope. ‘Equilibrium 2’ adds 17 all-Portuguese tracks to the cycle, bringing the full project to 32 songs and roughly 1 hour 33 minutes of music. —Guest artists. Thirteen collaborators span generations and genres, including Maria Bethânia, Alceu Valença, Mart’nália, MC Tha, and Grupo Ofá from Salvador’s Terreiro do Gantois. —Religious grounding. Tracks explicitly invoke Candomblé orixás, terreiro chants, and Afro-Brazilian spiritual imagery, with ‘Ogum Me Rodeia’ calling on the warrior deity Ogum. —Genre blend. The record weaves funk carioca, samba, MPB, reggae, forró and ijexá into a cohesive Brazilian sound critics have dubbed ‘macumbeats’. —Strategic pivot. Unlike earlier global-pop projects, ‘Equilibrium 2’ is almost entirely in Portuguese, marking a deliberate turn towards Brazilian roots and domestic cultural identity.

Anitta’s new album ‘Equilibrium 2’ unites funk, samba and Afro religions in a 17-track Portuguese-language project that Brazilian critics are calling the most personal and ambitious work of her career.

Anitta’s new album leans on funk, samba and Afro-Brazilian rhythms.

A Spiritual Sequel Built on Brazilian Soil

‘Equilibrium 2’ is the direct continuation of ‘Equilibrium,’ released in April 2026, which first established the Afro-Brazilian spiritual framework now deepened across this second volume. The combined cycle reaches 32 tracks and roughly one hour and thirty-three minutes of music, making it one of the most substantial artistic statements by any Brazilian pop star this decade.

Where the first instalment laid the conceptual groundwork, the sequel pushes further into Candomblé imagery, terreiro rhythms, and explicit invocations of orixás. Brazilian press coverage has consistently framed the project as Anitta’s most important work precisely because it centres Brazilian culture and Afro-Brazilian spirituality rather than chasing international pop formulas.

How ‘Equilibrium 2’ Afro Religions Theme Shapes the Sound

The album’s religious dimension is not decorative but structural. ‘Ogum Me Rodeia,’ featuring the legendary Maria Bethânia and Letícia Fialho, directly invokes Ogum, the Candomblé orixá of war, iron, and pathways, placing Afro-Brazilian devotion at the centre of a major pop release.

‘Deus Mãe’ with KING Saints and ‘Contemplação’ with Grupo Ofá, from Salvador’s historic Terreiro do Gantois, link contemporary song structures to terreiro chants and aesthetics. Tracks such as ‘Feitiço,’ ‘Sem Pressa,’ and ‘OKE’ return repeatedly to encruzilhadas — crossroads — a central symbol in Afro-Brazilian cosmology where the material and spiritual worlds meet.

‘Eu Não Sou Santa’ plays with religious syncretism, referencing devotion to Nossa Senhora while dialoguing with Afro-matrix beliefs, a tension familiar to millions of Brazilians who navigate multiple spiritual traditions simultaneously.

Funk, Samba and the ‘Macumbeats’ Aesthetic

Musically, the album stitches together funk carioca’s percussive bounce, samba’s rolling swing, and the sacred rhythms of ijexá alongside reggae, forró, and MPB. One Brazilian critic coined the term ‘macumbeats’ to describe this fusion of Afro-religious sensibility with pop production, and the label has stuck.

Recurring producers Los Brasileros anchor tracks like ‘Você Já Sabe’ with polished pop architecture that never flattens the Brazilian rhythmic DNA underneath. The result is a record that sounds unmistakably local while meeting international production standards, a balance Anitta has pursued across her career but arguably never achieved this fully.

Thirteen Guests, Three Generations, One Cultural Statement

The guest list reads like a curated map of Brazilian music across generations. Maria Bethânia, a towering figure of MPB since the 1960s, shares space with Alceu Valença, Mart’nália, and younger voices like MC Tha and Katú Mirim, the latter bringing Indigenous rap into the mix on ‘OKE.’

Alexandre Carlo of Natiruts, Mestrinho, KBrum, Brô MC’s, KING Saints, Los Brasileros, and Letícia Fialho round out the thirteen collaborators. This multigenerational assembly signals an artist thinking about legacy and lineage, not just streaming numbers.

The Business Read-Through: Why the Pivot Matters

For investors and industry watchers, ‘Equilibrium 2’ represents a calculated strategic shift. Earlier projects like ‘Funk Generation’ aimed squarely at global charts with English and Spanish versions.

This album is almost entirely in Portuguese, with only one Spanish version of Djavan’s ‘Azul’ breaking the rule.

The move bets that cultural authenticity can drive both domestic dominance and export appeal. Brazil’s recorded music market grew by over thirteen per cent in 2025, according to industry tracker Pro-Música Brasil, and streaming now accounts for more than eighty-five per cent of recorded revenue.

A Portuguese-language project rooted in local genres can monetise that domestic base deeply while the artist’s international profile draws curious global listeners.

Anitta’s brand partnerships and touring power also stand to benefit. Aligning with Afro-Brazilian spirituality and heritage positions her distinctively in a global pop landscape where cultural specificity increasingly cuts through algorithmic noise.

What Expats and Global Listeners Should Know

For expats and international audiences, ‘Equilibrium 2’ offers a genuine entry point into Afro-Brazilian religious culture that shapes daily life from Salvador to Rio’s suburbs. Candomblé and its musical expressions are not niche folklore; they are living traditions that influence Brazilian Portuguese, cuisine, dance, and social rhythms.

Understanding references to Ogum, encruzilhadas, and terreiro culture provides cultural literacy that extends well beyond music. The album functions almost as a syllabus in contemporary Afro-Brazilian identity, packaged inside highly listenable pop.

What to Watch Next

The full ‘Equilibrium’ cycle may yet spawn a visual album or live tour, given the scale of the project and Anitta’s history of ambitious staging. Any tour routing through Salvador, Rio, and São Paulo would likely incorporate terreiro aesthetics and guest appearances from the album’s collaborators.

Streaming performance in the first four weeks will indicate whether the Portuguese-only bet pays off domestically and whether international playlists embrace the record despite the language barrier. Early critical reception in Brazil has been strongly positive, but commercial data will tell the fuller story.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Anitta’s ‘Equilibrium 2’ about?

‘Equilibrium 2’ is the second part of Anitta’s ‘Equilibrium’ cycle, exploring faith, spirituality, and Afro-Brazilian ancestry through funk, samba, and Candomblé-influenced music. The 17-track album features explicit references to orixás, terreiro chants, and the concept of encruzilhadas, or spiritual crossroads, across collaborations with thirteen guest artists.

Which Afro-Brazilian religions appear in ‘Equilibrium 2’?

Candomblé is the primary religious tradition referenced, with the track ‘Ogum Me Rodeia’ invoking the warrior orixá Ogum and ‘Contemplação’ featuring Grupo Ofá from Salvador’s Terreiro do Gantois. The album also engages with religious syncretism, blending Catholic imagery like Nossa Senhora with Afro-matrix beliefs on tracks such as ‘Eu Não Sou Santa.’

Why is ‘Equilibrium 2’ almost entirely in Portuguese?

Anitta deliberately chose Portuguese to centre Brazilian culture and Afro-Brazilian spirituality rather than chase international pop markets with English or Spanish versions. The decision reflects a strategic pivot towards domestic authenticity, with only one Spanish version of Djavan’s ‘Azul’ appearing on the otherwise all-Portuguese record.

World.title: Kenya’s Maisha Namba Digital ID Reaches 1.7 Million Cards
World.content:
Kenya · Digital Rights

Key Facts —System components. Maisha Namba consists of a Unique Personal Identifier, the Maisha Card, the Maisha Digital ID and the Maisha national database. —Initial court halt. Justice John Chigiti stopped the rollout in late 2023/early 2024 after the Katiba Institute sued, citing the absence of a Data Protection Impact Assessment. —Injunction lifted. Justice Lawrence Mugambi lifted the suspension in August 2024, allowing the government to restart the digital ID scheme. —2026 rollout progress. The government has reportedly printed more than 1.7 million Maisha Cards and pushed birth e-notification above 90% of new births. —Petitioners and core concern. The Katiba Institute and Haki na Sheria Initiative argued that mass biometric collection began without a legally required Data Protection Impact Assessment.

Kenya’s Maisha Namba digital ID system is advancing in 2026 despite persistent privacy and data-protection pushback, following the lifting of a court injunction in August 2024.

A biometric passport; Kenya’s Maisha Namba centralises identity data despite privacy objections.

The 2026 rollout

The government reportedly cleared a backlog of more than 600,000 second-generation IDs and printed over 1.7 million Maisha Cards this year. Birth e-notification has reportedly exceeded 90% of new births, signalling an aggressive push to enroll citizens.

These 2026 figures come from secondary reports and indicate that the Maisha Namba infrastructure is being rapidly deployed. The rollout continues despite unresolved legal questions and concerns raised by civil society groups.

For a foreign reader, it helps to understand that Kenya’s previous national ID system relied on a physical card and a separate registration process that often left gaps in coverage. Maisha Namba is designed to close those gaps by linking birth records, biometric data and a lifelong unique number from infancy.

That ambition explains the government’s focus on birth e-notification as a foundation stone: every registered newborn becomes part of the system from day one, theoretically making it harder for anyone to fall through the cracks later.

How courts halted—then cleared—the project

In late 2023 or early 2024, Justice John Chigiti ordered a halt after the Katiba Institute challenged the rollout. The judge ruled that the government had not conducted a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) as required by Kenya’s 2019 Data Protection Act.

That injunction was lifted in August 2024 by Justice Lawrence Mugambi, allowing the rollout to resume. The court’s reversal removed the immediate legal barrier, enabling the registration drive seen in 2026.

A DPIA is a formal risk-assessment tool that forces organisations to map out how personal data will be collected, stored, shared and protected before processing begins. Under Kenya’s Data Protection Act, it is mandatory for any project that poses a high risk to individual rights—exactly the kind of large-scale biometric undertaking Maisha Namba represents.

The initial court halt turned on the absence of this document, not on a finding that the system was inherently unlawful.

The data-protection case

The Katiba Institute and the Haki na Sheria Initiative brought the legal challenge, arguing that mass biometric collection violated data-protection safeguards. They highlighted the lack of a DPIA, insufficient public participation, and overly broad biometric categories—though 2024 rules reportedly dropped items such as iris, DNA, voice and earlobe geometry.

Petitioners also pointed to risks of identity theft, surveillance and weak deletion and audit safeguards. These concerns remain at the centre of the debate, even as millions of cards are issued.

The narrowing of biometric categories shows that litigation can shape policy even when it does not stop a project outright. Still, the core complaint endures: collecting fingerprints and facial geometry at a national scale creates a single point of failure.

If the central database were ever breached, the stolen biometrics cannot be reset like a password, which is why deletion rules and independent auditing matter so much to privacy advocates.

Who could be excluded

Marginalised communities, including border and stateless populations like the Nubians, have historically struggled to obtain official identification. Critics warn that Maisha Namba’s digital ecosystem may deepen exclusion for groups that already face barriers to registration.

Without strong remedies for those without standard documentation, the system risks disenfranchising some of Kenya’s most vulnerable residents. The case filed by the petitioners specifically flagged this exclusion danger.

In many countries, digital ID systems promise to include people who lack paper documents, but the reality often depends on the flexibility of enrolment rules. If Maisha Namba requires a birth certificate or a parent’s existing ID to register a child, families that never had those documents could remain invisible to the state.

Whether the government introduces alternative pathways—such as witness affidavits or community-based verification—will determine if the system narrows or widens Kenya’s identity gap.

The wider stakes

The dispute encapsulates a global tension between digital identity expansion and privacy norms. Kenya’s 2019 Data Protection Act requires a DPIA for high-risk processing, a standard that mirrors the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation’s approach to accountability.

How Kenyan courts ultimately balance national ID ambitions with data-protection principles could influence other African nations crafting similar systems. The government’s allocation of about 6.88 billion Kenyan shillings (roughly US$53.3 million) in a 2024/25 budget line underlines the scale of the project.

This is not merely a domestic story. Several African countries are modernising their identity infrastructure, and Kenya’s experience—both its legal setbacks and its resumed rollout—is being watched by policymakers from Accra to Kigali.

A ruling that strengthens DPIA enforcement could raise the bar for government tech procurement continent-wide, while a permissive outcome might encourage faster, less consultative rollouts elsewhere.

Background on Maisha Namba

Maisha Namba is Kenya’s national digital identity scheme, built on a unique personal identifier that links a physical Maisha Card, a digital ID and a central database. The programme aims to unify fragmented identity systems into a single, interoperable digital footprint.

The initiative gained momentum with a reported budget allocation of 6.88 billion Kenyan shillings (approximately US$53.3 million) for 2024/25. Its rollout has been marked by legal battles that shaped, but did not permanently stop, the project.

What to watch next is whether the courts will issue a final ruling on the underlying petition, not just the interim injunction. An open question is how the judiciary will treat the adequacy of any DPIA the government may have produced since the injunction was lifted.

Another is whether parliament will amend the data-protection framework in response to the controversy, potentially clarifying the threshold for public participation in future digital-identity projects.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Kenya’s Maisha Namba digital ID system?

It is a national identity system comprising a Unique Personal Identifier, a physical Maisha Card, a digital ID and a centralised national database.

Why was the Maisha Namba rollout paused by the courts?

Justice John Chigiti halted the rollout in late 2023/early 2024 after the Katiba Institute sued, arguing the government had not carried out a mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment under the 2019 Data Protection Act.

Is Maisha Namba being rolled out now?

Yes, the injunction was lifted in August 2024 by Justice Lawrence Mugambi, and the 2026 rollout has reportedly printed over 1.7 million Maisha Cards with birth e-notification exceeding 90%.

World.title: Sebastião Salgado’s ‘Workers’: A Lasting Legacy
World.content:
Life · Photography

Key Facts —Death. Sebastião Salgado died on 23 May 2025 in Paris, France, aged 81, due to leukemia. —Workers Series. Shot between 1986 and 1992, it is a landmark black-and-white documentary photography series on manual labour. —Brasília Exhibition. The ‘Workers’ exhibition was displayed at SESI Lab in Brasília from 26 August 2023 to 28 January 2024. —Instituto Terra. Co-founded with his wife Lélia Wanick Salgado, it is a reforestation project in Minas Gerais, Brazil. —Other Major Works. Includes Migrations/Exodus, Genesis, and Amazonia; also co-founded Amazonas Images agency.

Sebastião Salgado, the Brazilian documentary photographer renowned for his ‘Workers’ series, died on 23 May 2025 at the age of 81.

Brasília, where Salgado’s ‘Workers’ was shown at SESI Lab in 2023-24.

The Workers Series

Sebastião Salgado’s ‘Workers’ series stands as a monumental achievement in the history of documentary photography, capturing the dignity and struggle of manual labour across the globe. Shot over six years between 1986 and 1992, the project took Salgado to dozens of countries, from the gold mines of Brazil to the shipbreaking yards of Bangladesh and beyond.

Through its stark black-and-white compositions, the series strips away the specificities of place to reveal the universal physical exertion and resilience of the working class. Salgado’s approach combined long-term immersion with a deeply humanistic lens, allowing his subjects to share their realities without intrusion.

The resulting collection of images not only cemented Salgado’s international reputation but also redefined documentary photography as a medium for social consciousness. Decades later, ‘Workers’ remains a powerful archive of a rapidly transforming global economy, preserving the dignity of manual labour for future generations.

What Workers Depicts

The ‘Workers’ series presents manual labour in an extraordinary range of contexts, from subsistence agriculture and artisanal fishing to heavy industry and mass construction. Salgado intentionally sought out both developing and developed nations, showing how labour connects humanity across economic divides.

Images of miners descending into perilous shafts, farmers toiling under the sun, and construction workers balancing on precarious scaffolding convey the raw physicality and danger inherent in such work. The series does not merely document tasks; it humanizes each worker, inviting viewers to see the individual behind the labour.

By transcending geographic and cultural boundaries, the photographs become a universal testament to the endurance of the human body and spirit. They challenge the viewer to consider the often-invisible hands that build the world’s infrastructure and produce its goods, shaping modern existence in countless unseen ways.

Remembering the Brasília Exhibition

The ‘Workers’ exhibition took up residence at the SESI Lab in Brasília from 26 August 2023 to 28 January 2024, marking a significant cultural event for the Brazilian capital. The show, now concluded, offered visitors a rare chance to engage with Salgado’s iconic series in a thoughtfully curated museum setting.

Presented as large-format prints, the photographs overwhelmed viewers with their scale and detail, drawing them into the physical worlds of the labourers. The exhibition’s design emphasized the tactile quality of Salgado’s gelatin silver prints, enhancing the emotional impact of each image.

For many Brazilians, seeing the work of their compatriot on such a grand scale was a moment of national pride and reflection. The exhibition demonstrated that, more than three decades after its creation, ‘Workers’ continues to speak urgently to contemporary issues of labour and inequality.

Salgado’s Death and Legacy

Sebastião Salgado passed away in Paris, France, on 23 May 2025, at the age of 81, succumbing to leukemia. His death brought forth an outpouring of tributes from the worlds of photography, environmentalism, and human rights around the globe.

The loss of Salgado marks a profound moment for documentary photography, as he was among the last of a generation that defined the genre with long-form, immersive projects. His unflinching yet deeply empathetic portrayal of humanity set a standard that will influence visual storytelling for generations.

Salgado’s legacy is not confined to his images alone; it lives on through Instituto Terra and the countless photographers he inspired. His work continues to challenge viewers to witness suffering and resilience without turning away, making him a moral force in the visual arts.

Instituto Terra and Wider Work

Together with his wife and creative partner, Lélia Wanick Salgado, he co-founded Instituto Terra in 1998 on their drought-stricken family farm in Aimorés, Minas Gerais. The reforestation project has since planted over two million trees, restoring a significant swath of Atlantic Forest and returning rare species to the region.

Beyond ‘Workers,’ Salgado produced several other monumental series, including ‘Migrations/Exodus’ (1993-1999), which documented the plight of refugees and displaced people, and ‘Genesis’ (2004-2011), a celebration of untouched landscapes and traditional communities. ‘Amazonia’ (2013-2019) continued his environmental focus, capturing the forest and its inhabitants before the breakneck pace of deforestation.

Collaborating with Lélia, he also established Amazonas Images, an agency dedicated to preserving and disseminating his work. All of Salgado’s projects reflect a consistent philosophy: that photography can serve as a bridge between worlds, fostering empathy, understanding, and meaningful action.

Workers’ Enduring Relevance for Latin America

As a Brazilian photographer who spent his career documenting global struggles, Salgado’s work resonates with particular intensity in Latin America. The region’s history of extractive industries and large-scale agriculture makes the ‘Workers’ series feel like a mirror held up to its own social fabric.

The SESI Lab exhibition in Brasília brought that connection into sharp focus, placing images of labourers from around the world in the heart of a city defined by its own construction and class divisions. For many visitors, the photographs were a stark reminder of the invisible labour that underpins Brazil’s economy.

Decades after the photos were taken, the series remains a powerful testament to the dignity of workers throughout Latin America and beyond. In a time of increasing automation and economic uncertainty, Salgado’s images serve as a lasting tribute to the human hands that continue to shape our world.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ‘Workers’ series by Sebastião Salgado?

It is a black-and-white photography series documenting manual labour around the world, shot between 1986 and 1992.

When did Sebastião Salgado die?

He died on 23 May 2025 in Paris, France, at the age of 81 due to leukemia.

What is Instituto Terra?

A reforestation project in Minas Gerais, Brazil, co-founded by Salgado and his wife Lélia Wanick Salgado.

World.title: San Luis Gold Tourism: Win 18-Karat Gold in La Carolina
World.content:
Frontier Tourism

Key Facts —The Offer. La Carolina will raffle 18-karat gold samples daily for 10 days during Argentina’s July winter school holidays. —How to Enter. Tourists automatically enter by keeping the parking ticket from the “Pueblo Peatonal” lot upon arrival. —The Source. The gold is extracted by local pirquineros, artisanal miners working the same streams that founded the town in 1792. —The Strategy. The giveaway is part of the provincial “Conexión San Luis” campaign, which bundles Banco Nación-backed discounts on lodging, gastronomy, regional products, and air travel. —The Scale. La Carolina has roughly 300 permanent residents, making this a high-impact play for a micro-destination in the Sierras Centrales.

A tiny mountain village in San Luis province is betting on its glittering past to secure its economic future, launching a San Luis gold tourism campaign that literally gives away precious metal to winter visitors.

Panning for gold; La Carolina in San Luis is reviving its 19th-century gold-rush heritage to lure winter visitors.

A 230-Year-Old Mining Village Plays Its Ace

La Carolina was founded in 1792 atop rich auriferous deposits and quickly became one of Argentina’s most important gold-producing centres in the 19th century. Today, with just 300 inhabitants, it is pivoting from extraction to experience, using its mineral wealth as a tourism magnet rather than a commodity export.

The mechanism is deliberately simple. Visitors driving into the historic centre park in the designated “Pueblo Peatonal” lot and receive a ticket.

That stub doubles as a raffle entry for that day’s draw, held each afternoon during the 10-day winter holiday window.

Winners receive a sample of 18-karat gold sourced directly from local pirquineros. These artisanal miners still work the streams and hillsides using methods largely unchanged for two centuries, turning a promotional gimmick into an authentic cultural artefact.

How the Gold Giveaway Actually Works

The rules are designed to reward genuine visitors and longer stays. Only parking tickets issued on the same day enter that afternoon’s draw, so tickets do not accumulate for future raffles.

The winner must present the original parking stub to claim the prize, a requirement that prevents digital gaming of the system. Municipal authorities have confirmed the raffle occurs once daily, with some local reports placing the draw at 17:00 and others at 18:00 at the Tourist Information Office.

The campaign runs for 10 consecutive days during the July winter school break, Argentina’s peak domestic tourism window. A family staying for a week could enter up to seven draws, materially increasing their odds of leaving with a piece of the Sierras.

The Economics of a Gold-Powered Tourism Pitch

For a village of 300 people, the calculus is straightforward. The marginal cost of the gold samples, sourced locally and measured in grams, is dwarfed by the spending power of even a few dozen additional tourist families on lodging, meals, and guided excursions.

Argentina’s domestic tourism market remains price-sensitive amid persistent inflation, making value-added promotions particularly effective. A free gold souvenir, however small, creates a powerful word-of-mouth narrative that paid advertising cannot easily replicate.

The initiative also diversifies La Carolina’s economic base beyond its narrow reliance on artisanal mining. By monetising heritage rather than ore, the town builds a more sustainable revenue stream less exposed to commodity price swings.

San Luis Gold Tourism and the Provincial Strategy

The gold giveaway is not an isolated stunt. It sits inside “Conexión San Luis,” the provincial government’s winter 2026 tourism push that bundles discounts on flights, accommodation, and gastronomy through partnerships with Banco Nación.

San Luis has long positioned itself as a nature and adventure tourism alternative to better-known Patagonian and Cuyo destinations. La Carolina’s mining heritage adds a cultural layer that differentiates the province from competitors offering only landscapes.

The province is betting that niche, story-driven attractions can capture a share of the winter holiday market typically dominated by Bariloche, Mendoza, and Córdoba. For investors watching Argentina’s tourism sector, the campaign signals a province actively diversifying its offering rather than relying on passive arrivals.

What This Means for Investors and the Tourism Sector

Argentina’s tourism industry is a rare bright spot in an economy grappling with currency controls and inflation. Domestic travel remains robust, and creative provincial campaigns like San Luis’s signal a maturing market where differentiation drives occupancy rates.

For expats and foreign investors, micro-destinations like La Carolina represent an under-the-radar opportunity. Property values in historic mining towns remain low relative to established tourism corridors, and provincial incentives may sweeten hospitality investments.

The broader read-through is that Argentina’s interior provinces are learning to monetise intangible assets—heritage, authenticity, and story—rather than competing solely on price or natural endowments. That shift, if sustained, could reshape the country’s tourism investment map over the next decade.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I enter the gold raffle in La Carolina?

Park in the “Pueblo Peatonal” lot when visiting La Carolina’s historic centre and keep your parking ticket. That ticket automatically enters you into that same day’s raffle.

No additional registration is required, and the winner must present the original stub to claim the gold.

When does the gold giveaway take place?

The raffle runs for 10 consecutive days during Argentina’s July winter school holidays. A draw is held once daily, typically in the late afternoon at the Tourist Information Office.

Only tickets issued on the day of the draw are eligible, so longer stays mean more chances to win.

Is the gold real and where does it come from?

Yes, the prizes are genuine 18-karat gold samples extracted by local pirquineros, artisanal miners who still work the gold-bearing streams around La Carolina. The town has been a gold-mining centre since its founding in 1792, and the giveaway uses locally sourced metal as an authentic cultural souvenir.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief — Sunday, July 26, 2026
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro — A cool, grey morning gives way to a bright afternoon — ideal for a late breakfast outdoors and a long, lazy pedal along the shore.

The city’s energy today is at the Hippie Fair in Ipanema, where the Sunday crowd makes for peerless people‑watching.

Latin American markets are closed for the weekend; Friday’s settled levels for Argentina’s Merval, Colombia’s COLCAP and USD/COP are on the WEEK IN FIGURES board.

Today is for doing very little, beautifully.

Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief for Sunday, July 26, 2026. Photo: The Rio Times archive.

Weather & What to Wear

FOUR-DAY OUTLOOK

SUN 26 22°C / 18°C 30% rain MON 27 23°C / 18°C 20% rain TUE 28 24°C / 19°C 25% rain WED 29 26°C / 20°C 10% rain

Expect overcast morning skies and a light south‑easterly breeze, with the sun breaking through by late morning. The low‑twenties air feels crisp by Rio standards — perfect for walking without breaking a sweat.

A light jacket or cotton sweater is your friend all day. Pack sunglasses and a small umbrella; the slim chance of a passing drizzle is real.

Monday and Tuesday stay mild and dry, making for a calm start to the working week, before Wednesday offers the warmest and brightest day of the set.

Sunset today: 5:23 pm · Posto 9 flags yellow this morning: moderate swell, clean sets, water near 20°C.

02

Day at a Glance

SNAPSHOT

— Weather: Morning cloud clearing to a 22°C afternoon; pack a cardigan. — The day’s event: Feira Hippie de Ipanema — Sunday‑only open‑air arts and crafts. — Venue/time: Praça General Osório, Ipanema, 9 am–6 pm. — Markets: Weekend close — all Latin American index and FX levels from Friday are final. — Weekend/outlook: Out‑of‑office Sunday; a quiet, no‑deadline 48 hours for most. — The day for: Bossa nova at brunch, browsing for leatherwork, and a sunset orange juice on the Arpoador rocks. A slow‑paced Sunday that feels like a holiday even when you have nothing to celebrate.

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — CRAFT & CAFÉ Hippie Fair Then a Walk to the Arpoador Rocks Start at the Feira Hippie de Ipanema in Praça General Osório, open 9 am to 6 pm every Sunday. The stalls sell excellent leather belts, hand‑printed linens and gemstone jewellery; many vendors now take Pix, though cash gets you a readier discount. Caffeine is a few steps east at Co.Ba Café (Rua Visconde de Pirajá 595, opens 7 am, espresso R$9), where you can grab a flat white and a pão de queijo. Its pavement terrace fills with freelancers by 10 am — early birds get the best seat. Once you’ve bought something you absolutely don’t need, stroll the three blocks south to Arpoador beach. The boulders between Ipanema and Copacabana are Rio’s finest sunset auditorium; locals clap the view almost every evening. Keep an eye on your phone on the rocks. The Jardim de Alah canal path links you back to the Lagoa cycleway if you’ve brought a rental bike from Bike Itaú. No bike today? Don’t try to summon a taxi right on Francisco Otaviano; walk one block inland for better luck with ride apps.

OUTDOORS — PARK & VIEWS For greenery, Parque Lage in Jardim Botânico opens at 8 am and admission is free. The mansion courtyard café serves cake and chemex‑brewed coffee under a giant imperial palm; go before 10 am to snag a courtyard table. The trailhead behind the café leads to Corcovado via the steep but shaded forest walk (start early, take water). If a full hike sounds too ambitious, the lawn and fish ponds alone are worth the Uber.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — IPANEMA & LEBLON Curto Café on Rua Joana Angélica in Ipanema has reliable Wi‑Fi, a courtyard garden and opens at 8 am on Sundays; their batch brew (R$10) is the pick. Workspace is limited, so share a communal table without a laptop squatting all day. In Leblon, Slow Bakery (Rua General San Martin 1247) opens at 7 am with sturdy sourdough, egg dishes until 1 pm and a back‑room table that suits two‑hour laptop sessions. Both spots are walkable from the Ciclovia if you’re coming from the beachfront bike lane.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — HIGH‑VIEW SANTA TERESA Swap sand for cobblestones and catch the bonde (tram) from Centro to Santa Teresa — R$20 one‑way, cash only, and runs roughly every 30 minutes on Sundays. Your target: Parque das Ruínas, a free cultural centre inside the shell of an old mansion with wrap‑around views of the bay. The in‑house café pours a cold chope for R$14 while DJs sometimes spin bossa nova on Sunday afternoons. Afterward, wander down to Bar do Mineiro for a R$55 feijoada and caipirinha; the neighbourhood feels like a hillside village dropped into the city.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Sunday night is low‑key by design. Lapa stays quieter than usual, so pivot to the Botafogo waterfront. Bar Urca is the classic move — no music charge, walls against the bay, and a crisp R$18 chopp served on the sea wall from 6 pm. For a more curated bar experience, Fogo by Companhia in Botafogo pours sourdough pizzas and natural wines until 11 pm (Rua Sorocaba 584, book a table via WhatsApp). If a completely different crowd is your thing, Galeria River in Largo do Machado shows talky films in a retro cinema setting — Sunday night tickets are discounted on the website to R$30 for the 8 pm session.

ALSO ON TODAY Parque Lage & Palacete do Lago — Jardim Botânico — free entry, 8 am–5 pm; perfect for a flat white among the hummingbirds. Museu do Amanhã — Praça Mauá, Centro — opens 10 am, R$30 full / R$15 half; strong air‑con alternative for a muggy morning. Jardim Botânico — Rua Jardim Botânico 1008 — open 8 am, R$15; Sunday guided tours in Portuguese at 10 am included in the ticket. Gabiroba Bar’s Sunday Jazz Trio — Rua Paschoal Carlos Magno, Santa Teresa — from 5 pm, free entry, plastic cups and courtyard music. The Mureta do Leme sunset — Leme — no ticket; a less‑crowded cousin of Arpoador where families gather with chilled coconuts.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô Linhas 1, 2 and 4 run a Sunday schedule from 7 am to 11 pm — the ‘domingueira’ single fare is R$7.50, no transfers included. The VLT in Centro operates from 7 am to 7 pm and serves Praça Mauá and Cinelândia if you’re museum‑bound; buy a RioCard at any VLT station.

The seaside Ciclovia lane from Leme to Barra is open for cyclists and skaters until 7 pm — car‑free on the beachfront side. Uber wait times are low across Zona Sul, but surge pricing is likely to hit Ipanema and Arpoador between 4 pm and 6 pm when the Hippie Fair and sunset crowd move together.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Grab a grilled‑hake plate with rice and beans at Via Sete (Rua Garcia D’Ávila 125, Ipanema, R$62), or try Galeto Sats in Copacabana (Rua Barata Ribeiro 7‑D, R$55 for the grilled chicken set with farofa and vinaigrette).

Dinner: Puro in Jardim Botânico (Rua Visconde de Carandaí 5, about R$120 per head) does a quiet Sunday terrace of wood‑fired fish. For a R$70 pizza and cold jazz, Bráz Pizzaria in Leblon stays open until midnight.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry R$100 in small notes for the Hippie Fair and the Santa Teresa tram — Pix is near‑universal at cafés and sit‑down restaurants but not every market stall or street vendor accepts it. An ID or digital copy is useful when picking up museum half‑price tickets.

Avoid the Lagoa path after dark on an overcast night when it rapidly empties. If you’re walking west from Arpoador rocks toward Copacabana with a phone in hand, keep it stowed and enjoy the view instead.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

The ‘Expats & Digital Nomads Rio’ WhatsApp group organises a casual 10 am coffee run most Sundays — message the admin on their Instagram story for today’s spot (often in Ipanema or Leblon). The Rio Digital Nomads Meetup page also lists a recurring Friday‑night drink but has nothing formal today.

For a low‑pressure plug‑in, head to CoWorking Leblon Space on Avenida Ataulfo de Paiva — it’s shut for hot‑desking on Sundays, but the associated café across the hall stays open until 3 pm and is full of freelancers polishing work ahead of Monday.

08

Game Day

THE SUNDAY LEAGUE PAUSE

No Campeonato Brasileiro or Carioca fixtures are scheduled today for Rio’s big four — Flamengo, Fluminense, Vasco and Botafogo all have a rest Sunday. The Maracanã is dark.

If you still need a pitch, the pelada games on the sands of Copacabana near Posto 4 kick off around 9 am and run until the afternoon heat; grab a cold mate leão from a cart and join the sideline commentary.

To watch whatever international match is hitting the screens, head to Blue Agave in Ipanema (Rua Vinicius de Moraes 68) or Mud Bug in Botafogo (Rua Arnaldo Quintela, courtyard screens). Check their Instagram before leaving, as Sunday match‑day hours change weekly.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Latin American equity and FX markets are closed for the weekend. Friday’s session levels for Argentina’s Merval, Colombia’s COLCAP and the dollar–peso rate USD/COP are final and shown in the Business & Markets / WEEK IN FIGURES board — no new settlements are created on a Sunday.

The past week’s moves followed a mixed‑data handover from US equities as traders priced divergent central‑bank paths across the Americas. Argentina’s broad index and Colombia’s benchmark drew flow driven by local legislative calendars, while the Colombian peso saw light Friday volume ahead of month‑end positioning.

Looking to Monday, the focus for expat professionals across LatAm will be the early US durable‑goods print and any Sunday‑night signals from Asian markets. A quiet Sunday is a good moment to review your firm’s exposure to the current settled levels before the open.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD Sun July 26 — Hippie Fair, Parque das Ruínas, then an Arpoador sunset — 22°C and clearing. Mon July 27 — Markets reopen; dry window for a morning run at Aterro do Flamengo before 23°C mid‑day. Tue July 28 — Fair weather, 24°C; light mail‑bag Tuesday, perfect for a post‑work Lagoa cycle. Wed July 29 — Warmest day at 26°C — block the afternoon for a long‑lunch in Santa Teresa. Thu July 30 — Weekend‑planning day; check Feira de São Cristóvão (opens Thursday) for Saturday forró.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — July 25, 2026.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief — Saturday, July 25, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is the Hippie Fair cash‑only or can I use card and Pix?

Around half the stalls are now taking Pix, but many artisans still work only with cash — especially those selling smallest items. Carry about R$150 in notes of R$10 and R$20, which will also help you haggle for a better price on leatherwork and silver jewellery. ATMs inside the shopping centre Galeria River (Rua Visconde de Pirajá 555, across from the square) are your nearest backup. They dispense R$50 notes, so don’t rely on getting small change from an elder stallholder who has been trading since 7 am.

Can I swim at Ipanema and Copacabana today, and is the water safe?

The Corpo de Bombeiros yellow flag at Posto 9 signals moderate conditions: experienced swimmers will find clean lines, but the side current is present. Families with young children should post up at the protected cove of Praia do Diabo, just south of Arpoador, where the bay calms the swell significantly. The latest balneabilidade bulletin generally keeps Ipanema’s central posts ‘própria’ (suitable); still, avoid fully submerging your head if you have a small cut, as this is a peak‑weekend bathing day with high numbers in the water.

World.title: BREAKING: Denvoy Bartley identified as tonight’s murder victim in Unitedville triple shooting
World.content:
BREAKING: Denvoy Bartley identified as tonight’s murder victim in Unitedville triple shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has confirmed that Denvoy Feliciano Bartley of Banak Street, Belize City, is the man who was murdered in a triple shooting in Unitedville Village on Saturday night.

Bartley was reportedly travelling with his twin brother and another man when the group was targeted near a bus stop while carrying out an errand in the village. All three men were rushed to the Western Regional Hospital, where Bartley later succumbed to his injuries. The two other victims remain hospitalized.

Bartley had previously survived a shooting in Belize City in April 2021. He was later charged in 2023 with the murder of Lionel Budna; however, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions discontinued the case in November 2024 by entering a nolle prosequi, and Bartley was released after spending more than a year on remand.

Police investigations into Saturday night’s murder are continuing.

World.title: BREAKING: Belize City man murdered in triple shooting in Unitedville, Cayo
World.content:
BREAKING: Belize City man murdered in triple shooting in Unitedville, Cayo

By Jose Luis Cruz: A Belize City man was murdered in a triple shooting that occurred on Saturday night in Unitedville Village in the Cayo District. The incident occurred near a bus stop in the village in the same vicinity that a policeman in uniform was also shot and killed.

A group of young men had gone to do an errand in the village when they were targeted by the gunman(men). Three (3) of the men received shooting injuries and were rushed to the Western Regional Hospital in Belmopan for treatment.

One of the shooting victims has succumbed to his injuries while the other two (2) are receiving treatment. The victim who died is a resident of Banak Street in Belize City.

This murder is the latest in a recent spike of shootings and murder that has occurred in Unitedville in the last two (2) years.

World.title: Man detained after young woman’s frightening bathroom ordeal
World.content:
Man detained after young woman’s frightening bathroom ordeal

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A man is in police custody after a young woman reported a deeply disturbing incident at her Trial Farm home, alleging that her mother’s common-law husband tried to force his way into the bathing room while she bathed, then grabbed and pulled her as she tried to escape, leaving her with injuries certified as harm.

According to the Belize Police Department, the young woman, accompanied by her mother, visited the Trial Farm Police Station on Monday, July 20, 2026, to make the report.

She told police that on the morning of Sunday, July 19, she was at home alone with her mother’s common-law husband when she went to bathe at about 10:00 a.m. While in the bathing room, she saw a shadow approaching and looked out to see the man coming toward her. With no door to the room, she grabbed the side of the shower curtain to keep him out as he struggled against her to get in, telling her in Spanish to let him in to bathe with her.

She held the curtain firm. When the man moved to close a window she had opened, she seized the moment, dressed quickly, and ran for her mother’s room. He ran behind her, according to her report, forcing his way into the room before she could shut him out, then grabbed her left hand and pulled her toward him as she struggled to break free, gripping her so hard that her arm hurt.

She managed to pull loose and ran outside, where a neighbour who saw what was happening took her into her home. From there she called her mother, waited as told, and later noticed pain through her entire arm and scratches on her wrist where she had been held.

She made her formal report the following day, and a doctor certified her injuries as harm. She has requested court action.

Police recorded her statement, and the man was detained. As he has not been formally charged, his identity is being withheld, along with the identities of the complainant and her family.

World.title: One checkpoint stop, three traffic charges for Belmopan rider
World.content:
One checkpoint stop, three traffic charges for Belmopan rider

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A routine vehicular checkpoint in Belmopan turned up a motorcycle missing every piece of required paperwork, and its rider now faces three traffic charges and a date with the Magistrate Court.

According to the Department of Transport, on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at about 8:10 p.m., a traffic warden conducting a vehicular checkpoint on Cemetery Road in the Maya Mopan Area of Belmopan City observed a woman approaching on a black motorcycle and directed her to stop, which she did.

The warden introduced herself as a Department of Transport officer and explained that checks were being conducted to ensure vehicles on the public road carried proper documentation. Asked for her driver’s licence, the rider stated that she did not own one, and she was informed of the offence and cautioned.

The checks did not stop there. Further inspection of the motorcycle revealed that it carried no insurance and was not licensed, adding two more offences to the night’s tally. The rider was informed of all the offences, cautioned again, placed under arrest, and escorted to the Maya Mopan Precinct pending charges.

At the precinct, she was identified as 32-year-old Francine Vanessa Recinos, a self-employed resident of the Salvapan Area, Belmopan City. She was informed of her constitutional rights in custody.

That same date, she was formally arrested and charged with three traffic offences: driving a motor vehicle not covered by third-party risk insurance, driving an unlicensed motor vehicle, and driving a motor vehicle while not being the holder of a Belize driver’s licence. Cautioned once more, she chose to remain silent.

Bail was granted in the sum of $500, and she is to appear at the Belmopan Magistrate Court at 9:00 a.m. on Wednesday, July 29, 2026.

World.title: School bag search lands San Pedro man with cocaine charge
World.content:
School bag search lands San Pedro man with cocaine charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A San Pedro Town man is facing a drug charge after police say a late-night stop in the Boca del Rio Area turned up suspected cocaine in the front pocket of the school bag he was carrying.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at about 9:15 p.m., officers on mobile patrol near a grocery shop in the Boca del Rio Area observed a man walking on the street with a dark blue school bag on his back. Upon seeing the marked police mobile, police reported, the man hurriedly hid something behind his back.

Finding the movement suspicious, an officer exited the vehicle, identified himself, and informed the man that a search would be conducted for drugs and ammunition. A search of his person found nothing incriminating, but checks inside the school bag, with the aid of a flashlight, produced a small transparent ziplock bag containing a white powdery substance, suspected to be cocaine, in the bag’s front pocket.

The man was shown the find, informed of the offence, cautioned, arrested, and escorted to the San Pedro Police Station with the suspected drugs in his view at all times.

At the station, he was identified as 24-year-old Edi Anderi Aban, a labourer of the San Juan Area, San Pedro Town. The suspected cocaine was weighed in his presence on a scale shown to read zero beforehand, amounting to 0.5 grams, then sealed in a labelled envelope which he signed voluntarily. He was served his rights in custody and granted a telephone call.

On Friday, July 24, 2026, police formally arrested and charged Aban with possession of controlled drugs. Cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

World.title: SUV run off the road at Punta Gorda Junction, driver flees
World.content:
SUV run off the road at Punta Gorda Junction, driver flees

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A woman escaped injury after her SUV was sideswiped into a roadside drain near Punta Gorda Junction on Friday evening, and police are now searching for the driver of a black car who never stopped.

According to the Belize Police Department, officers responded to a report of a road traffic accident at Punta Gorda Junction at about 5:55 p.m. on Friday, July 24, 2026.

On arrival, police met a 46-year-old Orange Walk Town woman, who explained that she was driving her grey Nissan Murano SUV from Punta Gorda Junction toward Bella Vista Village. Upon reaching the area of the three speed bumps, she told police, she saw a black car ahead of her travelling in the same direction, put on her left indicator, and attempted to overtake.

As she did, according to her report, the black car swerved into her vehicle, striking it between the rear passenger door and the bumper. The impact caused her to lose control and run into the drain on the right-hand side of the road.

The driver of the black car, she told police, never stopped.

Fortunately, no one was injured in the collision. Police are actively investigating the matter, and the identity of the fleeing vehicle and its driver remains unknown.

Anyone who witnessed the collision near the speed bumps at Punta Gorda Junction on Friday evening, or who has information about a black car with fresh damage, is asked to contact the Independence police.

World.title: Woman bitten by dog, owner allegedly refused to help
World.content:
Woman bitten by dog, owner allegedly refused to help

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Cowpen Village woman is nursing a dog bite, and police are seeking the animal’s owner, after she reported that the dog ran from his yard, bit her on the leg, and that the owner refused to assist her when told.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 37-year-old domestic of the Stann Creek District village visited the Independence Police Station on Friday, July 24, 2026, to make the report.

She told police that on the night of Thursday, July 23, at about 8:30 p.m., she was walking along a street in the village when a black and brown dog ran toward her and bit her on the left leg. According to her report, the dog ran from a nearby yard, and when she informed the owner that his dog had bitten her and that she needed assistance, he refused.

Police recorded a statement from the woman and issued her medico-legal forms, which are yet to be retrieved. A man has been listed as wanted in connection with the matter, facing the potential charge of permitting an unmuzzled ferocious dog to be at large. As he has not been detained or charged, his identity is being withheld.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Road safety must be more than just putting down concrete!
World.content:
Road safety must be more than just putting down concrete!

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Joe Awe: (Please note: I am no civil engineer. I am just a concerned citizen looking out for the better for the twin towns. I am not even interested in any mischief. I am willing to be corrected)

Let me start by saying something clearly: our children must be protected. Our pedestrians must be protected. And drivers must slow down.

There should be no argument about that.

But good road safety is not simply about installing a speed bump wherever there is a concern. Good road safety requires us to look at the entire road system: vehicles, pedestrians, intersections, emergency services and human behavior, and then make decisions based on proper traffic engineering.

That is why serious questions should be asked about the recently installed speed bump on Bullet Tree Road, reportedly about 300 yards from the four-way traffic lights at Joseph Andrews Drive.

This is a busy two-way roadway connected to a major signalized intersection. Vehicles turn from Joseph Andrews Drive onto Bullet Tree Road while other vehicles are approaching the intersection in the opposite direction. Any traffic-calming device placed along such a corridor should therefore be evaluated not only for the speed it reduces, but also for its effect on traffic flow, turning movements, sudden braking, vehicle queues and emergency access.

International traffic administration guidance itself treats speed humps as a traffic-engineering measure, not a one-size-fits-all solution. Their placement should consider the type of road, traffic volume, speed, intersection proximity and the role that road plays in the wider transportation network.

And there is another issue we cannot ignore: The San Ignacio Hospital is located down Bullet Tree Road. That changes the conversation.

Ambulances and other emergency vehicles may need to travel this corridor while transporting patients or responding to emergencies (and there are 5 speed bumps before the ambulance would get to this new one!). Research has documented that vertical traffic-calming devices can delay emergency vehicles, which is precisely why transportation guidance recommends special consideration for emergency routes and, where vertical traffic calming is necessary, alternatives such as speed cushions designed to allow larger emergency vehicles to pass with less disruption. – but there is no space for this engineering on this particular street.

So the question is not: “Do we care about children?” Of course we do. The real question is: Was this the safest solution available?

Because perhaps the bigger problem is standing only a few hundred yards away.

At the intersection of Joseph Andrews Drive and Bullet Tree Road, we already have a four-way traffic-light system and designated pedestrian-crossing infrastructure. That intersection should be one of the safest places for pedestrians, including schoolchildren, to cross.

But infrastructure alone does not educate people.

Do our children know exactly when to cross? Do pedestrians understand the pedestrian signals? Do motorists understand their responsibility when making left and right turns while pedestrians are crossing? Are the crossings clearly marked and visible? Is the timing adequate for children, older persons and slower pedestrians? Are we actively teaching people how to use that intersection safely? These questions matter.

International road safety guidance says pedestrian signals at signalized crossings are specifically intended to tell pedestrians when it is appropriate to cross, while proper signal timing must give people enough time to complete that crossing safely. Road-safety programs for children also combine engineering with education, supervision and other safety measures.

There is also a very real danger at intersections that we sometimes overlook: turning vehicles and pedestrians occupy the same space. Important pedestrian-safety materials specifically warn that drivers making left or right turns may fail to look for pedestrians. Modern signal strategies can even give pedestrians a head start before turning vehicles move, reducing conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles making left or right turns.

That is where our attention must also be focused.

A speed bump may slow a vehicle. Education changes behavior. A properly designed pedestrian system protects people at the precise location where they need to cross. Enforcement changes dangerous driving habits.

Good engineering anticipates what happens when an ambulance is rushing a patient to hospital, when two vehicles meet on a busy road, when a driver makes a right turn, and when a child steps into a crossing believing it is safe.

So perhaps it is time for the San Ignacio and Santa Elena Town Council to publicly explain the engineering reasoning behind this speed bump.

Was a traffic study conducted? Were ambulance and emergency-response movements considered? Was the hospital consulted? Were traffic volumes and vehicle queues studied? Were the turning movements from Joseph Andrews Drive assessed?

Were alternatives such as a raised pedestrian crossing, better markings, improved lighting or stronger enforcement considered?

And, critically, what sustained program is in place to teach our children and the wider public how to properly use the pedestrian crossing at the traffic lights?

These are not political questions. These are public-safety questions.

We should never have to choose between protecting a schoolchild and getting a patient to hospital quickly. A properly designed road-safety system should protect both.

Let us slow down where we need to slow down. Let us protect our children with everything we have. But let us also demand that every traffic-calming decision be based on sound engineering, public education, emergency access and the realities of how people actually use our roads.

Because sometimes the easiest thing to do is to build a speed bump. The harder, and more responsible thing is to build a complete culture of road safety.

And that is the conversation our Twin Towns need to have.

Touch lives. Change the world.

World.title: PEP transfer trap
World.content:
Head of the Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS), Anniona Jones, is urging parents to carefully consider requests to transfer their children to other high schools following the Primary Exit Profile (PEP) placement process, warning that such decisions should be based on what is best for the child’s development rather than the perceived prestige of an institution.

Jones also cautioned school administrators against accepting an influx of transfer students primarily for financial gain, arguing that overcrowding can undermine the quality of education and place unnecessary strain on teachers and school resources.

She said she is aware that some schools have received 60 or more transfer requests and, while she understands that every parent wants the best for their child, not every school is equipped to provide the type of academic intervention some students need.

“We have to be very careful about how we think of some schools as intervention schools or schools for children with low academic aptitudes, because as the children start to do better, people are still not going to want to place their children necessarily in those schools. You have schools that have low levels of enrolment, and then you have other schools that are bursting at the seams.

“It becomes an issue, though, for school governance to be able to say to a principal and have that conversation at the board level that, ‘Listen, this school was built for X amount.’ I still don’t know why we have schools on [the] shift [system] when we have so many schools that are underpopulated.

“It’s really…a policy issue, but a board can make a decision that we are going to limit our school sizes to no more than 22 to 30 children per class,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Jones argued that limiting class sizes is particularly important for schools offering science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) subjects, which she said are best taught in smaller classes. She added that smaller class sizes would also ease the burden on teachers by reducing the volume of books to be marked and allowing more targeted feedback and individual attention for students.

She noted that, in many cases, schools are reluctant to reduce enrolment because funding is largely allocated on a per-student basis, making lower student numbers financially disadvantageous. However, she welcomed the Government’s move toward a more equitable funding model, describing it as a positive step in the right direction.

Jones also expressed concern about the growing costs parents incur while seeking transfers, noting that some schools charge application fees between $1,000 and $5,000.

“If you look at the cost for transfer requests, you could have a school, in theory, getting a request of 100 children wanting to come in. If you charge each child $1,000, that’s $100,000 even if your school can only take in 20, so you could do a lot with an additional $100,000. Some parents are going around paying five schools $1,000 a pop or more,” said Jones.

She added: “Some schools, I hear, transfers are as much as $5,000 just to request a transfer, and they are not guaranteed to get in. Parents have to also look at that as well and understand that placing your child in a school where your child may be in the bottom quarter, or smack in the middle, may not be as good for your child as placing them in a school where your child may come first, second, or third and get a confidence boost, or placing a child in a school that can cater to their needs,” she reasoned.

Jones, who is the principal at Haile Selassie High School, added that, while traditional high schools often have a wider range of programmes and extracurricular activities, they can also place a greater financial burden on families.

In contrast, she said some non-traditional

schools may offer programmes that are better suited to a child’s interests and abilities while remaining more affordable.

“Sometimes we have to be very discerning that we don’t spend all the money to buy the car but turn around and can’t buy gas and can’t change the tyre, or can’t deal with the servicing and upkeep after the free servicing is finished.

“Schools need support to grow, so allow your child to be placed in an institution that can give you the financial wiggle room as well, to do some other things for your child. Otherwise, your child may go into these spaces, can’t function, and you can’t participate fully to keep the school offering what you say you want,” said Jones.

She further urged parents to do their part in ensuring that the children they send off to these institutions can have a positive impact, especially for non-traditional high schools that have a stigma of being violent environments.

“Send us the best version of your children, then we wouldn’t have to worry about the children, and every space can be a safe, developing, nurturing space for every child to be able to do all the things that they want to do, if parents are willing to help build it, fund it, create it,” she said.

She added: “We have the buildings, we have these teachers, we have the class sizes; it makes better sense to me to place your child in a smaller school to treat with the PEP score,” said Jones.

World.title: 140% spike in deportees to Jamaica last year
World.content:
In this Jamaica Observer file photo, Deportees from the US are on the move after arriving in Jamaica and being processed by local security officials.

SIXTY of the 1,317 people deported to Jamaica in 2025 were convicted of murder, manslaughter or attempted murder in the deporting country, with 52 of them being sent from the United States.

One was deported from Canada, five from England, and two from ‘other’ countries.

The information is outlined in the 2025 edition of the Economic and Social Survey Jamaica, a publication of the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ).

It listed 171 of the deportees having possession of drugs convictions, with a significant majority – 142 – coming from the USA. Two were deported from Canada, three from England, while 24 were sent back from other countries.

The 2025 list of deportees also included 134 people convicted for the serious offences of wounding, assault and battery.

The US again topped the list of these deportees with 115.

The sexual offences category listed 63 deportees last year, with the US sending back 50, Canada four, England five, while four came from other countries.

However for the vast majority of deportees, 610 were sent back to Jamaica for immigration violations including illegal entry, overstay of visa, and illegal re-entry.

There were 95 deportees convicted of firearm offences, with 88 running afoul of the law in the US. Other offences on the list included larceny, fraud/false document, kidnapping, and money laundering.

Of the total 1,317 deportees in 2025, 967 came from the US, which has a set policy of deporting Jamaicans to their homeland on the last Thursday of each month.

Last year saw Jamaica also receiving 70 deportees from Canada, 25 from England, and 255 from other countries.

The total represents a 140 per cent increase when compared to the 547 who were returned to Jamaica in 2024.

In May, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith said approximately 2,500 Jamaicans have been confirmed for deportation from the US this year.

Johnson Smith provided the update while speaking at a press conference at the Office of the Prime Minister as she moved to dismiss reports that some 4,000 Jamaicans are set to be deported from the US as part of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“Allow me to be clear that 4,000 Jamaicans are not being returned now. For some time it has been in the public domain that the US authorities had close to 4,000 persons in their records with final orders for deportation against their names.
