It is now our understanding that approximately 2,500 have been confirmed for removal over a period of time, to be determined by logistics, their own legal processes, and other factors,” said Johnson Smith.

She pointed out that the deportation of Jamaicans is not a new phenomenon, and said the Government remains committed to honouring its international obligations to receive its citizens while safeguarding national security and public safety.

“It is not a new phenomenon. For decades, Jamaica has facilitated the repatriation of its citizens under established international arrangements. We receive our citizens when they are returned to us. Just as we expect, and we do, repatriate foreign nationals who commit serious crimes or breaches of our immigration laws,” added Johnson Smith.

The foreign affairs minister further pointed out that the Government has expanded the National Reintegration and Rehabilitation Strategy to coordinate reintegration services for the deportees.

“On May 5th, Cabinet approved the establishment of a National Technical Working Group on Voluntary and Involuntary Migrants, recognising that not only is the grouping not homogeneous in and of itself, but we now have a sub-grouping of those who are returning of their own motion — determining the circumstances in the US to not be where they wish to remain — and those who are being returned, those who have the decision made for them. This technical group is chaired by the Planning Institute of Jamaica. Oversight is provided by the ministries of national security and foreign affairs and foreign trade; and the technical group comprises several ministries, departments, and agencies, as well as civil society partners.

“Its mandate is to coordinate reintegration services and to ensure that returnees are supported in a structured, sustainable manner — and this includes their reception, verification, health checks, security, vetting, and access to social and legal support where necessary,” Johnson Smith said as she sought to allay fears about the possible security threats the deportees might bring.

“Monitoring and detention measures are in place [and] they will be applied. Again, stakeholders play key roles in helping us as partners in this reintegration and return process,” declared Johnson Smith.

Meanwhile, the PIOJ also reported that the total number of voluntary returned migrants stood at 852 in 2025, an increase of 52.1 per cent when compared with the 560 who returned home in 2024.

Voluntary returned migrants are people who choose to return to their homeland.

World.title: Sunday Jones transforms ‘pain 2 power’
World.content:
Sunday Jones addresses the media launch for her five-day Jamaica Tour, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power, on July 20, 2026 at Sador’s Ethiopian Restaurant in Negril, Westmoreland. (Photo: Rosalee Wood Condell)

NEGRIL, Westmoreland — Poet and author Sunday Jones officially launched her five-day Jamaica tour, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power, on Monday, July 20, bringing a message of healing, reflection, and creative empowerment to audiences across Jamaica.

Rooted in the mission of transforming personal pain into purpose through spoken word, the July tour blends live poetry performances, youth engagement, and community building.

A native of Atlanta, Georgia, Sunday Jones is a poet, author, and community leader known for founding Sunday Jones Productions and the Prison Brat Foundation. She functions as an ordained minister, certified life coach, event curator, and radio personality dedicated to giving a voice to the unheard and unseen. Her work focuses on healing from childhood trauma, faith, and personal evolution.

“Ink Breath and Bars is the ink of our soul, of our journeys, our writings, our poetry, our life.” Jones explained to the

Jamaica Observer. “The breath is the breath that we take, through word sound, through healing, through all of the things. It’s the breath that we need to take sometimes. All the time we breathe, but we sometimes need to take breaths. And the bars are the lyrical word sound that come from the ink and the breath. The tour is about community, culture, love, and liberation. It is to bring people together, to pull light from people who don’t understand that they have the light, or to elevate those that do have the light and want to go further. That is Ink Breath & Bars, to sum it up shortly.”

The tour features a line-up of community showcases, school visits, and curated intimate gatherings designed to inspire, connect, and celebrate. The journey began on July 21 at Kingston Night Market, followed by a visit to Haile Selassie High School on July 23. On July 25 the tour headed to Sador’s Ethiopian Restaurant in Negril for a special community gathering. It concludes on July 30 with an exclusive healing experience and Jones’ Solar Return Celebration.

The Ink Breath and Bars tour has gained significant backing from internationally renowned Jamaican dub poet and performance artist Yasus Afari. He highlighted the vital role poetry plays in community upliftment and personal transformation, endorsing Jones’ vision to use creative expression as a vehicle for emotional wellness and youth empowerment.

“Let us use the language and the arts to heal and to redeem our people from what I described earlier as neurolinguistic sorcery, and so bring neurolinguistic healing, so that we can heal in a wholesome and full-some way. So that even our tongue can be an instrument of life. We don’t have to have so much dissing and cussing and quarrelling as a small country who have been through such great tribulation,” he stated.

The poet seized the opportunity to issue a charge: “So we are calling on our fellow so-called entertainers, which I prefer to call edutainers, let us rise to that occasion. We are a great country, unprecedented in human recorded history. We are a talented and great set of people. Let us use this gift of art, music, poetry, film, dance, comedy, literature, photography, videography to empower our people, to uplift our people, to heal our people, and to help fulfil Jamaica’s sacred, national pledge to advance the entire welfare of the entire human race. Honour, love, and prosperity. Rastafari blessings.”

In addition to live performances, the tour serves as a promotional platform for Jones’ latest book, The Art of Rising: A Love Letter to My Becoming, allowing readers and lovers of dub and spoken word poetry to connect deeply with her published works.

With stops spanning from the vibrant creative spaces of Kingston to the west coast in Negril, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power promises an uplifting cultural journey celebrating resilience, truth, and the transformative power of the Jamaican voice.

World.title: Breaking the cycle of underperformance
World.content:
Edwin Allen High School implemented a programme of extended learning that included Saturday mathematics classes, mathematics camps during school breaks, and mathematics marathons to provide intensive revision and examination preparation.

TARGETED intervention in 56 non-traditional high schools which were previously rated unsatisfactory or in need of immediate support by the National Education Inspectorate (NEI) has started to reap success.

The schools are beneficiaries of the National School Learning and Intervention Programme (NSLIP) introduced by the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information.

The programme was established in 2022 in response to the learning gaps/loss experienced by students from the disruption in the education system due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The tactical approach was developed to expedite school improvement by targeting the critical factors that influence student outcomes.

It included increased instructional time, strengthened leadership practices, data-driven decision-making, enhanced teacher support, improved student welfare, and stronger monitoring and accountability systems.

Its primary objective was to provide a structured and cohesive framework capable of achieving measurable gains within a relatively short time frame while promoting sustainable practices to support long-term school improvement.

The evidence emerging from NSLIP schools has provided one of the strongest arguments for sustained intervention.

In the 2025 Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) examinations, all 56 schools participating in NSLIP recorded improvement in English A, while 41 recorded improvement in mathematics, with several schools demonstrating dramatic gains.

Among the schools reporting improvement was Edwin Allen High School in Clarendon, which was placed under NSLIP after its CSEC mathematics performance declined to 25.4 per cent passes in 2024.

Following the targeted intervention, the school’s CSEC mathematics performance increased to 74.1 per cent passes in 2025.

Jermain Harris, principal of Edwin Allen, said he worked closely with the vice-principal of programmes, the head of the Mathematics Department, and the Ministry of Education’s mathematics specialists to ensure that the curriculum delivery was aligned with the CSEC mathematics syllabus and that curriculum pacing was closely monitored.

“Teachers used assessment data to identify priority content areas and adjusted instruction to meet students’ learning needs.

“To increase students’ exposure to quality instruction, the school implemented an extensive programme of extended learning, which included morning intervention classes before the start of the regular school day, afternoon classes conducted after the scheduled timetable, Saturday mathematics classes, mathematics camps during school breaks, and mathematics marathons to provide intensive revision and examination preparation,” Harris said.

“These interventions enabled teachers to revisit difficult concepts, address learning gaps, provide individualised support, and reinforce key mathematical skills. To promote a culture of excellence and continuous improvement, the school also introduced an incentive programme for both teachers and students,” added Harris.

He said students were recognised and rewarded for attendance, improvement, and academic achievement, while teachers were acknowledged for exceptional commitment, innovative instructional practices, and improvements in student performance.

“These incentives contributed to increased motivation, accountability, and ownership of the intervention programme,” declared Harris.

At St Thomas Technical, which posted a pass rate of 33.2 per cent in English A in 2024, the score was doubled to 67.4 per cent in 2025.

In addition, the school, which struggled with 6.9 per cent passes in mathematics in 2024, improved to 22.8 per cent in 2025.

“It was important for us, first, to critically address the whole issue of discipline,” said Principal Rochelle Taylor Brown.

“So we instituted a School Wide Positive Behaviour Intervention and Support Framework to promote positive behaviour, improve student discipline, and create a safe and orderly learning environment.

“Specific students received lunch and ‘shout out’ during general assembly, and the best class received a free field trip,” added Taylor Brown.

She said Alternative Pathways to Secondary Education (APSE) coaches — specialist educators supporting students requiring additional academic, behavioural or learning interventions — were engaged to bolster curriculum delivery for English A.

“The APSE coaches, who are one branch of the English language officer support team, provide support to teachers to better equip them to deliver high-quality instruction and increased student engagement. These officers conducted training sessions and collaborative lesson planning with the teachers, assisting them in interpreting assessment data for better placement of students.

“They also created intervention programmes for students who were deemed as ‘critical’ — those who were either performing or reading below their grade level,” said Taylor Brown.

She said the school’s improvement in mathematics, “though we must get better, was as a result of increasing the five periods [two hours and 55 minutes of teaching and learning time] for students to nine periods [five hours and 15 minutes)”.

Meanwhile, Charlie Smith High School moved dramatically from a 13.1 pass rate in English A in 2024 to 75 per cent in 2025, with its maths score shifting from 8.8 per cent to 18.2 per cent over the period.

“To break the cycle of underperformance we prioritised high-yield, research-backed interventions. The High-Dosage Tutoring method was applied, where students identified as critically underperforming received 45 minutes of small-group tutoring [3:1 ratio] three times a week. Research shows this is the single most effective tool for learning recovery,” said Principal Christopher Wright.

“The Tiered Response to Intervention Framework was, therefore, adopted: Tier 1 – high-quality, differentiated core instruction; Tier 2 – small-group targeted remediation; and Tier 3 – intensive, one-on-one specialist intervention. Importantly, we integrated local culture, music, and social justice topics into the academic content to dramatically increase engagement and relevance for our inner-city youth,” added Wright.

He argued that accountability in a rising inner-city school such as Charlie Smith High must be transparent, data-driven, and supportive.

“As a result, we have established a tripartite monitoring matrix. There is the Live Data Wall & Dashboard, where we use a digital student achievement dashboard that tracks real-time data from formative and summative assessments. Student progress is colour-coded, allowing us to spot regressions instantly.

“Teacher Performance Portfolio and Reflections is another highlighted area, where teachers maintain digital portfolios that map lesson plans against student mastery data. Finally, there is the Data-Driven Dialogue Meeting, where every three weeks I meet with grade-level teams for data dialogues. In these meetings, teachers must present their class data, identify students who are lagging, and detail the specific reteaching strategies they will employ,” said Wright.

Among the other secondary schools at which the NSLIP was implemented, which recorded improved performances in English A, were Bustamante High School, which moved from 12.1 per cent passes in 2024 to 51.9 per cent in 2025; Fair Prospect High School, which jumped from 9.5 per cent to 73.7 per cent; and Greater Portmore High School, which improved from 21.3 per cent to 78 per cent.

World.title: BRIGHT START
World.content:
Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls celebrate during netball competition at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, England, at which they won the silver medal.

Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls opened their Commonwealth Games netball campaign with an emphatic 81-22 win over Trinidad and Tobago at the Hydro Arena in Glasgow, Scotland, on Saturday.

The Sunshine Girls will be aiming for back-to-back wins today when they take on New Zealand in Pool B, after the Silver Ferns beat Scotland 74-44 in their opening game.

Led by 33 goals from 41 attempts from UK-based Azara Wilmot on her senior team debut, the Jamaicans dominated a young Trinidad and Tobago team.

Meanwhile, Sabrina Lyn qualified for today’s final of the women’s 100m breaststroke, while Jamaica’s 3×3 men’s basketball team won one of their three games.

Also today, Martez Cope will make his first appearance of the Games when he takes on Lesotho’s Pooana Khoahli in their men’s 65kg round-of-16 boxing contest.

At the Hydro Arena yesterday, Jamaica’s netball Captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey was pleased with the team’s execution after they restricted Trinidad and Tobago to a Commonwealth Games low in scoring.

Sterling-Humphrey said they had planned to stifle the Trinidadians’ offence and restrict their scoring chances.

“I’m really, really proud. I feel like each quarter we had a target,” she said after the match. “We started off at five, and then we lowered it. Unfortunately, they got, I think, seven in the second, but yeah, it’s good to keep them at two [in the final quarter] and know that we’re on target.”

Sterling-Humphrey said they were well aware of the advantage they had over their opponents and wanted to use the game as preparation for tougher matches.

“The emphasis lies on keeping possession of the ball. We cannot have that much turnovers when we come up against teams like Trinidad, because when it comes to the harder games, it will be much more difficult for us.”

The number-three-ranked Jamaicans led 24-5 after the first quarter, 43-12 at half-time and 60-20 after the third quarter before emptying the bench in the fourth, which they took 17-8.

The Jamaican defence also had 35 interceptions and 22 deflections, compared to four and seven, respectively, by their opponents.

Wilmot, who came off the bench in the second quarter, led the scoring with 33 goals from 41 attempts on her senior team debut.

Veteran Romelda Aiken-George scored 25 goals from 27 attempts, while Shanice Beckford converted all 16 of her attempts and Rhea Dixon scored seven from 11 attempts.

Afeisha Noel scored 17 of Trinidad and Tobago’s goals from 19 attempts, with Joelisa Cooper scoring the other five from seven attempts.

Lyn became the first Jamaican swimmer to reach a final after finishing fifth in her semi-final in 1:08.43 minutes at the Tollcross swimming centre. She had placed fourth in her first-round race in 1:09.11.

Lyn was also part of the Jamaican mixed 4x100m relay team that placed third in its first-round heat in 3:43.07, teaming with Collin McKenzie, Kito Campbell and Jessica Calderbank.

Today, Lyn and Calderbank will contest the women’s 100m butterfly, while McKenzie and Campbell are set to swim in the men’s 50m breaststroke.

The Jamaican men’s 3×3 basketball team beat Singapore 22-20 but lost 22-16 to England and 21-13 to Fiji in their opening games.

Also on Saturday, Jamaica’s Robert Simpson lost his third straight match in lawn bowls, going down 2-0 to Wales’ Ross Owen in the men’s singles.

Simpson is set to face England’s Sam Tolchard today and will complete his schedule on Monday against Pakistan’s Mohammed Ayub Qureshi.

World.title: Woman among three fatally shot by police in Mandeville shootout
World.content:
MANCHESTER, Jamaica — Police have confirmed that a woman is among three people who were fatally shot during an alleged shootout on Caledonia Road in Mandeville Saturday afternoon.

Preliminary reports are that about 4:00 pm, police were alerted to a robbery spree and subsequently intercepted a getaway vehicle near Horseshoe Curve.

A highly placed police source said the occupants of the intercepted vehicle opened fire on the cops who then returned fire. A shootout ensued resulting in a prolonged standoff and running gun battle.

Police said a woman and two men were taken from the intercepted vehicle and taken to hospital where they were pronounced dead on arrival.

The incident happened in the vicinity of last Saturday’s double murder where nursing student Deenekia Pounall and Sadefa Henry were gunned down in a taxi by a gunman who posed as a passenger.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: MegaMart Catherine Hall property goes on sale for US$15 million
World.content:
The former MegaMart Catherine Hall location is on sale for US$15 million.

The property that once housed MegaMart’s Montego Bay operations has gone on sale for US$15.09 million, or $2.41 billion, nearly eight months following the impact of Hurricane Melissa on western Jamaica.

Cost Club Limited, trading as Megamart Wholesale Club, occupied the 89,674 square feet property since December 2007 when it first opened to customers in western Jamaica. However, the location was closed following the devastation caused by the Category 5 storm which flooded the location and left substantial damage.

The former Catherine Hall location is being offered on an ‘as-is’ basis, with realtor REMAX Elite Realty indicating that the property could be used for a range of commercial uses.

The property and building is being sold by Wilco Ltd which acquired the property in April 2015 for US$1.05 million ($119.63 million). The location was developed at a cost of US$20 million ($1.3 billion).

The MegaMart Catherine Hall and Portmore properties were sold to a group of pension funds in 2013 as part of a sale and leaseback transaction that was arranged by Scotia Investments Jamaica Limited (SIJL). That deal, which was reportedly valued at $2.3 billion, resulted in MegaMart maintaining operations at both locations and receiving cash from the transaction, but paying a monthly lease cost under a 15 year lease arrangement.

The Portmore location closed on June 30, 26 years after it opened in September 1999. The loss-making location was effectively subsidised by the operations of the Catherine Hall location. The closure of both locations resulted in the loss of more than 300 jobs as Cost Club undergoes a strategic consolidation for its remaining two locations.

The Portmore property was transferred in January 2013 for $1.05 billion. The owner is listed as Scotia Investments Jamaica on the property title, but transfer documents lists the National Insurance Fund (NIF), SIJL NCB Insurance Company Limited, Montego Bay I.T. Centre Limited, Grace, Kennedy & Co. Limited Pension Scheme, Jamaica Money Market Brokers Limited (JMMB) and Appliance Traders Group Pension Scheme as paying a transfer tax. The future of this property is unknown at this time.

Scojampen Limited, The Bank of Nova Scotia Pension Fund, owns the MegaMart Mandeville location while Lord Nelson Investment Limited owns the Waterloo Road location in St Andrew.

World.title: Cape Verde star goalkeeper Vozinha heads to Chile
World.content:
Cape Verde’s goalkeeper Vozinha celebrates with his national flag after their 1-1 draw with Spain during the FIFA World Cup. (Photo: AFP)

SANTIAGO, Chile (AFP) — Vozinha, the 40-year-old goalkeeper who was one of the heroes of Cape Verde’s fairytale run at the World Cup, is signing for Colo Colo, the Chilean club announced.

“Vozinha is set to become a Colo Colo player; he will arrive in Chile in the coming days, undergo the necessary medical tests and will then be presented here at the Monumental Stadium,” club president Anibal Mosa told reporters ahead of a league match on Friday evening.

Vozinha starred at the World Cup with heroic displays in a 0-0 group-stage draw against eventual champions Spain and in a 3-2 extra-time loss to finalists Argentina in the knock-out rounds.

The goalie, whose full name is Josimar Jose Evora Dias, will move to Chile from Chaves of the Portuguese second division. Although he did not sign his first professional contract until he was 26, he has also played in Cyprus, Slovakia, Moldova and Angola.

“He’s in very good form; that’s why we’re signing him,” said Mosa.

Vozinha has also become a social media star, with help from Brazilian influencer Casimiro. The goalkeeper’s Instagram following has soared from 50,000 to nearly 30 million.

Colo Colo, 34-time Chilean champions, hold a comfortable lead in the table midway through the current season.

World.title: The Pentagon wants to build data centers. Congress would like a word.
World.content:
“The answer to this may be yes, may be no,” said Garamendi, ranking member of the House Armed Services Subcommittee on Readiness.

DOD officials and some congressional conservatives are pushing back, saying the military has already accounted for the impact of data centers. They also warn restriction would create a drag for military innovation at a time when the Pentagon is scrambling to stay competitive in the AI arms race.

But despite the administration’s resistance, some proposals are advancing and could become law as part of broader legislative battles over how to regulate the data center boom.

In many cases, lawmaker proposals addressing DOD data centers don’t seek to shut down the build-out. Most of them would simply require studies, evaluations or additional planning that would force the Pentagon to take into account — and be transparent about — proposed data centers’ consumption of energy and water, as well as the impacts they could have on local communities and the environment.

“Members ... understandably want to ensure there is careful consideration of impacts to local residents with regards to potential strain on the power grid and water supplies,” Rep. Ken Calvert (R-Calif.), chair of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, said in a statement.

The military’s data center drive gained momentum last year with President Donald Trump’s executive order directing the agency to identify suitable sites on military installations for AI infrastructure. The order required EPA and the White House’s Council on Environmental Quality to take steps to support data center construction.

World.title: Berlin police hunt suspect in attack on pride parade that left 1 dead
World.content:
Police are seen at the scene of the attack during CSD pride. | Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images

Manhunt is under way for the suspected attacker, who is considered “to be part of Berlin’s Islamist scene,” according to police.

A man drove a van into a crowd at Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade late Saturday, killing at least one person and injuring others.

Berlin police told POLITICO Sunday morning that one person was killed and 25 others were injured in the attack, some of them severely.

Police also said the suspect, identified as 21-year-old Abdul B., was “known to the police” before and is considered “to be part of Berlin’s Islamist scene.”

World.title: Romanian airspace violated by drones twice in 2 days
World.content:
Romanian Air Force F-16 fighter jets waiting for an aerial refueling, while they participate in an exercice. | Clement Mahoudeau/AFP via Getty Images

Romanian fighter jets shot down drones in separate incidents on Friday and Saturday.

Romanian fighter jets on Friday and Saturday morning shot down two drones that were violating the country's airspace.

On Saturday morning, Romanian radar "detected another unauthorized penetration of the national airspace by a drone operating in the vicinity of the Ukrainian border" and two Romanian F-16 jets shot it down in an unpopulated area close to the border, the Romanian defense ministry said in a statement. Romania already shot down another drone on Friday.

Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said that the drone shot down on Friday "was a Shahed-type drone, the same kind Russia launches, night after night, against Ukraine."

"Two incursions in 48 hours are not an accident, they are a pattern, and our answer to that pattern is consistency: detection, interception, protection of our citizens, full transparency with our allies," Toiu said.

In a social media post, European Council President António Costa "commend[ed] the Romanian authorities for their swift and effective response."

World.title: Record-breaking wildfires burned nearly 100,000 hectares in France, interior minister says
World.content:
Nearly 200,000 people have been evacuated because of the fires in southwestern France out of which more than 167,000 are in Gironde, the department of Bordeaux, and around 30,000 in the nearby Landes department.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday announced that he requested the activation of an EU emergency mechanism, which has prompted other EU countries including Portugal, Croatia, Slovakia and Sweden to send airplanes and helicopters to help France.

"Europe stands with France and Spain against the devastating wildfires that are hitting them," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote in a social media post on Saturday, stressing that France is already benefitting from five planes and two helicopters provided by other EU countries while four planes will arrive in Spain on Saturday.

France's Nuñez confirmed that Saturday afternoon an Airbus A400 military plane will start throwing a fire retardant product at the wildfires. That is on the top of Canadair and other French and European aircraft.

The wildfires have been the subject of political controversy in France in recent days, with both the hard-left France Unbowed and the far-right National Rally accusing Macron of underinvesting.

Spain has declared the state of emergency in the Madrid and Ávila regions.

"Our priority is to save lives, protect communities, and fight the fires," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Saturday. Around 80,000 people have been evacuated or are confined because of the wildfires, Spanish media report.

World.title: Italy’s defense minister offered adviser job to ousted Ukrainian defense chief
World.content:
The Italian minister said Fedorov was "moved" by the proposal and saw it as "a mark of respect and friendship," but he didn't elaborate on whether Fedorov accepted or not.

Crosetto strongly praised Fedorov, who has been credited with bringing a technology overhaul to Ukraine's military but also clashed with top generals.

“Fedorov embodies innovation; he is one of those who has completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield, enabling Ukraine first to hold its ground and then to take the initiative,” Crosetto said, adding that Fedorov was faced with "a resistance to change" that is also a problem in Italy, France and Germany.

Fedorov hasn't responded publicly to Crosetto's offer.

Crosetto, who is a top figure in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, also made clear that he is in favor of continuing to borrow via EU loans from the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme rather than financing defense spending through national public debt. But he made clear that it was up for the Treasury to make that decision.

Crosetto's comments come as the Italian government is mulling applying for only €5 billion to €7 billion under the SAFE scheme, instead of €15 billion, as initially planned.

World.title: NATO intern arrested over espionage suspicions
World.content:
The Canadian national of Chinese origin is suspected of spying for a third country and being part of a criminal organization.

Belgian police on Friday arrested an intern at NATO's strategic headquarters of the Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE,) suspecting her of "spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization," the Belgian Federal Prosecutor Office wrote in a statement on Saturday.

The intern, a Canadian national of Chinese origins, "had come to the attention" of the security services of SHAPE, NATO’s strategic command for operations in Mons, Belgium.

Belgian authorities searched her home and office on Thursday.

Belgian prosecutors gave no further details on what the woman is suspected of.

Camille Gijs contributed to this report.

World.title: Russian strikes across Ukraine kill at least eight over last 24 hours
World.content:
Russian strikes across Ukraine have killed at least eight people and injured dozens more over the last 24 hours.

 

On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one person was killed and nine were wounded in a drone attack on the northeastern city of Kharkiv.

"All the necessary emergency services have been deployed at the site," Zelenskyy said, adding that residential buildings had been hit.

In the Dnipropetrovsk region, two women aged 35 and 74 were killed after Russia struck three districts in the area with drones, artillery, and aerial bombs on Saturday, per local authorities.

One person died and 12 were hurt after further Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia Oblast in southeastern Ukraine.

Ivan Fedorov, the head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, said on Sunday morning that Russian forces had launched 1,029 strikes on 50 settlements in the region over the last day.

On Sunday, Fedorov said there were reports of another fatality following a Russian attack.

Another two people were reportedly killed and 24 were injured in Kherson Oblast this weekend.

"Russian forces struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential areas in the region’s settlements; in particular, they damaged 18 high-rise blocks and 17 private houses," Oleksandr Prokudin, who heads the Kherson Regional Military Administration, wrote in a post on Telegram. "The occupiers also destroyed a church, a petrol station, shops, gas pipelines, a farm building, private garages and cars".

In Sumy Oblast in northern Ukraine, a 53-year-old man was killed and eight people were wounded following Russian attacks.

It comes as Ukrainian authorities reported a hit on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih on Sunday. A fire reportedly broke out at an Epitsentr DIY store following the strike.

Kazakh leader calls for end to war

Kazakhstan's President Qasym-Jomart Toqayev on Saturday reportedly told his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin that he should end his war in Ukraine.

"It is a shame, young people are dying... All this has to be stopped," Tokayev said, per AFP.

Responding to the news on social media, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked Toqayev for his "realistic, timely, and wise message."

"Ukraine has proposed stopping the war along current frontlines and turning to diplomacy, but the Kremlin continues to reject this clear path to peace," Sybiha said in a statement posted to X.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov had already pushed back at Tokayev's comments, telling Interfax earlier on Saturday that it was "impossible" to "freeze" the war at the current time.

North Korea

Zelenskyy also warned in a video address on Saturday evening that Moscow was pushing for North Korea to send another 30,000 troops to support the Russian war effort in Ukraine.

Russian, left, and North Korea's servicemen attend the Victory Day military parade in Moscow, Saturday, May 9, 2026. AP photo

The Ukrainian leader said Russia has been making preparations to receive them in the Voronezh region since June and that Pyongyang was also looking to deliver additional launchers for ballistic missiles.

"This is a threat not only to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "Russia is helping North Korea learn how to wage war, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience in using them. All of this is a threat to everyone in Asia who is within range of North Korean missiles".

North Korea has been providing troops to support Russia's full-scale invasion since the autumn of 2024, when they were first deployed in Russia's Kursk Oblast.

World.title: Eurostar is launching a new direct route from London to Antwerp this December
World.content:
Planning to see Belgium beyond Brussels? Eurostar is launching its first direct London to Antwerp service this winter.

 

From 14 December, the high-speed rail service will operate four scheduled direct services from London St. Pancras to the Belgian port city daily.

Eurostar already connects Londoners to Belgium via its Brussels-bound route, with travellers keen to explore beyond the capital into a city like Antwerp having to alight at Brussels-Midi/Zuid to catch a SNCB train to Antwerpen-Centraal.

This current journey takes around 3 hours and 15 minutes. The new direct service will cut travel time to just 2 hours and 41 minutes.

However, there are currently no plans to introduce direct return routes.

This is because there are no dedicated UK border and customs facilities at Antwerpen-Centraal, Eurostar told Head for Points.

What to do in Antwerp

Often overlooked in favour of Brussels or Bruges, Antwerp is known for two things: fashion and diamonds.

The former is thanks to the Antwerp Six, who soared to fame in the 1980s and 1990s. You can learn all about them at the ModeMuseum Antwerpen, but if you want to shop from the city’s up-and-coming designers, you can head to Nationalestraa or Kammenstraat.

As for the latter, Antwerp’s diamond district is the largest in the world, with some 50% of the globe’s rough diamonds passing through here for polishing, making it perfect for anyone looking to accessorise their new look with some bling.

Belgium in general is known for its fries, known locally as frîtes, and there’s no better place to grab them than Frituur LO. To get your fix, you’ll need to pass through Sint-Anna’s Tunnel, which in itself is an experience as it’s home to authentic wooden escalators.

As we all know, nothing quite beats Belgian chocolate, and no trip is complete without sampling and having the willpower to bring some back home, too. At Pierre Marcolini's Antwerp branch, the quaint store pays homage to the Belgian chocolatier while offering visitors a selection of chocolates, truffles, biscuits, macarons, ice cream, and other confectionery as far as the eye can see.

For a different perspective of the city, Visit Antwerp also recommends heading out after dark when landmarks such as Centraal Station, Operaplein and the lively Het Zuid district are illuminated. Not only is it a chance to see Antwerp with reduced crowds as the city sleeps, but it also offers a striking look once night falls.

World.title: Pedro Sánchez: "The scale of the disaster we are living through is very hard to accept"
World.content:
Water Matters

Europe's water is under increasing pressure. Pollution, droughts, floods are taking their toll on our drinking water, lakes, rivers and coastlines. Join us on a journey around Europe to see why protecting ecosystems matters, how our wastewater can be better managed, and to discover some of the best water solutions. Video reports, an animated explainer series and live debate - find out why Water Matters, from Euronews.

World.title: Italy petrol tops €2.6: opposition and groups sound alarm, govt weighs variable fuel duty
World.content:
Fuel prices for petrol and diesel are once again causing concern in Italy. On Saturday in Milan, a price of €2.6 per litre for petrol was recorded at a filling station in the city centre. While opposition parties accuse the government of not having done enough to prevent a new economic crisis, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Minister for Business and Made in Italy Adolfo Urso are working on new measures to keep petrol prices in check.

 

Fuel prices in Italy have been rising since 3 July, when the cut in excise duties introduced by the government at the outbreak of the war between the US and Iran to tackle the price emergency came to an end. On Sunday, the ministry headed by Urso reported that, according to the latest data collected by the Fuel Price Observatory, the average price in "self-service" mode on the national road network stands at €1.981 per litre for petrol and €2.184 per litre for diesel. On the motorway network, meanwhile, the average self-service price is €2.071 per litre for petrol and €2.255 per litre for diesel.

Prices at the pump, however, rise significantly. According to local sources, on Saturday prices of over €2.7 per litre for diesel and €2.5 per litre for petrol were recorded on the A21 Turin-Piacenza, A4 Venice-Trieste, A22 Brenner-Modena motorways, and on the Milan-Brescia and Messina-Palermo routes. In Rome, several filling stations reached €2.3 per litre for petrol.

The alarm raised by associations and consumers

Consumer organisations have also sounded the alarm over the increases. According to Codacons, Italians' spending on fuel will reach €10.8 billion, almost €2 billion more than in 2025.

"The comparison with last year is merciless: with consumption unchanged and taking into account the average monthly price of fuels in July 2025, by the end of the month Italians will spend an impressive €841 million more solely on purchases of petrol and diesel than in the same period in 2025," Codacons explained in a statement released on Saturday.

At the same time, the research office of the Cgia di Mestre has estimated that in 2026 households and businesses will face almost €29 billion in additional costs for electricity, gas and fuels. Petrol and diesel show the largest increase, with extra spending of €13.6 billion, up 20.4% on 2025.

Government measures under review and opposition criticism

The government is looking at measures to reduce the impact of soaring fuel prices, including a variable excise duty mechanism that would allow prices to fall in line with the higher VAT revenue collected as prices rise. "To activate this system, we first need to wait for the Economy Ministry's calculations on the month's surplus VAT revenue, which will only be available next week and will determine the scale of the possible cut," he said in an interview with Corriere della Sera, and added: "The surplus VAT takings could be used to offset a reduction in excise duty, while any further measures would require additional funding".

The minister then defended the government's action against speculation, arguing that the Italian model of price control is being emulated by other countries and that thanks to this system fuel prices in Italy have risen less than elsewhere.

The opposition has called on the government to adopt more substantial measures to help citizens. "Meloni should now at least accept our proposal on variable excise duties, which would allow the price of petrol and diesel to be cut immediately. After all, those who once promised to abolish excise duties altogether, how can they now oppose this measure?" said Democratic Party secretary Elly Schelein.

"What we need here are serious measures, and we must act fast and invest to protect families and businesses: when will we start drawing resources from the windfall profits of banks, energy giants and the arms industry? When from the state's extra takings generated by the various price hikes and by the crazy spending on rearmament? When will we go to Europe and demand massive investment in an industrial and energy relaunch strategy, as we did during the pandemic with the NRRP? The country needs to be lifted up again and citizens need some breathing space. Enough with the whistling," Five Star Movement leader Giuseppe Conte wrote on social media.

World.title: 'Sea cannibal' spreads across the Baltic, threatening native species
World.content:
A species that resembles a jellyfish but, unlike a jellyfish, has no stinging cells reached Europe in the 1980s. As W.M. Graham and K.M. Bayha point out in the bookBiological Invasions by Marine Jellyfish (source in Polish), it was carried there by ships calling at Black Sea ports from the Atlantic coasts of North and South America. It soon became one of the dominant organisms in those waters.

 

In 1988, at the height of the invasion, the density of Mnemiopsis leidyi reached as many as 400 individuals per cubic metre. Shortly afterwards, however, as it consumed huge quantities of zooplankton, its main source of food, the comb jelly's population began to decline.

In the Baltic Sea this species has not yet reached such high numbers, but the latest research indicates that its spread is accelerating. One of the factors that may be aiding its expansion is the growth of oxygen-depleted zones, also referred to as oxygen deserts.

"Sea cannibal"

This remarkable invertebrate, which – as described, among other places, in an article published in Tutoring Gedanensis (source in Polish) – is capable of bioluminescence, poses a serious threat to fisheries. Species such as sprats and sardines are particularly at risk, because the comb jelly feeds on their eggs and larvae, thereby reducing the size of future fish stocks.

Studies have also shown that Mnemiopsis leidyi consumes vast amounts of zooplankton, competing for food with many other marine organisms and disrupting the ecosystem's natural balance.

What is more, this species has developed a unique survival strategy. When food resources begin to run out, the comb jelly is able to eat its own larvae, and adult individuals produce large numbers of eggs which, in periods of food shortage, can serve as an additional source of energy. This specific form of cannibalism allows it to survive even under unfavourable conditions.

It thrives best, however, in shallow, warm, nutrient-rich coastal waters.

In new ecosystems the comb jelly often encounters no natural enemies that could effectively keep its numbers in check. In the Baltic the situation is somewhat different: there is a species that can prey on the comb jelly's larvae. The problem is that ongoing environmental change is weakening this natural control mechanism.

Natural enemies

In January 2026 the journal Journal of Plankton Research (source in Polish)published the resuts of a study indicating that the three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus), native to the Baltic Sea, may act as a natural enemy of the comb jelly because it feeds on its larvae.

The latest observations, however, show that increasing hypoxia – a drop in the oxygen content of the water that leads to the formation of so-called dead zones – is limiting the activity of sticklebacks and reducing the extent of their feeding on comb jellylarvae.

This means that the invasive invertebrate's success in expanding its range depends not only on rising water temperatures linked to climate change, but also on the progressive loss of habitats suitable for its natural enemies.

Paradoxically, climate change is also contributing to a fall in the salinity of the Baltic Sea. This is not unequivocally beneficial for Mnemiopsis leidyi, because the species thrives best in waters with slightly higher salinity. The complexity of the processes taking place in the Baltic means that predicting future changes remains a major challenge for scientists.

An ecosystem under pressure: the Baltic in transition

The appearance of the "sea cannibal" is just one of many signals indicating that the Baltic Sea ecosystem is under severe pressure. In recent years scientists have observed, among other things, the growth of oxygen deserts, record fluctuations in water levels and increasingly frequent phenomena associated with climate change.

These processes are affecting living conditions for native species and may facilitate the expansion of alien organisms that are better adapted to the new environmental conditions.

However, not every alien species necessarily poses a threat to the Baltic ecosystem. Some of them gradually become part of the local web of interactions, and some may even increase biological diversity.

One example is the American crab, which has become an important source of food for cod, flounder and waterbirds, and the sand-burrowing clam małgiew piaskołaz – a species that buries itself deep in bottom sediments, where it helps to loosen them and improve their oxygenation.

The Baltic Sea therefore remains a dynamic and sensitive ecosystem in which natural processes are increasingly intertwined with the effects of human activity and global climate change.

World.title: Romanian forces shoot down third drone in three days
World.content:
A third drone has been shot down by Romanian forces in just three days, Romanian President Nicușor Dan has announced, adding to a string of drone-related incidents in the country.

 

In a statement on social media, Dan said a Romanian air force F-16 fighter jet had intercepted a drone over Romania's territorial waters at around 10:13 am on Sunday morning. The incident reportedly occurred in the Sulina–Chilia area of the Danube Delta, close to the border with Ukraine.

"I would like to congratulate the Romanian pilots and ground crews on the professionalism, courage and efficiency with which they carry out their missions," Dan wrote on X.

Romanian authorities reported that an F-16 shot down another unmanned aerial vehicle on Saturday morning, roughly 10 km west of the village of Sfântu Gheorghe in eastern Romania.

Two jets were scrambled to identify and intercept the target, and the drone was "safely shot down in an unpopulated area near the border," the Romanian Defence Ministry said in a statement on Saturday.

A third drone was shot down by a Romanian F-16 at around 11 am on Friday.

The Romanian Prosecutor General's Office has determined that the drone intercepted on Friday was of the Shahed-type used by Russian forces in its war against Ukraine, Romanian officials have said.

While investigations into the drones shot down on Saturday and Sunday are still ongoing, Dan said it was "intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace."

"Such actions are unacceptable and we are treating them with the utmost seriousness, alongside our allies," he added.

Romania's growing drone problem

Situated on NATO's eastern flank and on the shores of the Black Sea, Romania is particularly vulnerable to security challenges arising from Russia's war against Ukraine, which began after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022.

A small military patrol boat sails past the Romanian frigate Marasesti docked in the military port of Constanta following the explosion of a maritime drone. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Bucharest has seen a surge in drone-related incidents and incursions into Romanian airspace in recent months, prompting officials to pledge heightened security measures across the country.

In May, a Russian drone carrying explosives crashed into an apartment block in Galați, sparking a fire on the roof and injuring two people.

The following month, a Ukrainian sea drone also exploded in the Romanian port of Constanta. The Ukrainian military said it had veered off course as a result of Russian electronic warfare interference.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has labelled such incidents "a direct consequence of Russia’s war against Ukraine."

World.title: Car rams crowd at Berlin Pride event, killing one and injuring 16
World.content:
A car ploughed into a crowd celebrating Berlin's Christopher Street Day Pride event on Saturday night, killing one person and leaving at least 16 others injured.

 

The incident occurred at around 10 pm. Three people remain in a life-threatening condition.

According to initial information, a vehicle drove into a crowd on Lennéstrasse. The car then collided with a tree before the suspect apparently managed to flee.

Berlin police have since announced that they had identified a suspect who they said is "known to the police" and "believed to be associated with Islamist circles."

Police have released a photo of the suspect and named him as 21-year-old Abdul B.

Image released by Berlin police Polizei Berlin

They warned people not to approach him as he may be "armed and dangerous."

"What a despicable act in Berlin," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote in a statement published on social media.

"Hundreds of thousands of people from all over the world were celebrating peacefully at Christopher Street Day. They wanted us to treat one another with kindness and tolerance," he said. "This is an attack on our society".

The Pride parade was cancelled after the incident.

World.title: Revealed: Italy’s most popular beaches for 2026 – and Sardinia dominates
World.content:
Summer in Italy is practically synonymous with beach days – and with thousands of kilometres of coastline to choose from, the hardest part is deciding where to lay your towel.

 

From glamorous stretches of sand to hidden coves and crystal-clear waters, the country is home to some seriously spectacular seaside spots.

But which beaches are attracting the most attention right now?

Travel booking platform Holidu has crunched Google Maps data and reviews to reveal the 30 most popular beaches in Italy for 2026.

While the list features much of Italy’s coastline, it’s Sardinia’s beaches that are far and away the most popular in the ranking. In fact, 20 of the island’s beaches made the top 30.

Interestingly, the top five ranked beaches stayed in exactly the same position as in last year’s list, meaning they’ve maintained their quality.

From famous favourites to lesser-known gems, these are the Italian beaches set to be on everyone’s radar this summer.

The top five best beaches in Italy now

Rabbit Beach, Lampedusa, Sicily

This world-famous beach on the island of Lampedusa scored 4.9 out of five in Google Maps reviews, meaning it’s really rather special.

Rabbit Beach is widely considered one of Italy’s most beautiful beaches – and it’s not hard to see why. Tucked away in crystal-clear Mediterranean waters, the beach is known for its powdery white sands, turquoise sea and untouched natural surroundings.

Rugged cliffs and lush greenery frame the shoreline, giving the beach an idyllic, almost otherworldly feel. Its name comes from the wild rabbits that once lived in the area, although these days it’s the scenery that draws visitors from around the world.

Regularly ranked among the best beaches on the planet, Rabbit Beach is the perfect spot for those looking to experience the Sicily region at its most spectacular.

Cala Mariolu, Baunei, Sardinia

Following hot on Rabbit Island’s heels is this breathtaking spot in Sardinia, which scores 4.8 out of five in Google Maps reviews.

Cala Mariolu is one of Sardinia’s most famous beaches, often named among the world’s best, offering dramatic scenery and a secluded feel.

Tucked away on the island’s eastern coast, the small cove can only be reached by boat or via hiking trails, making getting there part of the adventure.

Rugged cliffs and lush greenery surround the beach, while the water shifts from deep sapphire to bright aquamarine around the pristine white pebbles.

For the best views, hike up the surrounding cliffs and look down over the cove – the contrast between the vivid blue sea and white shoreline is seriously spectacular.

The blue waters of Tuerredda beach are exceptionally clear and ideal for snorkeling Andrea Mancini/Unsplash

Tuerredda Beach, Teulada, Sardinia

In the south of Sardinia, you’ll find Tuerredda Beach, a spot often compared to the Caribbean thanks to its fine white sand and exceptionally clear blue waters.

Scoring 4.7 out of five in the Google Maps review ranking, the beach looks out towards the tiny islet of Tuerredda, just a few hundred metres from the shore and covered in fragrant Mediterranean scrub. You can swim or snorkel across the shallow, gently sloping seabed, or spend a few hours relaxing on the warm rocks and sand.

The coastline is a mix of soft sandy stretches and rugged rock formations, with smaller coves dotted between them.

The surrounding waters are home to plenty of marine life, while the islet itself attracts seabirds and other wildlife, making it well worth exploring beyond the main beach.

Is Arutas Beach, Cabras, Sardinia

Also scoring 4.7, Is Arutas is one of the most unusual beaches in Sardinia, known for its crystal-clear blue-green sea and distinctive grains of quartz that look almost like tiny grains of rice.

The sand is in shades of white, green and soft pink, creating a colourful shoreline unlike almost anywhere else on the island.

Set on the Sinis Peninsula, just over 10 kilometres from the town of Cabras, it’s an idyllic spot for a lazy day by the sea. Getting there takes you through the quiet village of San Salvatore, famous for its annual Corsa degli Scalzi – or Barefoot Race – and its starring role in several Spaghetti Westerns.

Porto Giunco is renowned for its shallow waters – and the possibility of spotting flamingos in the wild Divani/Unsplash

Porto Giunco ​​Beach, Villasimius, Sardinia

Another Sardinian beach to score 4.7 out of five, Porto Giunco is one of the best beaches in southern Sardinia, with white sand and vividly blue sea.

It sits in Villasimius, just over 40 kilometres from Cagliari, making it an easy choice for a day trip from the island's capital.

The beach is backed by the Notteri salt lagoon, where pink flamingos are often spotted wading through the shallow water. The sea is also relatively shallow, making it a good option for families, while the windier conditions attract surfers and windsurfers.

At one end of the beach, a rocky cape rises above the coastline, topped by a historic lookout tower with views across the surrounding landscape.

Porto Giunco can get busy in summer, but its long, wide stretch of sand means there's usually space to settle in. There are also plenty of facilities, including a beach bar, sun loungers and parasols.

Italy’s best beaches for 2026

The top 30 most popular Italian beaches for summer 2026, according to the Holidu research.

World.title: Israel's move to recognise Armenian genocide stalls under regional pressure
World.content:
The Israeli parliament's decision to postpone a vote on recognising the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey is being seen as a triumph for regional diplomacy, as Azerbaijan in particular seeks to avert a further escalation in tensions between its close allies.

Advertising

The Israeli government gave no official reason for postponing the vote to formally recognise the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey during World War I, which would have ratified a motion approved by the cabinet last month.

Ankara strongly denies the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Armenians constitute genocide.

While the motion's architect, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, called recognition a “moral duty”, critics say the move took aim at Turkey amidst rising tensions.

Based in Tbilisi, Israeli defence and security expert Eugene Kogan claims Israel badly miscalculated. “Foreign Minister Sa'ar could have waited and not just dropped a bomb that led to different repercussions coming from different sides,” he said.

Armenia, which is seeking to normalise ties with Turkey, reacted coolly, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan saying he saw no need to comment. Meanwhile, Israel’s close ally Azerbaijan reportedly lobbied Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drop the motion.

“At the end of the day, it might be either dropped or dismissed, and it will not come again to the new parliament agenda,” predicted Kogan.

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July and won't reconvene until after elections scheduled for 27 October.

Israel's recognition of the Armenian genocide unsettles Turkey and Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's influence

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that pressure from Azerbaijan tipped the scales, though officials deny it.

Azerbaijan supplies nearly 40 percent of Israel’s oil and is a major customer for Israeli arms. The two countries’ partnership involves frequent Israeli ministerial visits and strong military cooperation, especially crucial for Israel given Azerbaijan’s border with Iran.

Baku also maintains a deep alliance with Ankara, summed up in the phrase “one nation, two states”. As Israeli-Turkish tensions flare over the Gaza conflict and Ankara’s support for Hamas, Azerbaijan is walking a diplomatic tightrope.

Zaur Gasimov, a Caucasus expert at Istanbul’s Turkish-German University, believes Baku viewed the Israeli genocide motion as a direct threat to its difficult balancing act.

“I can imagine that there were negotiations and talks on various levels between political elites of both countries,” he said. “For Israel, Azerbaijan is still of paramount importance. I would even say it's much more significant than it used to be with regard to the situation in and around Iran. So Baku was and is maybe the key intermediary between Israel and the Republic of Turkey.”

In what may be a calculated move to turn up the heat on Israel, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev welcomed Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa this month. It was the first visit by a Palestinian leader since 2011.

“They [Israel] perceive it with a great sense of caution,” claimed analyst Kogan. “They don't know exactly what came out of this particular meeting between Aliyev and the Palestinian prime minister. And so there is a lot of guessing games right now taking place in both Tel Aviv and Jerusalem about the outcome.”

Such ambiguity over Baku’s intentions could strengthen its diplomatic hand, he suggested: “If Aliyev is involved in this Palestinian issue directly and no longer indirectly, it makes the situation very different for the Israelis.”

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Syrian precedent

Baku is already leveraging its strong relationships with both Israel and Turkey to cool tempers.

“We have organised meetings between Turkey and Israel in Baku, specifically at the very beginning of the change of the Assad regime in Syria, where both parties had their own legitimate concerns,” said Hikmet Hajiyev, chief foreign policy adviser to the Azerbaijani president.

Syria is viewed as a potential flashpoint, with Israel and Turkey having a military presence. One tangible outcome of Azeri-brokered talks was the establishment last year of a military hotline in Syria, providing a rare glimmer of hope as tensions continue to mount.

“It's not unavoidable that Israel and Turkey will reach confrontation. I think we can stop this process,” argued Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist in Turkish foreign policy at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies.

“They have a hotline between the Israeli Air Force and the Turkish Air Force, making sure that we will not have a collision in the skies of Syria, because we know both air forces are operating there. And the hotline has managed to keep the situation quiet. If I'm trying to find some anchor of reassurance that Turkish-Israeli relations can be controlled, it's Syria.”

As Israel approaches elections, a temporary lull in Turkish-Israeli tensions is anticipated. Still, since the main opposition shares the government’s concerns over Turkey, relations are set to remain fraught.

World.title: Can Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections calm tensions?
World.content:
Pakistan-administered Kashmir heads to the polls after weeks of deadly protests over seats reserved for displaced people from India-administered Kashmir. One local group has called for the elections to be boycotted.

The first phase of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir is scheduled for Monday, July 27, amid calls for a boycott from the recently outlawed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots alliance of civil society groups.

The JAAC has been demanding the abolition of 12 seats in the regional assembly reserved for people displaced from India-administered Kashmir and living in Pakistan. The group argues that only residents of Pakistan-administered Kashmir should be eligible to contest regional elections.

The dispute escalated after the Supreme Court of Pakistan-administered Kashmir ruled that the refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

The regional government outlawed the JAAC in June under anti-terrorism laws, citing threats to public order, and detained dozens of its supporters.

The ban came amid rising tensions over the refugee seats and ahead of violent protests sparked by the group's campaign to scrap them.

The unrest has left around 30 people dead since June, according to local estimates cited by Reuters news agency.

India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir in its entirety, but each country only controls a section of the territory, making the Muslim-majority region a longstanding flash point between the nuclear-armed neighbors since their independence from Britain in 1947.

Protests cast shadow over vote

Since early June, Pakistan-administered Kashmir — known locally as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — has witnessed weeks of protests and sit-ins. While the dispute over the refugee seats has become a major issue, JAAC has also campaigned for broader economic and governance reforms.

Following the unrest, authorities split polling into three phases, with voting in Mirpur set for July 27 and elections in the protest-hit Poonch division postponed until August 10.

Voting in the regional capital, Muzaffarabad, has been delayed until August 2 over security concerns. The JAAC continues to stage a sit-in in Rawalakot, near the Line of Control with India.

Demand for fair representation

A major question is whether the elections can restore public confidence or merely offer a temporary pause in public anger.

"We are just asking for fair representation, which is our right," Ali Raza, a 22-year-old student protester in Rawalakot, told DW. "The local people who live here should have the right to choose their representatives, not the refugees who settled here from India."

"The election is a major opportunity for the people of AJK to choose their representatives," said Shazia Marri, the central information secretary of the Pakistan People's Party, which currently rules the region. "The people want their rights protected, their issues addressed and a government that delivers on its promises."

Unrest keeps flaring up in Pakistan-administered Kashmir To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, JAAC leaders argue that elections alone cannot resolve the issues that brought thousands of people onto the streets.

"Our movement is not replacing one government with another over time; we need our rights, but there are just political slogans in the campaigns," one JAAC official told DW under condition of anonymity.

Imran Khan, a geopolitical expert and former director of the US Institute of Peace Pakistan, expects the movement to continue post-elections.

"While elections in AJK are important on their own merit and for the continuity of the political process, they will not address the political grievances and demands of the people who are supporting JAAC," Khan, no relation to Pakistan's former prime minister, told DW. "The protest is outside the assembly. They no longer trust those institutions fully."

Has JAAC changed Kashmir's political landscape?

Analysts have said the JAAC protests marked a significant shift in Pakistan-administered Kashmir's politics by bringing together citizens across party lines around economic and governance issues rather than traditional political rivalries.

For Khan, JAAC is a dominant political force in quite significant parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

"They have more street credibility than mainstream politicians and parties despite the allegations of foreign backing and funding. For now, they have disrupted the status quo politics in AJK," Khan said, noting that the Pakistani establishment has the means and methods to break up such political movements.

Experts caution that rebuilding trust will require more than campaign promises.

"[The] next government in AJK will be very weak, as it will be sandwiched between pressure from both the Pakistani establishment that controls AJK through administrative and security framework and the sentiment on the street, which is very pro JAAC," argued Khan. The next government would have "little credibility and limited room to govern unless it reaches an understanding with JAAC to ease political tensions."

But Marri of the Pakistan People's Party believes trust is rebuilt by listening to people's concerns, delivering practical solutions and empowering elected institutions.

Will protests return if reforms stall?

If key grievances remain unresolved, analysts warn that another wave of protests cannot be ruled out.

"It is too early to say that more waves of protests will be seen, but JAAC has the potential to become a lasting political force," said Khan, who suggested the group risks being weakened by internal divisions and pressure from the establishment.

"For now, both sides are treading carefully, with JAAC relying on mass support and the establishment avoiding a full crackdown while buying time," Khan added.

Kashmir tourism struggles post Pahalgam attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While the vote will determine who governs Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it is unlikely to resolve the broader constitutional dispute over Kashmir or eliminate long-standing frustrations with the region's governance.

"Governments must listen to public concerns and address them through dialogue and effective governance. Stability comes from listening to people, respecting the law, and delivering results," Marri added.

For Raza, the Gen Z protester, "the world has changed, and we have seen governments toppling through student protests in the neighboring countries; we won't stop, and protests will continue until our rights have been given to us."

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Sudan civil war: Civilians used as 'human shields'
World.content:
The situation in the besieged city of El Obeid in Sudan is worsening by the day, with rights organizations warning of mass atrocities. Children are traumatized and do not dare go to school.

Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of El Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet. Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan.

The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, project manager for the UK children's rights organization Plan International, and a native of El Obeid. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand internally displaced persons (IDP) — is under siege, he added.

There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long queues of IDPs at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days."

He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school.

"One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because always they are in fear of something happening again," he said, adding that Plan International tried "to provide psychosocial support" for people scared of drones that could hit a classroom at any time.

Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

El Obeid: trading hub in the desert

El Obeid is a strategically important location. The city is a trading hub in the middle of the desert on the only major route between Sudan's capital, Khartoum — which is controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — and the western Darfur region, large parts of which are under the control of the RSF. Since the war began in 2023, the city has been captured by the RSF and recaptured by the army and allied militias many times.

El Obeid is currently controlled by the army, which has some 13,000 soldiers stationed there, and has been on the front line since fighting shifted from Darfur to Kordofan at the beginning of the year. The RSF has deployed troops to about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) beyond the city limits, and has been using drones to bomb civilian infrastructure.

DW Documentary 'Sudan: A hospital in the shadow of war' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Hallmarks of genocide'

Analysts, aid organizations and the United Nations have warned that the RSF could soon capture El Obeid. They fear a similar scenario to that which unfolded in the city of El Fasher in the neighboring state of North Darfur in October 2025, when the RSF began by bombing infrastructure before storming the city after an 18-month siege.

Earlier this year, a UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan presented to the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva detailed atrocities in the capture of the El Fasher and identified "hallmarks of genocide."

A joint appeal issued by several human rights organizations warned that an escalation of the situation could lead to a repeat of atrocities and human rights violations, as documented in El Fasher. "We are alarmed by the ongoing hostilities around the city, including frequent drone strikes," said Pekka Haavisto, the UN secretary general's personal envoy for Sudan, in June: "These are already affecting the civilians and affecting humanitarian aid to the city. Any further escalation of the situation would place thousands of people at risk."

Who are Sudan's RSF? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Schools and hospitals turned into barracks

Adam Mousa Eshag, director of the Sudanese organization Darfur Victims Support Organization (DVS), is currently based in Kampala, the capital of Uganda. He is in constant contact with people in Sudan and El Obeid for his research, for which he also spoke to SAF soldiers. He explained that one reason the RSF was bombing schools is that SAF soldiers had turned classrooms into barracks.

He said that this was also the case in El Fasher, when the army "used schools and even hospitals as barracks." He said soldiers were repeating this scenario in El Obeid and that was "the problem," as when the RSF attacked, "civilians paid the price" because they were being used as "human shields."

Francesco Lanino, deputy country director of Save the Children in Sudan, said the drone strikes targeting schools and IDP camps were causing severe trauma. "We met several children who refused to talk," he said, reporting on a recent visit to the Tawila IDP camp near El Fasher. "It's hard for them to understand why all of this is happening."

This article was translated from German.

07/26/2026 July 26, 2026 Israeli settlers accused of setting fire to West Bank mosques after deadly clash

Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials said on Sunday.

Since the Gaza war began with Hamas's attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, settler violence against Palestinians ​in the West Bank has increased sharply.

Abdel Azim Wadi, mayor of the town of Qusra, south of the city of Nablus, told AFP and Reuters news agencies that settlers had torched a mosque in ​his village.

He added that the attackers sprayed slogans in Hebrew on the mosque's walls, including the word "revenge."

"The village has faced repeated attacks since 2011, and these attacks have increased since the war," ‌he told Reuters by telephone.

In a separate incident, "groups of settlers burned a mosque in the village of Kour in Tulkarem governorate and wrote racist slogans on its walls," according to the Palestinian Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs.

The attacks followed clashes in the village of Tell on Friday, which left two Israelis and four Palestinians dead.

Under international law, Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal — a position Israel rejects.

World.title: Vietnamese vessel sinks in South China Sea, 23 missing
World.content:
A Vietnamese-registered cargo ship carrying 62 crew members sank near Yongshu Reef in the South China Sea, one of the world's most important and contested maritime spaces.

Rescuers were searching on Sunday for 23 people, missing after a Vietnamese ship sank in the South China Sea, China's ⁠state media reported.

Authorities in the Chinese island province of Hainan said the cargo vessel Khoi ​Nguyen 18 ran into trouble near Yongshu Reef, also known as Fiery Cross Reef, state broadcaster CCTV said.

The ship was carrying 62 crew members, and 39 people were rescued from the water.

What we know about the sinking incident

A Chinese rescue ship, the Nanhai Jiu 115, first spotted what was believed to be a distress flare from the vessel shortly before 6:30 pm on Saturday (1030 GMT).

The Khoi Nguyen 18 is a Vietnamese-registered ship measuring just under 70 meters (230 feet) in length, according to state news agency Xinhua.

It added that six Chinese vessels, a rescue helicopter and a Vietnamese vessel were involved in the search-and-rescue operations.

How a small, disputed island wards off China's power claims To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Territorial disputes in South China Sea

Beijing claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea, despite the 2016 international ruling, initiated by the Philippines against China, that its assertion has no legal basis.

One of the most highly contested areas is the ​Spratly Islands, which China calls the Nansha Islands, where China has built runways ⁠and militarized artificial islands.

But ​Beijing's sweeping claims to the busy waterway overlap with those of other countries, including Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei, Malaysia and Taiwan.
