World.title: Berlin CSD: Latest in string of deadly vehicle attacks
World.content:
The attack at a Berlin Pride event is only the most recent incident on a long list where vehicles were used as weapons. The US, Canada, and China also saw similar attacks in recent years.

Berlin, Germany, July 25, 2026

A Christopher Street Day event in the German capital, which attracts thousands of people every year, was attacked on Saturday night by a 21-year-old suspect who police said was associated with the "Islamist scene" in Berlin. One person was killed and another 16 people were injured, while the suspect, named as Abdul B., fled the scene.

Leipzig, Germany, May 4, 2026

Two people were killed and 20 more injured in early May when a car drove through a crowd in the eastern German city of Leipzig. The suspect in the case was described as a 33-year-old German national and local resident, who had been known to police, though not for relevant offenses.

Mannheim, Germany, March 3, 2025

At least two people were killed and several were injured in the southwestern German city of Mannheim in 2025 when a motorist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of people, according to police and public prosecutors. Authorities identified the suspect as a 40-year-old German man. Law enforcement ruled out a political motive at the time, though the man had paid a fine under Germany's hate crime laws for a comment he made on a social media platform in 2018.

Emergency services work at the scene after a car drove into a crowd in Munich in February 2025 Image: Michaela Stache/AFP

Munich, Germany, February 13, 2025

A 37-year-old woman and her two-year-old daughter were killed in Munich in February last year when a car was rammed into a demonstration organized by the trade union Verdi. A 25-year-old Afghan man subsequently went on trial for their murder, as well as the attempted murder of the dozens of other people injured in the attack.

New Orleans, United States, January 1, 2025

A vehicle plowed into a crowd of New Orleans revelers early on New Year's Day 2025, killing 14 people and injuring dozens of others. The driver of the vehicle and two police officers were killed in a firefight soon after the attack, which took place at about 3:15 in the morning local time. The FBI said it was investigating the incident as an act of terrorism.

Magdeburg, Germany, December 20, 2024

At least six people died and more than 300 were injured when a man slammed a rented BMW SUV into a Christmas market in eastern Germany. The suspect, who was arrested at the scene, was a 50-year-old doctor originally from Saudi Arabia who had expressed anti-Muslim views and support for the far-right AfD party. In June 2026, he was sentenced to life in prison, with the court noting the severity of his crime, which more or less rules out the possibility of an early release.

The suspect in the Magdeburg attack is alleged to have hired a BMW SUV to carry it out Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

Zhuhai, China, November 11, 2024

A 62-year-old driver rammed a small SUV into people exercising at a sports complex in southern China on November 11, 2024, killing 38 people in the country's deadliest act of mass homicide in years. Another 48 were injured. Authorities said the perpetrator was upset about his divorce but offered few other details about his motive. The man was detained and sentenced to death, and executed in January 2025.

London, Canada, June 6, 2021

Four members of a Muslim family who were out for a walk were killed when an attacker hit them with a pickup truck in what then Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called "a terrorist attack, motivated by hatred." The 23-year-old white nationalist attacker was sentenced to life in prison.

The London Ontario attacker killed four members of the same family and united the Muslim community in grief Image: Ian Willms/Getty Images

Toronto, Canada, April 23, 2018

A 25-year-old Canadian man drove a rented van into mostly female pedestrians on the main thoroughfare in Toronto, killing 10 people and injuring 16. He told police he belonged to the online "incel" community of sexually frustrated men. He was sentenced to life in prison with no possibility of parole for 25 years.

New York, United States, October 31, 2017

An Uzbek national killed eight people and seriously injured 12 others when he swerved a rented pickup truck on a bike path in New York City. Reportedly spurred on by a call to action by militant group "Islamic State," he was sentenced to eight consecutive life sentences plus an additional 260 years in prison.

Barcelona, Spain, August 17, 2017

A man driving a van plowed into people on the Spanish city's crowded Las Ramblas boulevard, killing 14 and injuring many more.

The "Islamic State" claimed responsibility, with members of the same cell carrying out a similar vehicle attack in the nearby resort town of Cambrils before being shot dead by police.

The perpetrator of the Ramblas attack was killed by police on August 21 after spending several days on the run.

Police in Spain embarked on a manhunt after the attack, with the suspect shot dead days later Image: Getty Images/C. Court

Charlottesville, United States, August 12, 2017

A white supremacist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of protesters who were opposing a "Unite the Right" rally, killing one woman and injuring dozens of people. He was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

London, United Kingdom, March to June, 2017

The year 2017 saw a spate of vehicle attacks in the British capital starting on March 22, when a 52-year-old UK-born man rammed an SUV into people on Westminster Bridge, killing four before stabbing a policeman to death. The perpetrator — who was a convert to Islam — claimed to be waging jihad in revenge for Western military action in Muslim countries. He was shot dead.

On June 3, three Islamist attackers drove a van at pedestrians on London Bridge before stabbing people at the city's Borough Market. Eight people were killed and police killed the attackers.

The attackers on London Bridge went on to kill more people at the nearby Borough Market Image: Reuters/S. Wermuth

Later that month, on June 19, a 47-year-old man radicalized by far-right ideas drove a van at worshippers outside a mosque in London's Finsbury Park area, killing one man and injuring 15 people.

Melbourne, Australia, January 20, 2017

Six people were killed and more than 30 injured when a car hit lunchtime crowds at a pedestrian mall in Australia's second-largest city. The perpetrator was found to have been in a state of drug-induced psychosis.

Berlin, Germany, December 19, 2016

A rejected asylum-seeker from Tunisia drove a hijacked truck into a Christmas market in the German capital, killing 13 people and injuring dozens. The attacker was killed days later in a shootout in Italy. The attack was claimed by the "Islamic State" militant group.

Nice, France, July 14, 2016

A Tunisian-born French resident drove a rental truck for nearly 2 kilometers along a seaside promenade crowded with tourists. The attack on the French Riviera resort, which took place on France's Bastille Day holiday, killed 86 people — the deadliest of its kind.

(AFP, AP, dpa, Reuters)

This article was first published on April 8, 2025, and updated on July 26, 2026.

World.title: India news: Home minister backs Pradhan after resignation
World.content:
07/26/2026 July 26, 2026 Scenes from the protest site, late last night

At about 8:30 p.m. on Saturday evening, the Cockroach protest site at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi was dwelling in residual euphoria.

Hours earlier, the education minister had resigned and soon after the protest had been concluded. The instant celebration had been loud. Now, many had left, some remained and others walked in.

Many protesters held their phones up instead of traditional placards Image: Priyanshu Singh/REUTERS

For some working youths, who had been banking on the weekend to show their support, the news of Pradhan's resignation came a little too early. Robbed of their chance to be a part of the movement, they had decided to witness the last of the celebrations.

Popular songs blared from portable speakers and sweaty protesters jumped in celebration Image: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

At one end of the site, volunteers dismantled the stage where activist Sonam Wangchuk had been on hunger strike for over 20 days. It was the same stage where students sat in protest when Wangchuk had been removed without his consent, where CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke broke down in tears and where he first heard word on Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

Volunteers pack up temporary shelter to vacate the site Image: ANI/ANI News/IMAGO

A few meters away, people formed little circles around those who still danced in celebration. On the sides, protesters with witty placards proudly posed for those taking pictures, showing their creativity once more before putting it away.

Beyond the barricades, some congratulated strangers with water, words or hugs. Others leaned over ice cream carts which had finally made their way in.

And about two hundred volunteers still worked tirelessly, either to control the celebrating crowd, to show people the way out or to sweep the roads. Once in a while their eyes met, and a smile broke out on their faces.

World.title: Germany launches manhunt after Berlin Pride van ramming
World.content:
07/26/2026 July 26, 2026 Vehicle attacks 'a successful strategy' for Islamist groups, warns expert

Police named the suspect as 21-year-old Abdul B, who local media said was a German national of Lebanese origin Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

Islamist groups have stumbled upon a "successful strategy" of plowing vehicles into the public at major events across Europe, Rafael Bossong, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said.

"This is already a pattern — [the Berlin Pride attack was] the eighth or ninth attack of this kind in Europe," Bossong told DW.

He cited the most deadly atrocity, in July 2016, when a truck rammed into a Bastille Day celebration in Nice, France, killing 86 people and injuring hundreds more.

Bossong warned that there are over 9,000 Islamist radicals with apparent violent inclinations in Germany.

Although authorities are doing a better job of monitoring and foiling threats, he said that the Berlin attack appeared to have been carried out by "a minor figure, with a prior criminal record, but no clear affiliation [to Islamist terrorism] and no clear online warning that he was preparing to attack."

Asked how the suspect was able to drive into Berlin's Tiergarten so easily despite barriers being installed, Bossong said:

"It depends on the time and locality. In this case, Tiergarten is a large area, the ceremony was closing, so maybe the traffic restrictions had been relaxed."

World.title: Brazil denies entry to senior Trump officials ahead of elections
World.content:
Brazil rejected visas for two planned US envoys, alleging that Washington was seeking to shape Brazil's upcoming presidential election. The development adds to a deepening political tension between Brazil and the US.

Brazil has denied visas to two officials from United States President Donald Trump's administration who had sought to travel to the country to meet with electoral authorities ahead of the October presidential election.

A spokesperson for Brazil's foreign office said on Saturday that Assistant Secretary Riley M. Barnes from the ​US State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, had requested a visa on July 20, along with Samuel Samson, a deputy assistant secretary.

The delegation's visa request was rejected on Friday, the spokesperson said.

What has Brazil said?

The Washington Post had first reported on the planned visit of the two envoys, citing senior Brazilian officials who said they had learnt of a US "ploy" that was "completely incompatible with Brazilian democracy."

The denial of the visas was ‌based on "evidence pointing to a renewed attempt to politically exploit the situation and undermine the electoral system", news agency Reuters quoted a Brazilian official as saying.

What has Washington said?

The US State Department said later on Saturday that Barnes and Samson planned to go to the South American country's capital, Brasilia from July 27 to 30 to discuss "election integrity," religious freedom and freedom of expression with government officials, religious leaders and others.

The Associated Press quoted the department as saying that the visit was routine and "any insinuation of a 'ploy' to undermine a democratic nation's election is a baseless lie."

Brazil gears up for elections

Brazil's presidential election is slated to be held on October 4.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is seeking reelection against Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The right-wing Liberal party confirmed Flavio as their candidate for the presidential race on Saturday.

The senior Bolsonaro, Jair, is under house arrest as he serves a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election.

The former Brazilian leader had also presented unsubstantiated allegations that his country's electronic voting system was vulnerable to fraud.

Flavio recently repeated some of his father's claims.

Bolsonaro-Trump ties

Jair is a friend and ally of Trump and the Bolsonaro family has ties with the Trump administration.

In May, Flavio and his brother Eduardo had visited US officials in Washington, including Trump.

The Trump administration classified two of Brazil's largest drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations, in a move opposed by Lula.

Jair was dubbed "Trump of the Tropics" during his tenure.

Trump had railed against Jair's trial, deeming it a "witch hunt".

World.title: A San Andrés de Teixido, por el Camiño Vello
World.content:
Una ruta a pie por la salvaje Costa Ártabra, en el extremo septentrional de España, buscando el segundo santuario más visitado de Galicia, que se alza desde tiempos remotos al pie de los acantilados más altos de Europa

Dicen que “a Santo André de Teixido vai de morto quen non foi de vivo”. ¿Y eso es malo? Respondamos gallegamente: depende. Si para ir allí, uno se reencarna en una babosa y se arrastra a cámara lenta por un camino abarrotado de peregrinos, corriendo el serio peligro de acabar espachurrado bajo una suela Vibram, no es bueno. En cambio, si se reencarna en una bolboreta, en una mariposa macaón o en una blanca esbelta ­–por citar dos especies habituales en el extremo norte de la Península–, y se va parando en cada flor a libar y copular, no está mal.

Probablemente Dios y san Pedro no pensaron en esta posibilidad cuando hallaron a san Andrés triste y solo en su santuario coruñés, pues no recibía ni la milésima parte de visitas que el de Santiago, y le prometieron que a su templo vendrían todos los mortales y que aquel que no lo hiciera en vida, lo haría reencarnado en un animal. O no lo pensaron bien o no sabían de mariposas.

Más información 13 razones por las que queremos viajar

Tras los pasos del Padre Sarmiento

Al santuario de San Andrés de Teixido, como al de Santiago, llevan todos los caminos. Hay casi tantos como peregrinos, que son legión –unos 70.000 al año– desde que se enteraron de que Dios y san Pedro habían prometido lo que prometieron a san Andrés. Todos valen, pero el original, el primero del que hay noticia fidedigna, es el que siguió el ilustrado Padre Sarmiento en 1755. Este escritor y erudito benedictino, que había pasado su niñez y parte de su juventud en Pontevedra, se interesó como ningún otro en su tiempo por todo lo gallego, en especial por la lengua y la geografía, a tal punto que iba anotando en un cuaderno los nombres exactos de los lugares por los que andaba. Gracias a eso, hoy puede seguirse sin dificultad el camino que hizo. Bueno, y gracias también a la Diputación de A Coruña, que lo señalizó en 2001 con monolitos de granito en los que un pescado rojo indica la dirección correcta. Para más facilidad, en Wikiloc están la descripción, el mapa y el track de este camino de 39 kilómetros, que suele hacerse dividiéndolo en dos etapas de unas seis horas de duración cada una.

El santuario de San Andrés de Teixido, destino final del histórico Camiño Vello y uno de los principales centros de peregrinación de Galicia. Andrés Campos

El Camiño Vello, que así se llama –aunque también podría llamarse Bello, con be, porque lo es– arranca en el monasterio de San Martiño de Xuvia, en la parroquia de O Couto, en Narón, junto a la ría de Ferrol. Bordeando ésta se sube hasta el molino de mareas de As Aceas –de mediados del siglo XVIII, que llegó a ser una de las mayores fábricas de harina de Galicia­­­–, donde el camino se desvía tierra adentro para ir en busca del Pazo Libunca, un palacete modernista de 1922 cuyo primer dueño y constructor, el indiano Francisco Montenegro, dicen que se encendía los puros con billetes de mil pesetas. Ahora es un hotel muy majo pero carillo, donde se necesitan al menos 24 de aquellos billetes –unos 145 euros– para dormir una noche de verano. Pasando después por la necrópolis prehistórica del Monte dos Nenos y por el Marco de Portonovo de Valverde –pedrusco milenario donde confluyen los términos de Narón, Valdoviño y San Sadurniño– se llega, ya casi al final de la primera etapa, a la ermita de Liñeiro, más conocida como la Capela da Fame, la Capilla del Hambre, nombre popular que suena fuerte y claro, como las tripas del peregrino después de caminar 22 kilómetros.

Las caldupeiras de Porto do Cabo

En Porto do Cabo –pueblo chico pero de hermosos y extensos dominios, divididos entre los municipios de Valdoviño, Cedeira y Cerdido–, se acaba la primera etapa del Camiño Vello y también la fame, el hambre que cualquiera arrastra tras andar seis horas por el monte. Aquí, alrededor del puente medieval, se ponían antaño las caldupeiras, mujeres que por poco dinero –un patacón de cobre– daban a los peregrinos una cunca rebosante, no de aguachirle, sino de guiso sustancioso: un caldo gallego, vaya. Y aquí se siguen poniendo, con pañoletas, mandiles, zuecos de cuero y ollas humeantes, las mujeres de la Asociación Veciñal Porto de Cabo, cuando se celebra la romería más importante a San Andrés de Teixido, el primer fin de semana de septiembre.

Vecinas de Porto do Cabo caracterizadas como caldupeiras durante la romería de San Andrés de Teixido, una tradición que recuerda a las mujeres que alimentaban a los peregrinos. Andrés Campos

Una de estas caldupeiras, Antonia Martínez, y su marido y presidente de la asociación vecinal, José Picallo, son los propietarios de Casa do Morcego, bautizada así en recuerdo de los muchos murciélagos que la habitaban antes de ser transformada en un hotelito rural encantador, el mejor de la ruta. Murciélagos ahora se ven pocos. En cambio, hay bolboretas a patadas: mariposas de los muros, vanesas pintadas, mantos oscuros, colias, níspolas… El huerto está lleno de ellas y también de verduras que acaban en la cocina de la casa y en las tripas cada vez más silenciosas del caminante.

Casa do Morcego es un lugar que envicia, donde uno se estaría, no una noche, sino una semana explorando los contornos de la mano de Antonia Martínez y José Picallo. En el mismo Porto do Cabo se conservan la histórica hospedería Casa da Bastona y el puente medieval sobre el río das Mestas, el cual desagua en la ría de Cedeira cerca de un lugar donde se acaba la poca fame que el caminante pueda aún tener: Taberna do Puntal. Tampoco se come mal en el restaurante O Castro, con vistas a la playa de Pantín, la catedral gallega del surf. Ni en Badulaque, en el puerto de Cedeira, a tiro de caña de la lonja. Más frescos, los rapes y las almejas no pueden llegar. Luego lo suyo es dar un largo paseo digestivo viendo el casco viejo de Cedeira, el castro Sarridal, el Castelo da Concepción y el atardecer desde el mirador de San Antonio de Corveiro.

Bichos y bestas de la Serra da Capelada

Tras desayunar y sellar el pasaporte de peregrino en Casa do Morcego, comienza la segunda etapa del Camiño Vello subiendo por espesos y fragantes montes de eucaliptos para, a los cinco kilómetros –una hora y media a paso regular– pararse a desayunar otra vez en Panadería Prados (981 48 24 58), en A Venta, en la parroquia cedeiresa de San Román de Montoxo. En este horno de leña, además de un pan irresistible –lo habitual en Galicia–, hacen ricas cocadas, bollas de manzana, bizcochadas y empanadas de raya. Conviene llevar una mochila XXL porque todo, dentro del cuerpo, no cabe.

La ermita de San Roque de Reboredo marca la entrada a la Serra da Capelada en la segunda etapa del Camiño Vello. Andrés Campos

Siguiente parada, en la capilla de San Roque de Reboredo, ermita del siglo XVII que señala la entrada a la Serra da Capelada. Quienes peregrinan a Teixido han de mirar siempre bien dónde pisan, por si alguien que no fue allá en vida está haciendo el camino transmutado en insecto, anfibio o reptil, pero aquí deben extremar las precauciones porque el prado de la ermita está plagado de ranas galaicas y de luciones, lagartos ápodos, sin patas, también conocidos como culebrillas de cristal. A los que pasen sin despanzurrar ninguno, san Andrés se lo agradecerá. Y san Roque, patrón de los peregrinos y amigo de los animales, no digamos. Esta era una de las muchas capelas habitadas por ermitaños que dieron nombre a la Serra da Capelada, orónimo que el Padre Sarmiento explicó en 1755, cuando peregrinó anotando todo en su cuaderno de viaje.

A partir de aquí, el paisaje se vuelve más agreste. Se puebla de bestas, los caballejos semisalvajes que cada primavera rapan y marcan con festiva algazara los ganaderos de la comarca. Y se puebla también de amilladoiros, montones de piedras en los que el peregrino previsor arroja la que ha transportado en la mochila desde su lugar de origen para que el día del Juicio Final demuestre que ha estado aquí en vida y no tenga que volver desde el más allá, convertido en un bicho. Eso, si es que es capaz de encontrarla, sepultada como está bajo hogazas de pan, dulces varios y empanadas de raya.

Un artesano elabora y vende sanandresiños, los tradicionales amuletos de pan asociados a la romería de San Andrés de Teixido. Andrés Campos

En el mirador Chao do Monte, a un kilómetro justo del final, se obtiene la primera vista del santuario de San Andrés de Teixido. Si el caminante no supiera que está en la esquina más norteña de Galicia, diría que aquella iglesia de allá abajo y aquellas casitas de piedra casi negra con llagas blancas, rodeadas de acantilados y de verdores tan intensos que hacen daño a la retina, son un pueblecito de la isla canaria de La Gomera. Y si no supiera que san Andrés no pisó nunca España y que terminó atado a una cruz en forma de aspa en la ciudad griega de Patras, diría lo que dice la leyenda: que aquella peña oronda que aflora del mar al pie del blanco caserío, cual navío panza arriba, es la barca de piedra en la que vino a Galicia, emulando a Santiago, y con la que naufragó al llegar, demostrando que estos acantilados no son un buen lugar para atracar.

“A San Andrés van dos y vuelven tres”

Una vez en San Andrés de Teixido, la tradición manda acercarse a los puestos de productos típicos –exvotos, licores, herba de namorar, rosquillas, juncos del bien parir, pines con forma de percebe…– para comprar los sanandresiños, amuletos hechos con masa de pan sin fermentar, endurecidos al horno y pintados de vivos colores, que tienen diferentes formas, adecuadas al uso que se les va a dar: la flor, para conseguir el amor; la mano, para formular un deseo; la sardina que pescó san Andrés, para conjurar las envidias… Son muy bonitos y prometedores, pero para comer no valen. Para eso, están los percebes y todo lo que sirven, sin florituras, en la Taberna Hermanos Bouza.

Lo segundo que hay que hacer en San Andrés de Teixido es entrar en la iglesia, erigida sobre la roca viva, y pedir la bendición del titular, a cuyos pies suele haber gran variedad de ofrendas: fotos de carné, extremidades de cera, barquitos de madera… Por haber, hay hasta ataúdes de personas que, gracias al santo, no llegaron a necesitarlo. Y lo tercero, dirigirse a la fuente de los Tres Caños, de los cuales tres hay que beber para que se cumpla un deseo. Si se arroja una miga de pan y flota, también es buena señal. Y si se tiene una verruga y se lava con esta agua, puede que se caiga o puede que no. En el peor de los casos, se tendrá una verruga lustrosa. Las que tienen una piel preciosa, verde brillante con reticulado en negro y ocelos axiales azules, son las lagartijas serranas (Iberolacerta monticola) que pululan en el merendero aledaño.

Una lagartija serrana junto a la fuente de los Tres Caños, donde la tradición invita a beber tres sorbos para pedir un deseo. Andrés Campos

Antiguamente, también era tradición bajar hasta la rompiente en busca de la hierba de enamorar, hacer un ramito con ella y depositarla en el santuario como ofrenda. Ahora, que hay más conciencia ambiental, se recomienda comprar la que venden en los tenderetes, procedente de cultivos. A la Armeria pubigera se le atribuyen propiedades enamoradoras –una pizca en el bolsillo del otro obra el milagro–, afrodisiacas y empreñadoras. Y no falla, según lo que dicen: “A San Andrés van dos y vuelven tres”.

Acantilados gigantes y playas salvajes

En San Andrés de Teixido termina el Camiño Vello, pero el viaje a pie se puede alargar una jornada más –tres en total– bordeando los acantilados situados al noreste del santuario, que hay quienes dicen que son los más altos de Europa continental, aunque otros, más cautos, añaden que están a la par con los de Irlanda y Noruega. En el filo más elevado, a 620 metros sobre el océano, descuella la Vixía de Herbeira, un puesto de vigilancia costera del siglo XVIII desde el que los barcos enemigos debían de verse, si es que se veían, como microbios. El mar sí se ve, pero tan lejos que no se oye. Aquí, incluso en verano, sopla un viento recio, fresco, de jersey obligado. En ir y volver desde San Andrés de Teixido se tarda cuatro horas, siguiendo esta ruta de Wikiloc.

La playa de Fornos, en el municipio coruñés de Cariño, destaca por sus aguas transparentes y su entorno prácticamente virgen. Andrés Campos

El cabo Ortegal, ya en el vecino concejo de Cariño, es el segundo más norteño de la Península después del de Estaca de Bares. Y el más afilado, con el sitio justo para la carretera y un faro como de juguete. Le acompañan tres temibles islotes, Os Aguillóns, como si él solo no diera ya bastante miedo. Los que saben de percebes dicen que aquí se cogen los mejores de Galicia. Y los que saben de rocas, que estas son las más antiguas de la península Ibérica, de hace 1.156 millones de años. De la Vixía de Herbeira al cabo Ortegal hay 11,5 kilómetros de camino, unas tres horas sin parar apenas.

A la Vixía de Herbeira y al cabo Ortegal también se puede ir en coche, si es que uno no tiene las fuerzas o las ganas suficientes para prolongar a pie el Camiño Vello. Pero a donde solo se puede ir andando es la playa de Teixidelo. Escondida al pie de los tremendos acantilados de la Serra da Capelada, es la única playa del mundo de arena negra no volcánica. Su misterioso color es producto de la erosión de rocas ricas en peridotita y olivino. Para descubrirla, se ha de caminar desde el mirador de Teixidelo, muy cerca de San Andrés de Teixido, siguiendo una ruta de circular breve pero muy abrupta y empinada, de seis kilómetros y casi tres horas de duración, solo para senderistas expertos. Los que no lo sean se moverán mucho mejor por estos vertiginosos vericuetos de la Serra da Capelada acompañados por los guías de Portal Norte.

Otras playas salvajes alucinantes, con acceso más sencillo, son las que rodean la península de Figueiroa, en el vecino concejo de Cariño. A un lado de la península está la de Fornos, de 400 metros de largo por 60 de anchura, cuyas aguas verdes nada tienen que envidiar a las del Caribe. Salvo la temperatura, lógicamente. Al otro, la de Figueiras, más pequeña –260x15 metros– y recogida, frecuentada por las mariscadoras que siembran y luego recogen, rodilla en tierra, su cosecha berberechil. Y en medio, la más seductora, la de Os Cabalos o de A Postiña –350x30 metros–, solo accesible a pie desde las otras dos cuando la marea baja. Las fuertes corrientes de la ría y las violentas mareas hacen casi imposible bañarse en ella. Si nos gusta bajar a la playa cinco minutos, a deshora y sin gente, es perfecta.

World.title: Blood on Her Tongue: A modern vampire tale not for the squeamish
World.content:
Johanna van Veen’s gothic horror Blood on Her Tongue offers up a classic vampire tale with some modern contemplations.

The book follows Lucy Goedhart as she is called to the ominously named Zwartwater (black water) estate, where her sister has taken ill. In 1887, there isn’t much in the way of medical treatment, but Lucy’s sister Sarah isn’t fighting off a regular illness.

Sarah has become obsessed with a body found in the bog of the vast estate and since interacting with the 300-year-old corpse she has become increasingly incoherent, struggles with taking care of herself and has developed an insatiable hunger.

As Lucy tries desperately to save her sister, she finds that her sister’s husband, her sister’s doctor and childhood friend, and several other characters who are present at the remote manor house all have their own interests and motivations – some as dangerous as whatever condition is plaguing Sarah.

The book is not for those easily bothered by gore. The title – Blood on Her Tongue – is a pretty good indication of what is to come. Van Veen does not shy away from the horror elements, including two separate scenes of eyeball gouging.

Like any good horror novel, the macabre monster is not the scariest part. The threats Lucy faces are from the men surrounding her sister. Her brother-in-law attempts to seduce Lucy while badgering her to send Sarah away to an asylum.

Sarah’s doctor expresses his own interest in Lucy, pushing his vision of the future while supposedly devoting himself to his patient. The mores of 19th-century upper-class society may be the biggest piece of villainy of all.

In the tradition of Dracula, Blood on Her Tongue tells its story through letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The personal correspondence adds to the claustrophobia of the work, with everyone limited to an isolated house, but the media reports remind the reader that the world outside does exist.

The work is the second book from Dutch author Johanna van Veen. It was published in 2025 in English and became a USA Today bestseller. Her first book, My Darling Dreadful Thing, was nominated for the Bram Stoker Award for best horror novel. Van Veen grew up in the Netherlands as a triplet, something that influenced her writing about the sisters Lucy and Sarah.

If horror is your thing, Blood on Her Tongue will creep you out and keep you turning the pages.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Thousands cross finishing line as Nijmegen Vierdaagse ends
World.content:
The 108th edition of the Nijmegense Vierdaagse (four-day march) ended on Friday, with tens of thousands of walkers being welcomed with flowers by well-wishers.

British walker Simon Brownlee crossed the finishing line ahead of the rest of the walkers for the 27th time, local media reported. Brownlee, who completed the distance before 10am, told local broadcaster Omroep Gelderland that the walk “felt like home”. “I’m happy it is over and I can now relax,” he said.

Wheelchair participant Ronald van Dort was the very first person to finish, picking up his seventh medal for completing the event.

Over 45,000 walkers from 70 countries took part in this year’s series, which is proving increasingly popular among the young. Ten years ago, 7.5% of the walkers were aged 21 to 30, but this year their number rose to over 20%.

This year the event was marred by a fatal shooting just outside the area where the Vierdaagsefeesten, the street festivities accompanying the annual four-day marches, were taking place. One man has been arrested.

The shooting, and other crowd problems, led the organisers to cancel performances by urban scene artists such as Ronnie Flex and Lil’ Kleine because their presence was “attracting the wrong sort of people”, the AD reported.

World.title: Dozens of women forced into prostitution by Romanian gang
World.content:
Dozens of women may have been forced into working as prostitutes in Amsterdam’s red light district by a Romanian gang, Dutch police confirmed on Friday.

The statement follows a joint Dutch and Romanian campaign against human trafficking in the area earlier this month. Seven men were arrested during a string of raids on July 14 – four in the Netherlands and three in Romania. All were Romanian nationals.

Shortly after the arrests, police issued a video interview with one of the victims speaking Romanian, which has led more women to come forward and has resulted in other information reaching the police, the statement said.

Police now say they have spoken to several victims and say they believe more women have been trafficked. They too are said to be Romanian.

The women were lured to Amsterdam with the promise of high earnings but found themselves forced into working in brothels and handing over their earnings to the gang. They were also forced to pay “rent” for their rooms.

None of the men had jobs but were big spenders, buying expensive clothes and cars and gambling heavily, the statement said. The gang also treated part of the red light district as their “personal kingdom”.

Four men remain in custody in the Netherlands, one of whom was extradited from Romania. Another man may also be extradited soon, RTL said. They are all suspected of human trafficking and forming a criminal organisation.

According to the Parool, two of the suspects are half brothers aged 44 and 45 who have earlier convictions for trafficking in women in Romania.

More arrests have not been ruled out.

A year ago, Dutch and Romanian police arrested 13 people in a joint investigation into human trafficking and the forced prostitution of Romanian women, mainly in and around Amsterdam.

World.title: Singer Sophie Straat cleared of discrimination over mosh pit
World.content:
Discrimination hotlines in both the Netherlands and Belgium have concluded that Dutch singer Sophie Straat did not discriminate when she asked “all white men to step back” during two of her recent performances.

Last month at the Best Kept Secret festival in Beekse Bergen, Straat — real name Sophie Schwartz — asked for space for women, queer people and people of colour in the “mosh pit”, an area in front of the stage where fans dance chaotically.

She made the same request on Monday during a performance in Ghent, Belgium.

The Dutch discrimination hotline Discriminatie.nl said it received hundreds of complaints but maintains that Straat’s comments do not amount to discrimination against white men based on their colour or gender.

“The call only concerned one short, one-off mosh pit for these groups,” said the hotline. “Therefore, visitors were not refused entry to the concert.”

Belgian authorities reached the same conclusion after receiving some 200 complaints following her performance in Ghent.

“Although the statement may be perceived as polarizing or offensive, in this context it must be seen as a symbolic and artistic expression,” a spokesperson for the Belgian discrimination hotline Unia told the Flemish broadcaster VRT.

“According to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, artistic and political expressions enjoy broad protection under freedom of expression, even when they provoke, shock or offend.”

Hate messages and death threats

Straat wrote on Instagram earlier this month that she has received “a wave of sexist, antisemitic hate messages and (death) threats, some more explicit and creative than others”.

She has also questioned where the left-wing media has been in all this, saying the public narrative is being controlled by the right.

The singer, who was raised in a Jewish home in Amsterdam’s de Pijp neighbourhood and is known for her protest songs, has said she never wanted to exclude anyone but rather wanted to make room for people who feel unsafe in a mosh pit.

World.title: Youngster arrested for participating in sadistic online network
World.content:
Police have arrested a young man from Noord Holland who they suspect of being part of the sadistic online Com network “764”.

The public prosecution department reported the arrest on Thursday, saying the suspect encouraged underage girls to cut themselves and write his online name on a wall with their own blood—so-called “bloodsigns”.

He also is said to have prompted them to write his name on their bodies with a marker, known as“fansigns”. Both are practices within the Com movement—short for The Community—for members to gain prestige.

The suspect himself, who was also charged with aggravated assault, exploitation of underage girls and possession of images of sexual child abuse, was a minor at the time of the alleged crimes. Because of that, no further details are being released.

The Com network consists of various chat groups where members recruit vulnerable young people and force them to commit acts including assault, sexual abuse and murder.

The members, from all corners of the globe, then share images of these acts online in private chat groups, using such platforms as Telegram and Discord.

According to NOS, at least 70 Dutch people are involved in this movement known as “nihilistic extremism” because the incitement to commit such extreme violence doesn’t have a clear ideological motive.

The phenomenon is especially attractive to young men.

World.title: Dangerous drivers face extra surveillance under points system
World.content:
The police and justice ministry officials are working on a system which would see traffic offenders being given points for dangerous driving – which will lead to persistent offenders coming under extra surveillance.

Motorists who have collected six points for using a mobile phone while driving or not wearing a seatbelt would come under the tougher regime, RTL Nieuws reported on Friday. No start date has yet been set.

The points will be awarded in addition to regular fines. The number of points will depend on the seriousness of the offences and speeding tickets recorded by camera will not be included.

The new system is being devised in an effort to tackle persistent offenders who do not change their behaviour despite being fined multiple times, RTL said. Last year, almost 30,000 people would have had at least six points if the new system had been in existence.

“Research shows that people who don’t stick to the rules are often responsible for accidents,” Achilles Damen from the public prosecution department told the broadcaster.

The privacy implications of monitoring specific individuals are still being assessed, RTL said.

World.title: Ajax beat Vojvodina in Conference League qualifier, Twente lose
World.content:
Ajax kicked off their European football campaign with a 4-1 win over Serbian club Vojvodina in the second qualification round of the Conference League competition in Novi Sad on Thursday evening.

The simple win sets the Amsterdammers up in a strong position ahead of the return match next week. If Ajax win again, they will meet either Irish side Shelbourne FC or Estonian club Nõmme Kalju in the third qualification round for the third-tier European competition.

The Amsterdam goal total included one for 16-year-old debutant Mohamed Abdalla, who became the youngest player to score for a Dutch club in Europe.

There was disappointment for FC Twente, who are hoping to qualify for the group stage of the Europa League. They lost 1-2 at home to Hungarian side Ferencváros and will have to pull out all the stops during the away leg next week to remain in the competition.

If they do lose, Twente will move down to the qualification rounds of the Conference League.

PSV Eindhoven and Feyenoord have qualified directly for the Champions League while NEC is taking part in the qualification competition. AZ, as winners of the KNVB Cup last season, will take part in the Europa League competition.

World.title: Unilever backs London for food division secondary listing
World.content:
Unilever’s food division, which is being sold to US sauce and spice producer McCormick, will have a secondary listing on the London stock exchange, despite an intensive lobbying campaign to list in Amsterdam.

Unilever itself has been based in London, and listed there, since 2020.

Unilever said in a statement that the secondary listing is separate to McCormick’s plans to establish an international headquarters in the Netherlands and maintain Unilever Food’s R&D facilities and operations in Wageningen.

This “reflects its commitment to the European market and the critical role the Netherlands will continue to play in the combined company”, the statement said.

Economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert said in a reaction to the sale when it was announced in March that the cabinet had already discussed developments with Unilever and would talk to the new owner “such as about a listing on the Amsterdam stock exchange”.

Unilever’s ice cream arm, spun off in 2024, is listed on the Amsterdam stock exchange as the Magnum Ice Cream Company and is headquartered in the Dutch capital.

The sale of the food arm means there is nothing left of the original Dutch part of Unilever, which was set up in 1930 through the merger of the Dutch Margarine Unie and British soap maker Lever Brothers. Unilever now focuses on personal care and household cleaning products.

World.title: Poland identifies remains of legendary anti-communist resistance fighter
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz (pictured above on the right), a prominent figure in the underground resistance that fought against the Soviet-installed communist authorities in the years after World War Two. Dziemieszkiewicz, who was killed by the communist security services in 1951 and dumped in an unmarked mass grave, was identified through a combination of historical detective work and genetic testing, including exhuming the remains of his deceased mother and sister to obtain DNA samples. “Once again, we can say that the communist authorities did not win. Heroes prevail,” declared Krzysztof Szwagrzyk, deputy head of the IPN. “Even in the most difficult situations, we must seek the truth, find those of whom no trace was supposed to remain, and restore their names.” While World War Two officially came to an end in 1945, tens of thousands of Poles, known as the “cursed soldiers” (żolnierze wyklęci), continued to fight against the Soviets and the communist regime they installed in Poland. While most had laid down arms by 1947, some continued fighting well beyond then, including Dziemieszkiewicz, who operated under the nom de guerre “Rój” (meaning “swarm”). Dziemieszkiewicz, who was 20 years old when the war ended, came from a family that had been part of Poland’s wartime resistance. His anti-communist views were hardened when his elder brother, Roman, was killed by Red Army soldiers in 1945. After being conscripted that year into the Soviet-backed Polish People’s Army, Dziemieszkiewicz defected and joined the underground resistance forces, where he rose to command a unit tasked with eliminating regime officials and members of the communist Polish Workers Party (PPR). Dziemieszkiewicz’s group killed around two dozen members of the communist security services and more than 20 informants, according to the IPN. In 1950, the communist authorities intensified efforts to dismantle Dziemieszkiewicz’s unit, using threats and blackmail to recruit hundreds of agents and informants in an effort to locate the resistance fighters. Eventually, one such informant gave up Dziemieszkiewicz’s location in exchange for a promise to release her parents from captivity. Dziemieszkiewicz found himself surrounded by several hundred soldiers and was killed while trying to escape. After his body had been identified by his family, Dziemieszkiewicz was buried in a section of Powązki Cemetery in Warsaw where the remains of those killed by the communist security services were placed en masse in unmarked graves. Exhumations by the IPN, which was established after the fall of communism to investigate communist and Nazi crimes in Poland, have located over 200 complete bodies at that site as well as several thousand bone fragments. During that work, one set of remains was found buried with an eagle symbol and remnants of a black cloth. IPN researchers realised that the item was similar to a beret that appeared in posthumous photographs of Dziemieszkiewicz’s body taken by the communist security services. That prompted them to carry out genetic testing on the remains and compare them to samples taken from Dziemieszkiewicz’s mother and sister, who were buried in a cemetery in the town of Maków Mazowiecki. “We have found ‘Rój’, commander of one of the longest-fighting units of the independence underground,” declared the IPN on Friday, announcing the confirmation of his identity. They described Dziemieszkiewicz as “legend in life and a symbol of the fight against communist oppression”. The identification was announced today during a press conference at @PrzystanekH. The identification is the result of many years of work carried out by the IPN. It was preceded by extensive archival and investigative research, the analysis of forensic evidence, archaeological… https://t.co/Rcf4wemJFc pic.twitter.com/XgMUAgSQc6 — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) July 24, 2026 At a conference announcing the findings, the IPN noted that Dziemieszkiewicz’s remains had been located right next to those of another prominent anti-communist resistance fighter, Zygmunt Szendzielarz, who fought under the nom de guerre “Łupaszko”. “It is an incredible situation that two great and distinguished soldiers of the Polish underground lie next to each other in this part of the Powązki Cemetery,” said Szwagrzyk. However, Szendzielarz, who was executed by the communist authorities in 1951, has a contested legacy, given evidence that his unit was involved in the massacre of dozens of Lithuanian civilians. Some other “cursed soldiers” have faced similar accusations of war crimes. While it was often IPN historians who uncovered evidence of such actions, the institution has more recently begun to honour those figures, particularly under the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice government between 2015 and 2023. Opposition MPs walked out of parliament yesterday as the chamber commemorated an underground officer who fought against Nazi-German occupation and the imposition of communism in Poland, but has also been accused of a war crime against civilians https://t.co/MIY7krOxTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 9, 2022 Dziemieszkiewicz himself, however, like most of the cursed soldiers, has not faced such accusations. In 2007, President Lech Kaczński posthumously awarded Dziemieszkiewicz the Commander’s Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta, one of Poland’s highest honours. In 2020, his image was featured on a commemorative silver coin issued by the National Bank of Poland. Through a combination of brutal repression and offering amnesties, the communist authorities managed to end most resistance efforts by 1947. However, the last “cursed soldier” to die in combat, Józef Franczak, was killed in 1963, 18 years after the end of the war. World.title: Three quarters of Poles support cooperation with Ukraine against Russia despite historical dispute
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A new study shows that, while most Poles were angered by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, they still overwhelmingly support cooperation with Ukraine and believe that Russia benefits from the dispute. The study, carried out by Polish state research agency CBOS, also finds that a large majority of Poles believe good relations with Ukraine will only be possible once historical issues are resolved. The polling was carried out this month in response to the ongoing diplomatic crisis that began in May, when Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. The UPA is widely revered in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-backed Soviet rule. However, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians – mostly women and children – were slaughtered during World War Two, often with great brutality. Zelensky’s decision sparked anger in Poland, where the massacres are regarded as a genocide (though Ukraine strongly rejects that label). In June, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest honour, which he had received in 2023. In its new survey, CBOS found that 59% of Poles support Nawrocki’s decision, while only 28% oppose it. However, they were divided over the consequences, with 41% saying it would bring Poland more losses than benefits and the exact same proportion saying the benefits would outweigh the costs. More broadly, 84% said the Polish state should react when another country glorifies historical figures responsible for crimes against Poles. However, when asked if Ukrainians have the right to honour their own historical heroes, even if those figures left a negative mark on Polish history, 44% agreed and 42% disagreed. At the same time, over three quarters of respondents (77%) said that good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past, but a similar proportion (73%) also believe that politicians on both sides “fuel conflicts between Poles and Ukrainians for their own political gain”. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Yet the survey also showed that, for Poles, historical disputes have not displaced security concerns, and in particular the view that, for Poland and Ukraine, Russia is a shared enemy. Some 75% of respondents agreed with the statement that “Poland and Ukraine should, above all, cooperate in the face of the threat from Russia, rather than focus on the issues that divide them”. The most frequently cited priorities in relations with Kyiv were security cooperation (61%), building good neighbourly relations (46%), commemorating victims of the Volhynia massacres (43%), strengthening Poland’s regional leadership (41%), and ensuring Polish companies participate in Ukraine’s reconstruction (40%). Just over half of Poles (52%) agree that “Poland and Ukraine have more common aims and interests than conflicting ones”, while 32% disagreed. A huge majority (80%) agreed that “Russia benefits from the Polish-Ukrainian dispute”. W ocenie społecznej zdecydowanym priorytetem w relacjach z Ukrainą powinna być współpraca na rzecz bezpieczeństwa – wskazało ją 61% badanych.📊 ➡️Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Wokół polsko-ukraińskiego sporu o imponderabilia i nie tylko":https://t.co/pIvYbu8gyz#Ukraina #relacje pic.twitter.com/LOpmAKNnXn — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) July 23, 2026 Based on the answers in the survey, CBOS identified three broad groups of respondents classified by their views of the dispute. The largest, described as “moralists”, accounted for 46% and placed greater emphasis on historical grievances. Among this group, 99% supported Nawrocki’s decision and said good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past. “Pragmatists”, who made up 34% of respondents, placed greater emphasis on future cooperation. Some 96% said Poland and Ukraine should cooperate against the Russian threat rather than focus on historical disputes. The smallest group, labelled by CBOS as “withdrawn”, represented 20% of respondents who were more likely to lack a clear view on Polish-Ukrainian relations. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Recent weeks have seen moves from Ukraine towards finding a diplomatic solution to the crisis. In early July, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha visited Warsaw to propose an “anti-crisis package” of measures. Last week, Zelensky himself outlined a five-point plan to alleviate the dispute, including opening up Ukrainian historical archives and permitting more exhumations of victims of the massacres, most of whom remain buried in mass graves in Ukraine. The Polish authorities have cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement, though also emphasise that they are waiting to see concrete action. Meanwhile, there is no indication that Zelensky will change his decision to name a unit after the heroes of the UPA. World.title: Poland bans chaining of dogs and cats
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Those who are found to have violated the new law can be fined between 1,000 and 100,000 zloty (€232-23,166). If they are deemed to have acted with “extreme cruelty”, they can also face a prison sentence of up to five years, reports the Forsal news service. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. A dog who throws a ball to passers-by from a balcony above one of Poland’s most famous streets and waits for them to throw it back has become a star. Videos of her game have been viewed millions of times and people visit in the hope of playing with her https://t.co/A9p9t0hWSD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 9, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Police and park rangers step up joint patrols in Poland’s Tatras after series of tourist offences
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Police officers and rangers have stepped up joint patrols in Poland’s mountainous Tatra National Park during the peak summer season, following a spate of rule-breaking including swimming in the park’s lakes and ponds, driving cars and going off marked trails. Meanwhile, national park authorities have repeated warnings that bathing, littering and breaking other rules can damage the park’s fragile ecosystem. Local police officers have joined Tatra National Park rangers on patrols on popular tourist routes. On one such patrol last week, officers focused on education and prevention, reminding visitors not to leave marked trails or litter and explaining how to behave safely and responsibly in the mountains. They also checked that organised groups were accompanied by qualified mountain guides, as required by law. Fines for such offences range from 50 zloty (€11.55) to as much as 1,000 zloty (€231) in the event of environmental damage or multiple offences. Police said that all visitors encountered during the patrol were complying with the park’s regulations. However, they added that similar patrols would continue on a regular basis. The Tatra National Park, home to Poland’s highest peaks, and the nearby mountain resort of Zakopane are among the country’s most popular holiday destinations, with crowds taking to park trails in the summer season. The park, the most visited of Poland’s 23 national parks, welcomed a record 5.3 million visitors in 2025 and offers 275 km of marked hiking trails, including high-altitude routes that connect at several points with the adjacent national park in Slovakia. 🚨 Ukraiński Influencer wjechał nielegalnie samochodem na Morskie oko 🗣️: Jesteśmy pierwszymi ludźmi w historii, którzy wjechali samochodem nad Morskie Oko. To było jedno z miejsc, do których chcieliśmy dotrzeć podczas tej podróży i wszyscy znajomi oraz przyjaciele mówili, że… pic.twitter.com/tA9shZ6Rqk — Pigułka 💊 (@informacyjnie) May 23, 2026 This season has already seen a number of high-profile cases of transgressions of the park’s strict rules. In May, a Ukrainian social media influencer sparked outrage after driving a sports car along a road closed to traffic to Morskie Oko, a picturesque lake nestled between the mountains. As a result, he was banned from entering Poland and other Schengen Area countries for five years. Tourists have also been filmed entering Morskie Oko and other protected lakes and ponds, which is not permitted in the national park. This month, a group of young Dutch tourists were filmed bathing in Przedni Staw Polski in the Valley of the Five Lakes, one of the Tatras’ best-known hiking destinations. Witnesses repeatedly warned the group that entering the lake was prohibited, but they ignored the warnings, reports Gazeta Wyborcza. Park authorities have responded to such incidents by reminding visitors of the reasons for the strict rules. “Tatra ponds are incredibly delicate ecosystems. Cosmetics, UV filters, insect repellents, and bacteria entering the water can have a long-lasting impact on its chemical composition and the organisms living in the lakes,” they warned. A national park in Poland’s southern mountains has completed testing of an electric bus that could replace horse-drawn carriages carrying tourists to a famous lake. World.title: Polish opposition PiS party set to split, with over 30 MPs being expelled
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. More than 30 MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, have effectively resigned after refusing to sign a loyalty pledge, party leader Jarosław Kaczyński has announced. The dispute centres around a more moderate faction in the party aligned with former prime minister and deputy PiS leader Mateusz Morawiecki, who is one of those now set to be expelled from the party. They have for months been unhappy with PiS’s move in a hard-right direction. 💬 Prezes PiS Jarosław Kaczyński @OficjalnyJK. 👉 Udostępnij pic.twitter.com/bycjE0Yq0f — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 24, 2026 “Around 30-something…of our group’s MPs have resigned,” revealed Kaczyński at a press conference on Friday. He added that their departures would be formalised at a meeting of the party’s political committee scheduled for Tuesday next week. Kaczyński’s announcement came after a deadline expired at midnight on Thursday for its MPs to sign a pledge of loyalty to the party that included a commitment not to be members of any external political associations. That measure was aimed in particular at an association called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) founded by Morawiecki in April. The former prime minister had always insisted that his organisation was intended as complementary to PiS, rather than a rival to it. However, many figures in the party saw it as an attempt by Morawiecki to create a separate centre of power, and potentially to use the association as a launchpad for creating his own party ahead of the autumn 2027 parliamentary elections. The right-wing opposition PiS party has threatened disciplinary action, including exclusion from electoral lists, against dozens of its MPs who have joined a new internal group led by former PM @MorawieckiM and intended to appeal to more moderate voters https://t.co/y62Cm361U2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 17, 2026 After PiS issued a resolution on Wednesday last week requiring that its parliamentarians pledge to withdraw from any such associations, most of its 186 MPs quickly complied. However, a group of between 30 and 40 who are part of Development Plus refused to do so. “Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” said Kaczyński on Friday. “And so they made the decision they did.” “In this situation, we cannot view the [Development Plus] association as anything other than a component of a plan…to split our party,” he added. However, although its supporters will now leave PiS, “we want to part ways without any animosity”, said Kaczyński. After Kaczyński’s announcement, senior figures from Development Plus made clear that no one from their association had resigned from PiS. They had simply not signed the declaration of loyalty demanded by the party. Later, Morawiecki himself held a press conference in parliament surrounded by his supporters. He claimed that an unnamed “small group of schemers” within PiS had been seeking to turn Kaczyński against him and push him out of the party. “We fought for the unity of Law and Justice until the very end,” declared Morawiecki, who said that his group included 40 MPs, one senator and three MEPs. However, three of the MPs are not members of PiS, and therefore were not expected to sign the loyalty declaration. Szanowni Państwo! 🟦Do ostatniej chwili walczyłem o jedność Prawa i Sprawiedliwości. Nie o stanowiska. Nie o osobiste ambicje. Nie o wpływy. 🟦Walczyłem o jedność obozu, który przez osiem lat zmieniał Polskę – budował jej bezpieczeństwo, rozwijał gospodarkę i przywracał godność… pic.twitter.com/PP7sOkzMHp — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 24, 2026 If the expulsion of Morawiecki’s supporters is confirmed, it will mark a major shake-up of Poland’s political landscape. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, PiS has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemyszław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Morawiecki, who was an international banker before joining PiS to become finance minister and then prime minister, wants the party to focus on more technocratic issues, such as economic development, rather than Euroscepticism and culture wars. That has led to frequent public sparring between his supporters and others in the party. In April, PiS threatened disciplinary action against members of Development Plus. Kaczyński and Morawiecki then reached an agreement that allowed the association to continue. But that uneasy truce has now fallen apart. World.title: Polish president renews bid for referendum on EU climate policy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has submitted a second request to parliament for a nationwide referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the European Union’s climate policies, which he argues are too costly. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, first proposed a referendum in May. But it was rejected by the Senate, the upper house of parliament, where the more liberal government has a majority. Senators argued that the proposed referendum question was “absurd”. The president has now submitted a revised proposal featuring a simplified question and again proposed holding the referendum on 27 September this year. Nawrocki’s originally proposed question was: “Are you in favour of implementing EU climate policy, which has led to an increase in citizens’ cost of living, energy prices and the cost of running business and agricultural activity?” However, following criticism in the Senate that the question was clearly intended to elicit a specific answer, this time he has proposed a more neutral one: “Are you in favour of Poland implementing the European Union’s climate policy?” “I’m looking for compromises, looking for solutions,” said Nawrocki on Thursday while announcing the new referendum bid. “The Senate wasn’t satisfied with the [previous] question”, so “we prepared a different one…[that] does not suggest anything”. However, the president has also proposed that the ballot paper would include information on what answering “yes” or “no” would mean in practice. Voters would be told, for example, that maintaining EU climate policy would result in, among other things, “Poland bearing costs estimated at 3.5 trillion zloty by 2040”, “burdens on agriculture”, “increasing costs for industry” and “obligations for owners of buildings”. By contrast, voting “no” would mean “negotiating exceptions and exemptions for Poland with the relevant EU bodies that will protect Polish industry and citizens from the burdens of climate policy”. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Under Poland’s constitution, the president may call a referendum with the approval of a majority of senators in a vote where at least half of all members of the 100-seat chamber are present. The ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk controls 63 seats in the Senate, making approval of proposals brought forward by Nawrocki, who often clashes with the government and regularly vetoes its bills, unlikely. While the government is generally pro-EU, it has also been critical of Brussels’ green policies, arguing that they place too great a burden on Poland. After the European Commission last Friday unveiled changes intended to soften the impact of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), the EU’s flagship climate policy, they were welcomed by the Polish government as a step in the right direction. Dzisiaj robimy milowy krok w zmianie systemu ETS. Po raz pierwszy Komisja Europejska proponuje rozwiązania, które łagodzą, a nie zaostrzają wpływ systemu na gospodarkę i obywateli. To efekt konsekwentnych działań Polski i zbudowania silnej koalicji państw w UE. Dzisiejsza… pic.twitter.com/5AMd9KCBVa — Ministerstwo Klimatu i Środowiska (@MKiS_GOV_PL) July 17, 2026 However, in his written justification for the new referendum proposal, Nawrocki wrote that, while he had “given the government time” in its push for ETS reform, the final result was simply “technical adjustments” that postpone some elements but do “not change the direction” or ultimate outcome. “ETS will remain an increasingly expensive, increasingly extensive system, and increasingly burdensome for the Polish economy,” wrote the president. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), which is the main opposition and supported Nawrocki’s bid for the presidency last year, wants Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS. Government figures warn, however, that there is no way to do so without either accruing enormous fines or leaving the EU entirely. When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Nawrocki’s new referendum proposal was met with criticism by figures from the ruling coalition. “There is no possibility of one country suspending part of EU law,” wrote Stanisław Gawłowski, a senator from Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party. “This referendum is pure fraud.” Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, also from KO, wrote that, “as the Brits have learned, the Europhobe’s dream world, in which one enjoys all the privileges of EU membership without any obligations, does not exist”. However, Nawrocki’s initiative was welcomed by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of PiS, who wrote that, “on such fundamental matters as climate policy, Poles should decide, not Brussels bureaucrats”. Zaproponowane przez @NawrockiKn pytanie referendalne jest wybiórcze. Kontrpropozycja: „Czy jesteś za likwidacją unijnych dopłat do inwestycji i dla rolników?” Jak przekonali się Brytyjczycy, świat eurofoba, w którym ma się same przywileje członkostwa w UE, nie istnieje. — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) July 23, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
