World.title: Poland appoints new human rights commissioner
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has chosen Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram as Poland’s new human rights commissioner. She will take office after the five-year term of the incumbent, Marcin Wiącek, expires today. Gregorczyk-Abram is a prominent lawyer and activist, who is particularly well known for opposing the overhaul of the judiciary by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. PiS, which is now the main opposition party, strongly opposed her election, arguing that she is politically aligned with the current, more liberal government. Gregorczyk-Abram herself, however, has pledged to “put all my beliefs and views aside” when she takes up the new role. Senat wyraził zgodę na powołanie Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram na Rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich. pic.twitter.com/gz3rwGy3hi — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) July 22, 2026 The commissioner for human rights (widely known by its Polish initials, RPO) is appointed by a resolution of the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, with the consent of the upper-house Senate. Candidates must meet certain requirements, including not belonging to any political party and having legal expertise and relevant experience. As well as acting as a watchdog for human rights, the RPO also has the power to submit motions to the Constitutional Tribunal to assess the constitutionality of laws and to file so-called cassation appeals to the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative Court against rulings by lower courts. Poland’s human rights commissioner has written to the government expressing concern that a "temporary" ban on asylum claims by most migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus remains in place after more than a year https://t.co/9SA2TypQdK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Gregorczyk-Abram was last month nominated as a candidate to be the new RPO by the main ruling party, Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), along with one of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica). PiS proposed a rival candidate, Adam Borowski, a veteran of Poland’s anti-communist struggle in the 1980s. However, critics argued that Borowski, an activist and former PiS election candidate, does not appear to have the requisite legal knowledge and experience. In a Sejm vote last Friday, the ruling coalition supported Gregorczyk-Abram, who won 233 votes to Borowski’s 177. On Wednesday, her candidacy was also supported by the Senate, with 59 votes in favour and 25 against, confirming that she will become the new RPO. Gregorczyk-Abram is best known as one of the founders and leaders of the Free Courts (Wolne Sądy) initiative launched in 2017 amid a wave of protests against the then-PiS government’s efforts to take greater control over the judiciary. Free Courts was prominent in efforts to defend the rule of law. Many of its leading figures are now associated with the current ruling coalition: Maria Ejchart is a deputy justice minister, while Michał Wawrykiewicz is a member of the European Parliament representing KO. In April last year, Gregorczyk-Abram was made chairwoman of a commission established by the current government to look into cases of abuse of power against civil society under the former PiS administration. In September, her commission published its first findings, in which it said that public media outlets under PiS control had “carried out systematic repressive and defamatory actions against activists, non-governmental organisations, and civil society”. Poland's public media “carried out systematic repressive actions against activists, NGOs and civil society” during the rule of the former PiS government, a report commissioned by the new government has found https://t.co/S2MO9KGssC — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2025 PiS argues that Gregorczyk-Abram’s previous activity makes her unsuitable as a suitable candidate for RPO, which is meant to be a non-partisan role. They also point to claims that she was involved in a group of legal figures that discussed the Tusk government’s controversial takeover of public media in December 2023. “[She] is a discredited and extremely politicised person who should be brought to justice, and not receive the laurels of the commissioner for human rights,” former PiS justice minister Marcin Warchoł told the Do Rzeczy weekly last month. After a Sejm committee hearing on Gregorczyk-Abram’s candidacy earlier this month, former PiS deputy justice minister Sebastian Kaleta criticised her for ignoring questions over her alleged “role in the illegal takeover of public media”. Zadałem Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram serię pytań o jej działania i możliwe spotkania z Ewą Wrzosek w sprawie przejęcia TVP, w tym możliwego tworzenia dokumentów prokuratorskich w prywatnej kancelarii. Kandydatka ostentacyjnie zdecydowała się ignorować te pytania. Ma bardzo dużo do… — Sebastian Kaleta (@sjkaleta) July 15, 2026 Speaking to state broadcaster TVP on Wednesday after her appointment was confirmed by the Senate, Gregorczyk-Abram declared that, “from the moment I take the oath and assume the position of commissioner, I will be independent and sovereign”. She pledged to “put all my beliefs and views – because each of us has them – aside and become an advocate for all citizens, regardless of what they believe in, how they live, or who they vote for”. Gregorczyk-Abram said that among her priorities as RPO would be the justice system, supporting the rights of disabled people and their carers, protecting older people, and fighting hate speech. With regard to the last of these issues, she noted that certain politicians present some groups as “enemies”, pointing to how this previously happened with LGBT+ people and judges, and is now being directed towards Ukrainians. Those are all groups who have at various stages been targeted by PiS and other right-wing parties. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. World.title: New Railway Tunnel to Cut Prague to Pilsen Journey to 45 Minutes
World.content:
The Czech government has approved the next phase of one of its largest railway infrastructure projects: a new tunnel connecting Prague and Beroun.

Construction is expected to begin in 2032, with completion scheduled for 2044.

The 24.7-kilometre double-track tunnel will significantly shorten travel times on one of the country’s busiest rail corridors.

Once completed, trains will travel between Prague-Smíchov station and Beroun in around 13 minutes, reducing the current journey time by more than 30 minutes.

The project will also improve connections towards western Czechia and neighbouring Germany. The journey from Prague to Pilsen is expected to take approximately 45 minutes, while international rail services to Munich and Nuremberg will become faster and more reliable.

New railway line designed for speeds of up to 200 km/h

The planned railway route will include a new high-speed section designed for trains travelling at up to 200 km/h. The tunnel will begin near Prague-Smíchov station, pass beneath the Barrandov area, and emerge near Beroun.

A separate connection on the Prague side is also planned, linking the new line with Braník Bridge and Prague-Krč. The additional infrastructure will improve connections within the capital while increasing capacity on the wider railway network.

Construction preparation underway

Preparatory work for the tunnel is already in progress. Geological surveys and technical documentation are currently being completed, with the application for a construction permit expected to be submitted between 2028 and 2029.

After the approval process, Správa železnic will launch a tender to select the construction company responsible for building the tunnel.

The Czech Railway Administration estimates the total cost of the project will continue to rise due to inflation and increasing construction expenses. However, its director general Tomáš Tóth said the estimated cost of around CZK 3 billion per kilometre remains comparable with similar railway tunnel projects abroad.

The project is expected to increase railway capacity towards western Czechia, improve timetable reliability, and strengthen connections between Prague, Pilsen, and major German cities.

World.title: Thailand Brings Its Culture and Flavours to Prague at Thai Market 2026
World.content:
The colours, flavours, and warm spirit of Thailand return to the capital on Friday, 4 September 2026, as the Royal Thai Embassy proudly hosts Thai Market 2026 at the historic Písecká brána.

Organised alongside Team Thailand—comprising the Thai Trade Centre and the Tourism Authority of Thailand in Prague—this year’s flagship event is held in active cooperation with the Prague 6 Municipality.

“Thai Market has become a meaningful platform to bring Thailand closer to the Czech public through friendship, creativity, and people-to-people connections,” said H.E. Mr. Pichit Boonsud, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Thailand to the Czech Republic.

“This year, we are thrilled to celebrate Prague 6 Day with our Thai Market to show our true partnership with the local municipality. This event is a heartfelt cultural exchange and our way of actively engaging with the wonderful community that hosts us.”

Open to all ages with free admission, the event will offer a full day of authentic Thai experiences, from traditional cuisine and refreshing drinks such as Thai iced tea to popular desserts including Mango Sticky Rice and Thai tea ice cream.

Visitors can also take part in interactive workshops, including a mini Loy Krathong celebration with origami lotus basket-making, traditional Thai clothing photo sessions, and postcard design with Thai stickers.

The programme will also feature live stage performances, premium Thai products from Czech importers, traditional Thai massages, and activities where guests can win vouchers to spend at the event.

A dedicated tourism section will provide inspiration and information for those planning their next trip to Thailand. Thai Market 2026 promises to be a vibrant celebration of Thai culture, flavours, and community in the heart of Prague.

Event Details Event:

Date: Friday, 4 September 2026

Time: 11.00-17.30

Venue: Písecká brána, K Brusce 5, 160 00 Prague 6 – Hradčany

Admission: Free entry

World.title: Future of Prague’s Výtoň Bridge Could Be Decided by the End of This Year
World.content:
The Railway Administration (Správa železnic) is expected to decide on the future design of Prague’s Výtoň Railway Bridge by the end of this year.

If the final plan is approved, construction could begin in 2028.

The long-delayed project has become the centre of a dispute between transport authorities and heritage experts. While railway officials argue that a new three-track structure is necessary to meet future transport demands, conservationists continue to push for the preservation of the existing historic bridge.

The Railway Administration has warned that the current condition of the bridge requires a final decision soon.

Dispute over historic structure

The main proposal currently under consideration is the construction of a new three-track railway bridge. Správa železnic selected a project team last year, but the plan remains controversial due to opposition from heritage authorities and groups seeking to preserve the original structure.

The debate has also attracted international attention. UNESCO representatives are preparing a Heritage Impact Assessment (HIA), which will examine how the planned changes could affect Prague’s cultural heritage.

The Transport Association supports the construction of a new bridge, arguing that rebuilding the existing structure would be more expensive and would not provide enough additional capacity.

Construction could start in 2028

According to earlier plans from Správa železnic, work on the project was originally expected to begin sooner. A tender process was completed in 2025, with companies SUDOP Praha and TOP CON SERVIS selected for the preparation of the three-track bridge project.

The estimated cost of the entire project is around CZK 3.4 billion.

Because of the bridge’s deteriorating condition, trains currently operate on only one track and must reduce speed when crossing the structure. The construction of the additional third track alone is expected to cost approximately CZK 129 million.

World.title: Prague Compared to 11 European Cities: Housing, Jobs, Transport,
World.content:
A new report from the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR) compares life in Prague with 11 other European cities, following a typical resident’s day—from housing and commuting to work, education, and leisure.

Based on verified data collected directly from partner cities, the study highlights both Prague’s strengths and its biggest challenges.

Prague Has Some of Europe’s Least Affordable Housing

The report found that Prague has the least affordable owner-occupied housing among the cities compared.

Buying an apartment requires more than 13 years of gross salary, placing Prague alongside cities such as Barcelona, Munich, and Amsterdam. Unlike many Western European cities, Prague also lacks relatively affordable rental housing.

Renting a 60-square-meter apartment costs around 40% of the average salary in Prague. By comparison, the same apartment would consume about 28% of average income in Munich and just 14% in Vienna.

Strong Job Market, But Lower Incomes

Prague continues to have one of the lowest unemployment rates in Europe, making it relatively easy to find work.

However, real incomes remain below those of most Western European capitals. Workers in Munich earn roughly 50% more than those in Prague, while wages in cities such as Copenhagen have grown steadily over the past decade.

Although Prague residents now work fewer hours than they did ten years ago—less than 39 hours per week on average—they still work around three hours more each week than people in many Western European cities.

Public Transport Is One of Prague’s Biggest Strengths

Prague ranks among Europe’s top cities for public transport.

Around 70% of residents use public transport regularly, while 87% report being satisfied with the service. The city’s extensive tram, metro, and rail networks make commuting easy, and the system stands out for its reliability, dense coverage, and affordability.

A monthly public transport pass costs less than 1% of the average monthly income, making Prague one of the most affordable cities for public transport after Barcelona.

Car Ownership Continues to Rise

Despite having one of Europe’s best public transport systems, Prague continues to see a steady increase in car ownership.

Together with Warsaw and Bucharest, Prague is one of the few cities in the study where the number of registered cars is still growing significantly. By contrast, cities such as Stockholm, Copenhagen, and Vienna have between one-third and one-half fewer cars per capita and a much higher share of electric and hybrid vehicles.

The report warns that increasing car ownership contributes to traffic congestion, road accidents, poorer air quality, and greater pressure on public space.

World.title: Meet the Four Prague Pizzerias Recognized in 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026
World.content:
Prague’s growing pizza scene gained international attention after four local restaurants were recognized in the 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026 guide.

The biggest success went to Pizza Nuova, which secured 30th place among the best pizzerias in Europe outside Italy. While the restaurant slipped a few places compared with last year’s ranking, it remains the only Czech establishment to appear in the guide’s main European list.

Located near Prague’s Kotva department store, Pizza Nuova has built its reputation on authentic Neapolitan pizza made with premium Italian ingredients. The restaurant also holds certification from the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana, an organization that promotes traditional Neapolitan pizza-making standards.

Prague’s recognition extended beyond a single restaurant. Three additional venues received the guide’s Excellent Pizzerias distinction, awarded to restaurants that consistently demonstrate outstanding quality.

This year’s recipients are Da Pietro, Sasy The Original, and Diskotéka in Prague’s Dejvice district.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pizzeria Da Pietro Praha (@dapietropraha)

Diskotéka is one of this year’s notable newcomers. Shortly after opening, the restaurant attracted attention for its distinctive interior, centered around a large silver pizza oven designed to resemble a disco ball.

Alongside its food, the venue hosts DJ nights and combines a traditional pizzeria with a relaxed social gathering space.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Diskotéka Pizza (@diskoteka.pizza)

The annual 50 Top Pizza rankings are compiled by anonymous inspectors who visit restaurants without prior notice. Their assessments go well beyond the pizza itself, taking into account ingredient quality, dough preparation, baking technique, service, beverage selection, atmosphere, and the overall dining experience.

World.title: Czech Women Earn About CZK 109,000 Less Per Year Than Men
World.content:
Czech women earn significantly less than men on average, with the annual difference estimated at CZK 109,000.

New figures based on Eurostat data show the country’s gender pay gap remains above the EU average.

Across the EU, employed women earn an estimated CZK 93,800 less annually than men on average. The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), which converted the hourly wage gap into annual earnings, estimates that the combined difference across the bloc amounts to more than CZK 8.65 trillion every year.

Czech Republic exceeds the EU average

According to Eurostat, women across the European Union earned 11.1% less per hour than men in 2024. In practical terms, women received CZK 88.90 for every CZK 100 earned by men. The figures cover companies with at least ten employees.

Applying that methodology, the ETUC estimates that women in the Czech Republic earn roughly CZK 108,700 less per year than men, placing the country above the EU average.

Only a handful of member states recorded larger estimated annual gaps. Finland ranked highest at around CZK 183,500, followed by Austria (CZK 165,600), Germany (CZK 146,200) and Sweden (CZK 123,600).

At the opposite end of the scale, Luxembourg was the only EU country where women earned slightly more than men on average. There, women’s hourly earnings exceeded men’s by 0.8%, equivalent to roughly CZK 11,500 annually in their favor under the ETUC model. Estonia recorded the largest percentage gap in the bloc, at 18.8%.

Different methods produce different figures

National Czech statistics paint a somewhat different picture because they rely on a different methodology.

Data from the Czech Statistical Office shows that in 2025 the median gross monthly wage reached CZK 41,068 for women and CZK 47,648 for men. That represents a monthly difference of CZK 6,580, or just under CZK 79,000 over a full year.

The discrepancy does not mean either calculation is incorrect. Eurostat measures average gross hourly earnings, while the Czech Statistical Office compares median monthly wages. Because the indicators measure different aspects of income, the results cannot be directly compared.

Eurostat uses an unadjusted gender pay gap, which reflects a range of labor market factors, including differences in occupations, industries, management roles, work experience, career interruptions, age and the balance between public and private sector employment.

World.title: Spicy, Not Spicy: How This Chef Is Bringing Authentic Chinese Street Food to Prague
World.content:
At Manifesto Market, the aroma of Sichuan peppercorns and chili oil stands out among the usual mix of street food and drinks.

It comes from Lá Bù Lá Street, the more casual sibling of the restaurant Lá Bù Lá, both founded by Wen, a Chongqing native who wants to introduce Prague diners to the real flavors of her hometown.

Wen arrived in Prague in 2019 after being accepted into a Master’s program at the Prague University of Economics and Business. But studying was only part of the reason she moved. At 22, she wanted a new beginning and the chance to discover a different version of herself.

“There was something about Prague that attracted me immediately,” she says. “The architecture, the pace of life, the atmosphere of the city —

it all felt very charming. I wanted to see what kind of person I could become here.”

That decision eventually led her into the restaurant business, with four concepts launched over the years — two that closed and two that continue today.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lá Bù Lá Street (@labula_street)

Beyond the Stereotypes

For Wen, opening a Chinese restaurant in Prague was never only about selling food. It was also about showing people that Chinese cuisine is far more diverse than many stereotypes suggest.

“China is a huge country, and every region has its own culture and food traditions,” she says. Through her restaurants, she hopes guests become more curious about where dishes come from, how ingredients are used, and how different regions eat.

She also wants Chinese food to be seen as something connected to special occasions, not only a quick meal.

“Chinese food can create beautiful memories too,” she says. One example is Chongqing chili, which is often associated only with heat. Wen says there is much more to it.

“Many people think Chongqing chili is only about being spicy. But it is also about aroma,” she explains. The same applies to Sichuan peppercorns, where the famous numbing sensation is only part of the experience.

Learning the Hard Way

Wen’s path has not been simple. Her first two projects, Chi Xiao Mian and Mi I’m, did not succeed as she had hoped, but she sees them as important lessons.

“They taught me how to work with people, how to manage a team, and how important communication is,” she says.

The experience also taught her to stay focused on her original vision. Running a restaurant requires listening to others, but also knowing when to trust your own ideas.

“Building something meaningful always requires finding a balance between dreams and reality,” she says.

A Restaurant, and Then a Street

Today, Wen runs two concepts: Lá Bù Lá and Lá Bù Lá Street. The name, meaning “spicy, not spicy,” reflects the idea that Chongqing cuisine is about much more than just heat.

The original restaurant offers a deeper introduction to traditional Chongqing dishes, while Lá Bù Lá Street at Manifesto Market has a more relaxed atmosphere.

“It is more spontaneous and more social,” Wen says. The concept is inspired by street food culture in Chongqing, where people gather, share dishes, and spend time together.

At Manifesto, surrounded by music, travelers, and international crowds, the idea has naturally evolved. Some dishes work better for sharing, while others simply encourage people to stay longer.

“For us, food tastes better when shared,” Wen says. “Passed around a table. Offered to a friend. Or quietly stolen from someone else’s plate.”

Growing Step by Step

Like many restaurant owners, Wen faces daily challenges, from managing a team to introducing unfamiliar flavors to new customers. Building a group of people who share her values has been one of the most difficult parts.

When asked about opening more locations in Prague, she says the ambition is there — but there is no rush.

“Of course, I would love for more people to discover the food of my hometown,” she says. “But I am not in a hurry.”

For now, Wen is focused on improving the restaurants she already has and building a stronger team.

“When my team and I are truly ready, we can always begin the next journey,” she says. “For now, we are happy to keep growing step by step.”

World.title: Prague and Stockholm Launch Cross-Border Public Art Project
World.content:
Visitors in Prague and Stockholm will soon be able to communicate across borders through a pair of interactive public art installations designed to exchange anonymous messages between the two cities.

The linked installations, created by the Czech initiative Praho! project and its Swedish partner Stockholm! project, will open in Stockholm on August 20 and in Prague on August 31.

The installations are designed as private spaces intended for one visitor at a time.

After entering, participants answer a series of questions before listening to an authentic audio recording left by someone in the other city. They are then invited to record their own message, creating an ongoing exchange between residents and visitors in Prague and Stockholm.

According to the project team, the concept explores what happens when anonymous thoughts become personal through the human voice.

“The installation creates a space where you first listen to someone else—and only then can you speak,” the organizers said. “We want to explore how connecting two different cities through shared experiences can foster understanding.”

The initiative is part of Art & Design Without Borders, an international collaboration supported by the Erasmus+ programme. The project brings together organizations from the Czech Republic and Sweden to promote participatory art, community engagement and new approaches to public space.

Although they work closely together, Praho! project and Stockholm! project operate as independent non-profit organizations. Their partnership reflects a shared history rather than a branch structure.

Praho! project was founded in 2021 and focuses on participatory art in public and digital spaces. Through text-based interventions and an online platform, it has collected more than 30,000 anonymous responses addressing personal experiences and broader social issues. Those contributions have since been transformed into publications, exhibitions and artistic installations.

The concept, however, began even earlier. Founder Annamarie Čermáková first developed the idea in 2019 while studying at Stockholm University of the Arts. Returning to Sweden inspired the creation of Stockholm! project in 2025.

The project extends beyond the installations themselves. Organizers will also host workshops, educational programmes, international internships and prepare a methodology guide documenting best practices in participatory public art across different European settings.

World.title: Don’t try to swim here! Bathing banned at five Lake Velence beaches
World.content:
Bathing has been temporarily banned at five popular beaches on Hungary’s Lake Velence, as well as one beach on the Danube, after routine water quality tests detected bacterial contamination above legal limits. The restriction will remain in force until follow-up laboratory tests confirm the water is safe again.

The Fejér County Government Office has ordered a temporary bathing ban at six natural bathing sites following the latest official water quality monitoring. According to the authority, laboratory tests found bacterial contamination exceeding permitted levels, prompting the immediate precautionary measure.

The ban affects five beaches on Lake Velence, one of Hungary’s most popular summer destinations, as well as the Szalki Island Free Beach in Dunaújváros.

Which beaches are affected?

The following beaches are currently closed to swimmers:

Agárd Park Beach Camping (Gárdony-Agárd)

Tini Beach (Gárdony)

Velence North Beach

Velence Korzó and Free Beach

Velence Resort & Spa Beach

Szalki Island Free Beach (Dunaújváros)

Officials stressed that the restriction is temporary and will be lifted as soon as repeated laboratory tests confirm that water quality once again complies with microbiological standards.

Enterococcus bacteria detected

According to reports, self-monitoring water samples collected by beach operators on 21 July showed Enterococcus bacteria levels above the legal threshold at several Lake Velence beaches. As a result, the microbiological quality of the bathing water no longer met public health requirements.

The government office has ordered operators to suspend bathing, inform visitors about the restrictions and ensure the ban is enforced until the water is declared safe.

Alleged failure to enforce the closure

The situation has also sparked controversy in the town of Velence. According to the municipality, the operator of Velence Korzó and Free Beach allegedly failed to comply with the official order, FEOL writes. Local authorities said they instructed the operator to close the beach immediately, install warning signs and prevent bathing, but claimed they received no response.

During a site inspection on 24 July, municipal officials reportedly found that the beach remained open, visitors were still swimming, and information boards continued to display “good” or “excellent” water quality ratings despite the bathing ban.

The municipality has urged visitors to respect the restrictions and choose alternative activities in the area until the water quality improves. Officials highlighted that the Lake Velence region continues to offer hiking opportunities, cultural events, restaurants, wellness facilities and other leisure activities.

If you missed it: Lake Velence property prices defy climate change, but can they stay up forever?

Drought adds to Lake Velence’s problems

The closures come as Lake Velence is already facing severe environmental stress from prolonged drought. Low water levels have significantly altered parts of the lake, with some areas appearing unusually dry after months of exceptionally hot and arid weather.

The authorities are continuing control water quality tests, and the bathing bans will be lifted without delay once the results confirm the affected beaches meet the required health standards again.

World.title: Hungarian forint is the weakest since elections, still manages to hold on
World.content:
The Hungarian forint strengthened on Friday against all three major foreign currencies, recovering from recent losses and ending the week on a firmer footing. While the domestic currency remains weaker than it was at the start of June, it has posted solid gains since the beginning of the year.

Forint rebounds after recent pressure

The Hungarian forint started Friday on a positive note in the interbank foreign exchange market, reversing some of the weakness seen earlier in the week.

During Thursday’s trading, the euro briefly climbed close to HUF 365, raising concerns that the forint’s recent decline could continue. However, sentiment improved overnight, allowing the Hungarian currency to recover.

By 9 AM on Friday, the euro had fallen to HUF 363.10 from HUF 364.58 on Thursday evening. The US dollar slipped from HUF 320.50 to HUF 318.65, while the Swiss franc eased from HUF 392.24 to HUF 390.54, writes Tőzsdefórum.

Stronger finish by the afternoon

The forint continued to strengthen throughout the day. By 6 PM, one euro was trading at HUF 362.19, compared with HUF 364.12 early in the morning. The US dollar fell from HUF 320.04 to HUF 318.12, while the Swiss franc declined from HUF 391.48 to HUF 389.55.

Market data also showed an even stronger late-afternoon performance, with the euro briefly trading around HUF 361.05, the dollar at HUF 317.55, and the Swiss franc at HUF 388.16. Overall, the forint gained around 0.5% against both the euro and the Swiss franc during the day, while strengthening 0.6% against the US dollar.

Still below June levels, but ahead for the year

Despite Friday’s recovery, the Hungarian currency remains weaker than it was at the beginning of June. Compared with the start of the month, the forint is still down by 1.7% against the euro, 1.8% against the US dollar and 0.9% against the Swiss franc.

The broader picture for 2025, however, remains considerably more positive. Since the beginning of the year, the forint has appreciated by:

5.8% against the euro,

2.8% against the US dollar,

5.7% against the Swiss franc.

This might also interest you: The art of selling property in Hungary — Getting the best price in 2026

Key economic data could drive next moves

Friday’s trading session was expected to remain sensitive to fresh macroeconomic data. Hungary’s Central Statistical Office (KSH) was due to release employment figures, while the afternoon brought purchasing managers’ index (PMI) data from both the eurozone and the United States.

These indicators are closely watched by investors and could influence currency markets in the short term. And although the forint has regained some lost ground, analysts will be watching whether the latest rebound marks the beginning of a more sustained recovery or merely a temporary correction.

World.title: The art of selling property in Hungary: Getting the best price in 2026
World.content:
My previous columns looked at the Hungarian property market almost entirely through the buyer’s eyes – how foreign nationals can purchase, where to look, how the process works and what happens on inheritance. This piece is about the other side: the seller’s. The occasion is a natural one – those who inherit property often wish to sell it, and those who bought years ago are now weighing a sale after an exceptional run of price growth. Selling property in Hungary well, however, takes at least as much expertise as buying well, and the rules are the same across the whole country.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Timing: what the 2026 market means for a seller

2025 – with the highest nominal house-price growth in the European Union – was an extraordinary seller’s market. 2026 is different: prices are stabilising, buyers are more selective and negotiation is once again part of the process. This is not bad news for sellers; it is a different task. A good property at a good price still sells quickly, but the market no longer forgives overpricing. A seller who starts at a realistic price negotiates from strength; one who starts at an unrealistic price advertises for months and often closes below the realistic level in the end.

The art of pricing

The most common seller mistake is the “we can always come down” logic. On the public market every listing’s age is visible, and a property that lingers acquires the stale label – which buyers then use as negotiating leverage. The correct starting price rests not on hopes but on actual comparable transactions: not asking prices, but what similar homes genuinely sold for. This is where an advisor who knows the local market adds the most to the outcome.

Public or discreet sale?

Not every property should be advertised publicly. For an average apartment, broad visibility is an advantage; for a significant, characterful home – a Buda villa, a Danube-front residence, a Balaton estate – discretion itself often protects value. A long-standing pattern across international premium markets is that a substantial share of the most valuable homes changes hands privately, without a public listing: the seller’s privacy is protected, the property does not “age” on the portals, and only genuinely qualified buyers ever see it. Choosing between the two routes is the first strategic decision a seller must make.

Preparation: what the buyer sees, and what their lawyer sees

Preparing a property for sale happens on two levels. What the buyer sees: tidy, well-lit spaces, professional photography, home staging where needed – these are not costs but investments in defending the price, and they also count as deductible selling expenses for tax purposes. What the buyer’s lawyer sees: a clean title deed, settled encumbrances, accessible condominium documents and an energy certificate. With a well-prepared property, the buyer’s due diligence takes days; an untidy title can stretch the process by weeks or months, or sink the deal entirely.

The deposit from the seller’s side

Home staging: not a trend but a measurable return

The most frequently misunderstood element of preparation deserves a section of its own. Home staging is neither decoration nor a passing fashion: it is the deliberate preparation of a home so that the buyer sees not square metres but a life. And its result is not a matter of taste but of numbers: according to the latest survey by the US National Association of Realtors, professionally staged homes typically sell for 1–10% more, and in the premium segment the difference can reach 15% – while time on the market shortens noticeably. Industry data tracking actual transactions shows that a substantial share of staged homes sells above the asking price, with the investment returning a multiple of its cost. For a home of significant value this is no longer an exercise in style but the most cost-effective instrument of price defence. And as noted above: the documented cost of staging is deductible from the tax base – so the result shows up not only in the sale price but on the tax return as well.

The foglaló binds the seller too: if the deal falls through by the seller’s fault, double the amount received must be repaid. Choosing between offers is therefore never purely a question of price. A mortgage-financed buyer, a non-EU buyer awaiting an acquisition permit and an immediately liquid cash buyer represent three different risk profiles – and the highest offer is not always the surest closing. The contract’s conditions should be built accordingly, with funds routed through an attorney’s escrow account.

Taxation when selling property in Hungary: the five-year rule

The main tax a seller faces is the 15% personal income tax on the gain – which, however, shrinks step by step with each year of ownership. In the year of acquisition and the following year the full gain is taxable, in the second year 90%, in the third 60%, in the fourth 30%, and from the fifth year the sale is entirely tax-free. For inherited property, the acquisition date is the date of the deceased’s death and the acquisition value is the value established in the probate proceedings – so someone who inherits and sells a home long held in the family is typically in a favourable position. Documented selling costs – agency fees, photography, home staging, advertising – and value-adding improvements are also deductible from the tax base.

When the buyer is foreign

It is increasingly natural on the Hungarian market for the best offer to come from abroad. Where the buyer is a non-EU national, the seller should know that the buyer needs an acquisition permit with a statutory 45-day deadline – this stretches the schedule but does not increase the risk if the terms of the contract handle it properly. A staged, permit-conditional payment structure through an attorney’s escrow protects both parties, and the entire process can be completed without the buyer’s physical presence, by power of attorney.

In closing

Selling property in Hungary is not a single decision but a sequence of them – price, channel, buyer, conditions, taxation. In the more balanced market of 2026, these decisions carry more weight than at any point during the price surge of recent years. Successful transactions depend on a precise understanding of the local legal and tax environment.

If you missed it: From the offer to the land registry extract: how a safe property purchase works in Hungary

Emese Széll, an expert in the Hungarian premium real estate market, premiumingatlanok.com

World.title: New 2,500-ton railway bridge installed in major Budapest rail upgrade! – Photos
World.content:
A 2,500-tonne steel railway bridge has been lifted into place over Soroksári Road in Budapest as part of the ongoing Southern Circle Railway (Déli Körvasút) development, Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced on Facebook on Saturday.

Vitézy, who observed part of the installation on site, described the operation as a major milestone for both Budapest’s and Hungary’s railway network, while acknowledging that the project has previously faced criticism over procurement procedures and construction costs.

“Regardless of those concerns, we should not lose sight of the fact that a genuinely useful and meaningful investment is now being built,” he wrote.

Future Közvágóhíd station begins to take shape

According to the minister, the newly installed bridge will form part of the future Közvágóhíd railway station, one of the most important elements of the Southern Circle Railway project.

The station is designed to become a major transport interchange, allowing passengers travelling on suburban and long-distance trains crossing Budapest via the Southern Circle Railway to transfer directly to HÉV suburban rail services, trams and buses. Vitézy said the station is expected to become the new southern gateway to Budapest’s city centre, both in transport and urban planning terms.

Second bridge to complete four-track station

The current bridge is only the first phase of the new railway crossing. A second steel bridge is scheduled to be installed next summer, creating a four-track railway corridor with two island platforms at the new Közvágóhíd station.

Seven years in the making

Vitézy recalled that the concept for the Southern Circle Railway was first developed seven years ago together with railway planners and transport experts. He said it was a rare experience to see a project that had spent years on the drawing board finally becoming reality.

“It is a special feeling when something you’ve worked on for years is built before your eyes,”

he wrote, adding that he had been the first person to step onto the platform of the new station after the bridge had been positioned.

Photo: MTI

Thanks to workers and motorists

The minister also thanked engineers, contractors, MÁV railway specialists and everyone involved in carrying out the complex weekend operation. He also expressed gratitude to motorists using Soroksári Road for their patience during the bridge installation, which required significant traffic restrictions.

The Southern Circle Railway is one of Budapest’s largest ongoing railway infrastructure projects and aims to increase rail capacity through the capital while improving connections between suburban, regional and urban public transport services.

World.title: Trump: I’m considering resuming full-scale war with Iran if we don’t get 100% of what we want
World.content:
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he was considering resuming a full-scale war with Iran “if we don’t get 100% of what we want.”

In a phone call with French News Channel LCI, Trump said that he would resume a full-scale war with Iran “if we don’t get 100% of what we want, absolutely.” According to a report by Axios, Trump directed the US military not to launch new strikes on Iran on Friday, ending nearly two weeks of daily attacks.

After approving daily strikes for the previous 13 days, Trump reportedly declined to authorise Friday’s plan. It remains unclear whether the pause is temporary or marks a broader shift. When asked if he has any message for his European allies, Trump responded by saying: “They’re lucky they have me as their friend.”

Daily life continues despite late-night US airstrikes targeting Iran and rising tensions between the two countries in Tehran, Iran on 22 July 2026. Photo: Anadolu Agency

Trump did not comment when asked if he was considering imposing more tariffs on the EU, saying: “I don’t want to comment on that. Thank you very much.” On Friday, Trump threatened to impose tariffs on the European Union after accusing the bloc of unfairly targeting major US technology companies with multibillion-dollar fines.

“The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, citing penalties imposed on Apple, Meta, Amazon and Google. He also said the penalties imposed by the EU “will be entirely reversed” and that his administration expects to impose “a substantial TARIFF” on the European Union “at the earliest possible moment.”

World.title: Could Budapest’s beloved Planetarium finally reopen? Government launches talks after nine years of closure
World.content:
After nearly a decade standing empty, Budapest’s iconic Planetarium could finally be on the path to reopening, as the Hungarian government prepares to launch expert consultations on the future of the landmark attraction.

Several options on the table

Zoltán Tanács, Minister for Science and Technology, announced that discussions involving several government ministries will begin in early August with the aim of presenting a long-term proposal to the government. The initiative is expected to determine whether the facility will reopen in its current form, undergo a full renovation, or be replaced by a modern science museum and interactive experience centre.

According to the minister, officials are working towards a comprehensive strategy that would secure the Planetarium’s long-term future. Among the options under consideration are:

a temporary reopening of the existing facility;

a complete reconstruction of the current building;

the creation of an entirely new science museum and educational experience centre.

Tanács said the objective is to develop a proposal that would make it possible for the Planetarium to welcome visitors once again, writes HVG.

The Planetarium in 2008. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

A Budapest landmark closed since 2017

The TIT Planetarium first opened its doors in 1977 and quickly became one of Hungary’s best-known science attractions. For decades, it introduced generations of visitors to astronomy and space science, attracting an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 visitors annually.

However, the building was forced to close in 2017 after serious structural problems with its roof made it unsafe to operate. The deterioration had become increasingly apparent in previous years. In 2016, severe storm damage caused extensive leaks, forcing the Planetarium to suspend operations for six weeks during the summer.

Although emergency repairs were carried out and the roof was later restored with HUF 128 million (EUR 354,800) in funding by 2019, the comprehensive renovation needed to reopen the building never began. Plans for a full refurbishment were drawn up as early as 2018, but the project stalled.

Ownership complicates redevelopment

One of the main obstacles to restoring the Planetarium is its ownership structure. Although regarded as one of Budapest’s most beloved scientific attractions, the building is not owned by the Hungarian state.

Instead, it is operated by the Society for Dissemination of Scientific Knowledge (TIT), meaning that any major modernisation project would require substantial government funding and close cooperation between the owner and the state.

More on the Hungarian capital: Budapest’s busiest M3 metro to be extended after EU funding secured!

They want to give the Planetarium a purpose

Following a recent site visit with experts from both the Ministry of Science and Technology and the Ministry of Transport and Investment, Tanács argued that previous governments had failed to prioritise the Planetarium despite repair plans already being available.

He said the upcoming consultations are intended to finally resolve the future of a venue that provided unforgettable educational experiences for generations of Hungarians.

If the government approves the forthcoming proposal, Budapest’s long-shuttered Planetarium could once again become one of the capital’s leading science attractions, whether through the restoration of the historic building or the creation of an entirely new educational complex.

World.title: Tisza nominates renowned constitutional law expert for Hungary’s Constitutional Court
World.content:
Hungary’s Tisza parliamentary group has nominated Dr. Pál Sonnevend, one of the country’s leading constitutional law scholars, to fill the vacant seat on the Constitutional Court following the end of Csaba Hende’s mandate.

Tisza nominates a leading constitutional law scholar

The nomination was announced after Parliament’s Committee on Justice and Constitutional Affairs invited parliamentary groups to propose candidates for the vacancy. According to Tisza, the party’s parliamentary leader, Andrea Bujdosó, formally submitted Sonnevend’s name to the committee on Friday.

Sonnevend is the head of department at the Faculty of Law of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) and previously served as the faculty’s dean. Tisza described him as an internationally recognised expert in constitutional and international law with decades of experience in both academia and public service.

He used to work with former presidents

During his career, he worked at Hungary’s Constitutional Court alongside former President László Sólyom, one of the country’s most influential constitutional lawyers. He later served as a constitutional law adviser to former Presidents Ferenc Mádl and László Sólyom.

His academic work focuses on human rights, international law and the rule of law. Sonnevend has also represented Hungary before the International Court of Justice in The Hague and has appeared in cases before both the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union.

According to Tisza, his professional achievements have earned him recognition both in Hungary and internationally.

Tisza claims judges should answer only to the law

In a Facebook post announcing the nomination, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said the Constitutional Court’s role is to protect Hungary’s Fundamental Law, limit the exercise of state power and safeguard citizens’ fundamental rights.

He argued that the party had deliberately selected a candidate whose “professional competence, international reputation and constitutional commitment are beyond question”.

Magyar added that Hungary needs constitutional judges who make their decisions “solely on the basis of the law, their conscience and constitutional values”, describing Sonnevend’s nomination as reflecting that principle.

Election could come within days

Under Hungarian law, Parliament has up to 60 days to elect a new member of the Constitutional Court following a vacancy. However, the vote could reportedly take place as early as Monday, significantly earlier than the legal deadline.

Stay up-to date: Orbán changes tone at Tusványos — Fidesz recast its role as “resistance politics” shifts into gear

The prospect of such a rapid appointment has already drawn criticism from Amnesty International Hungary, which issued a statement before the nominee’s identity was announced.

The human rights organisation argued that there was no justification for the accelerated timetable, noting that the 60-day period exists to allow for broad professional and political consultations to identify the most suitable candidate.

Amnesty worded harsh criticism

Amnesty also claimed that the current procedure effectively eliminates even the limited consultation provided for under existing rules, arguing that it mirrors previous constitutional court appointments carried out without meaningful cross-party or professional consultation.

World.title: Romanian director Alina Șerban’s debut film “I Matter” to premiere at Venice Film Festival
World.content:
“I Matter” (“Eu contez”), the feature film debut of Romanian director Alina Șerban (in photo), will have its world premiere at the 83rd edition of the Venice International Film Festival, taking place from September 1-12.

Written and directed by Alina Șerban, one of the few Roma female directors in the world, “I Matter” is a co-production between Romania (microFILM), Germany (2Pilots Filmproduction), and Belgium (Frakas Productions, Lemming Film), exploring themes such as overcoming fear, hope, and self-acceptance, according to the press release.

Spoken in Romanian and Romani, the film tells the story of Rebeca, a young Roma woman who is about to leave the foster care center where she grew up.

“We very rarely see Roma characters who live complex human experiences beyond stereotypes. And stories about what it means to be a girl, Roma, and part of the child protection system are almost nonexistent. Through ‘I Matter’ I wanted to build a bridge toward a deeper understanding of these experiences and, above all, to tell a story about humanity. The fact that this film is beginning its journey in Venice means a great deal to me,” said Alina Șerban.

The film was developed over more than four years together with young people from the social protection system. During this period, Alina Șerban created several documentary short films and theater performances alongside them.

The film’s cast includes Denisa Farcaș, Sorin Mihai, Angelina Pavel, Vanessa Dancea, Raisa Mihai, Juno (Alexandru Stancu), Alina Berzunțeanu, and Natalia Călin. Alongside them, 16 children and young people residing in the Casa Iosif and Casa Sara foster centers, part of the Măgurele Christian Social Ensemble in Bucharest, also appear in the film.

The Venice International Film Festival / Mostra Internazionale d'Arte Cinematografica will take place from September 2-12, 2026. “I Matter” has been selected alongside seven other titles in the Spotlight section, dedicated to audience films characterized by innovation and creativity in the way they engage with viewers. The film is competing for the Audience Award offered by Armani Beauty and the Luigi de Laurentiis Award for Best Debut, awarded by an international jury.

Winner of the Best Actress award at the German Actors’ Association Awards for her role in Gipsy Queen (2019), Alina Șerban is a graduate of the prestigious Tisch School of the Arts (New York), Royal Academy of Dramatic Art – RADA (London), and UNATC. In 2024, she was decorated by the president of Romania with the Order of Cultural Merit, in the rank of Knight.

She is the first Roma film and theater director in Romania and, for more than a decade, has developed artistic projects dedicated to children and young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, as well as Roma communities.

(Photo source: Cornel Brad via press release)

World.title: Anti-corruption prosecutors detain three directors of state-owned Romanian defense companies
World.content:
Romania’s National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) officially announced on Friday, July 24, that it has detained three directors from companies within Romania's defense industry, all accused of taking bribes.

The three are Mihai Rafiu (general manager of Uzina Mecanică București), Tiberiu Alexandru Pîrvu (general manager of Uzina Mecanică Plopeni), and Liliana Sorescu (commercial director of Uzina Mecanică Plopeni).

Alongside the three, an administrator of several commercial companies was also detained, accused of giving bribes and complicity in giving bribes.

During searches, prosecutors found EUR 500,000 in cash at the home of Tiberiu Pârvu Alexandru. Authorities say Rafiu, for his part, allegedly received RON 48,000 from the businessman detained in this case, divided into 12 installments, according to the official DNA statement.

Tiberiu Pârvu Alexandru also allegedly received RON 25,900 from the same businessman "related to contracts concluded with the commercial companies effectively managed by defendant V.M."

The same businessman allegedly also bribed Liliana Sorescu. According to DNA, the total amount she allegedly received as bribes was RON 24,250, in several installments.

In addition, DNA also claimed that another businessman, who owns a company with contracts with Uzina Mecanică Plopeni, allegedly gave Liliana Sorescu USD 3,800, for "placing orders and carrying out the formalities necessary for the acceptance of the goods delivered by the respective companies."

Liliana Sorescu allegedly claimed that the dollars she received were counterfeit and requested the same amount once again, which she allegedly received in lei. "The contracts concluded by the two factories with the aforementioned commercial companies mainly concerned maintenance services, the purchase of materials, and the provision of services," DNA emphasized.

Reacting to the detention of the three directors, economy minister Irineu Darau said that "in general, the defense industry is an extremely sensitive subject. I am convinced that for some it is also a subject of temptation. A strong Romanian state must identify anyone connected to the defense industry who engages in dishonest activities.”

ROMARM, Romania's national state-owned defense company and the country's primary producer and exporter of military equipment, said in connection with the detention that it will support any legal action aimed at strengthening and reviving the defense industry.

The company noted that the problems within its subsidiaries have been known for some time and have been repeatedly brought to the attention of the Ministry of Economy, without answer.

The company's general manager, Răzvan Pîrcălăbescu, said in a statement cited by Digi24 that the reform plan was drafted by ROMARM's management, discussed with institutional partners, approved by the Board of Directors, and submitted to the Ministry of Economy for final approval, but so far the institution has made no decision.

World.title: Asia-born home improvement chain MR.DIY opens location at Bucharest’s Colosseum Mall
World.content:
MR.DIY, one of the world’s leading home improvement and lifestyle retailers, announced the opening of a location at Bucharest’s Colosseum Mall on Thursday, July 23.

Spanning over 800 sqm and developed following an investment of nearly half a million euros, the new MR.DIY store represents one of the most important openings within the retailer’s current national expansion plan, according to the press release.

The store offers a comprehensive one-stop-shop format offering customers access to thousands of practical everyday products across categories such as home improvement, household items, home organization, hardware and tools, stationery, toys, decorations, electrical accessories, car accessories and lifestyle products.

The opening is part of a process of diversification ongoing at the mall. Earlier this spring, Colosseum Mall also welcomed dm dogerie markt and Planeta Arthur bookstore.

The new store has been designed to deliver an accessible and efficient shopping experience, allowing customers to discover a broad assortment of products for everyday needs under one roof.

“This new store reflects our commitment to bringing the MR.DIY concept closer to Romanian consumers through accessible locations, a broad product assortment and affordable prices. Romania is an important market in MR.DIY’s European expansion strategy, and each new opening represents another step in building a strong long-term presence locally,” said Cătălin Secăreanu, representative of MR.DIY in Romania.

Established in Malaysia in 2005 with a single hardware store in Kuala Lumpur, MR.DIY has grown into one of Asia’s leading home improvement and lifestyle retailers, with a continuously expanding international presence across multiple markets. Today, MR.DIY operates in 15 countries worldwide, with more than 5,700 stores across Asia, Europe and other international markets.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: EUR 80 million refinancing for Bucharest underground telecommunications network operator Netcity
World.content:
Meridiam and its partners have successfully closed the EUR 80 million refinancing of Netcity Telecom, the operator of Bucharest's underground telecommunications network, the company announced.

According to the company, the refinancing operation, led end-to-end by Meridiam, represents the first project finance bond issuance in the country, and establishes a new market record with tenors of up to 26.5 years, surpassing Meridiam's previous 18-year market benchmark achieved in 2022.

The operation also provides flexibility to support a future expansion of the Netcity Telecom network and new digital infrastructure developments across Bucharest, Meridiam said.

Netcity Telecom has been operating the underground telecommunications network in Bucharest since 2008, in a 49-year concession agreement with the Bucharest City Hall.

It has so far developed more than 3,000 kilometers of underground telecommunications infrastructure across Bucharest, while removing overhead cables. Today, the network serves around 70,000 buildings, representing approximately half of all buildings in the city, and provides internet access to nearly 600,000 homes and office premises.

Netcity Telecom has worked with several districts of Bucharest in designing and deploying dedicated fiber networks for municipal CCTV projects. The company has also contributed to the implementation of the pilot phase of the new Bucharest Traffic Management System, and is currently involved in Smart School initiatives.

Meridiam has an 80% stake in Netcity Telecom, alongside E-INFRA Group (20%), a Romanian group active in the energy, construction, and telecommunications sectors.

Meridiam, an independent investment Benefit Corporation and asset manager, was founded in 2005 by Thierry Déau. The firm specializes in the development, financing, and long-term management of public infrastructure across three sectors: sustainable mobility, critical public services, and innovative low-carbon solutions. With offices in Addis Ababa, Amman, Dakar, Istanbul, Johannesburg, Libreville, Luxembourg, Paris, Vienna, and Washington, Meridiam manages USD24 billion and more than 130 projects to date.

(Photo: Jakub Krechowicz | Dreamstime.com)

World.title: Romanian manufacturer TeraPlast inaugurates polyethylene pipe factory in Spain
World.content:
Romanian building materials manufacturer TeraPlast Group inaugurated its TeraPlast Iberia polyethylene pipe factory in Spain, strengthening its expansion into Western European markets. The facility, located near Bilbao, is expected to serve customers across Spain, France, and North Africa.

The factory, inaugurated on July 23, is located in Okondo, in Spain's Álava province, about 20 kilometers from Bilbao. It has an annual production capacity of 16,000 tonnes and employs 79 people.

The opening follows TeraPlast's acquisition of the facility and forms part of the group's international expansion strategy after earlier investments in the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria, and Croatia.

“Romanian industry can compete and thrive at European level, and we demonstrate it through actions, not idealistic speeches. Following our expansion into the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria and Croatia, our entry into the Spanish market marks another important step in our international growth strategy,” said Dorel Goia, chairman of the TeraPlast Board of Directors.

The company plans to invest EUR 4 million in the Spanish factory over the next three years to increase production by 60% and achieve an EBITDA margin of more than 10%.

“The expanded production capacity will serve the markets of Spain, France, and North Africa. This will enable us to reduce leverage while generating returns on our investment for the benefit of the group's shareholders," Goia added.

According to the company, the factory has an established customer base in Spain, France, and Germany and will serve as a regional hub for the group's operations in Western Europe.

TeraPlast Group is the largest polymer processor in Southeastern Europe and operates production facilities in Romania, the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria, Croatia, and Spain. Its parent company, TeraPlast SA, is listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange under the symbol TRP.
