World.title: Teens charged after alleged machete brawl in Melbourne's CBD
World.content:
Police have charged four young people, who were all on bail, after an alleged machete brawl in Melbourne's CBD early on Sunday morning.

Two people received serious injuries during the altercation at the intersection of Elizabeth and Flinders streets, near Flinders Station.

Police said the incident occurred at about 5am after a verbal dispute between two females escalated.

"Others within their respective groups got involved," a spokesperson said.

"The incident escalated and one male brandishing a machete chased two males and allegedly slashed both, causing serious injuries to the hand of one male and the arm of the other."

Six people, aged between 16 and 23, were arrested in relation to the incident.

Four of those were charged with various offences, including committing an indictable offence while on bail.

A 17-year-old male from the Brimbank area was also charged with intentionally causing injury in circumstances of gross violence, affray, as well as possessing a prohibited weapon and drugs.

A 19-year-old man from Bacchus Marsh and a 16-year-old female from the Banyule area were both charged with affray, while a 23-year-old man from Laverton was charged with theft.

The 16- and 23-year-olds were let out on bail to appear in court at a later date.

Police said they gave a 17-year-old girl a caution for possession of drugs, while another young woman was released without charge.

The investigation continues, and police have urged any witnesses to come forward with information.

World.title: WA government considering new gas-fired power plant as coal phases out
World.content:
The Western Australian government is investigating building and running a new gas-fired power plant in the south of Perth as it prepares to switch off coal by 2030.

The government has identified a site at Naval Base for a 300-megawatt (MW) power station that is expected to cost more than half a billion dollars.

WA Premier Roger Cook said his government was committed to being the "first and only state" to switch off "all our state-owned coal-fired power stations by 2030".

"A clean energy transition involves renewable energy, backed by battery and firmed by gas," he told reporters on Sunday.

"That's why we need to do careful planning; I stress at this stage we are just going to the community consultation and planning phase."

The state will not be increasing its reliance on gas, according to the WA government.

Roger Cook says his government is committed to shutting all state-owned coal-fired power stations by 2030.

Mr Cook said this project, like the gas turbines at the Pinjar power station that was commissioned in 1989, would "replace existing assets that are coming to the end of their lives".

The energy needed to replace coal would come from renewables, including wind farms in the Mid-West, a government spokesperson said.

However, the state government has not put a price tag on the proposed project as it is still at an early stage.

Mr Cook says the proposed project aims to replace aging assets that are due to retire. (Supplied: APR)

This year, independent operator AGL stated it funded a similar 220-megawatt expansion at its Kwinana Swift Power Station for $450 million.

The ABC understands the state-owned project will be bigger and without existing infrastructure, with the cost expected to be higher.

A decision on the gas project is expected by the end of the year, as the state government is under pressure to meet its 2030 goals.

Bipartisan support

The project has rare bipartisan support, with the opposition suggesting it had the idea first.

"I do support this plan, because we built the exact same plan … two years ago," said WA Liberal energy spokesman Steve Thomas.

But Mr Thomas said the proposed power plant needed to do more than just replace existing gas turbines, if coal was to be switched off.

Steve Thomas says the state government needs new and additional gas to meet its goal. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"There is no way the government is closing down its coal fleet, on its current time frame, unless they have significantly more gas generation; that means they need new and additional gas, not just replacing old units," he told the ABC.

"They will need to have more than 300MW of new gas in total if they are going to keep the lights on past 2029."

He added that it would be "another failure of the transition plan" if the government was not putting more gas generation into the system.

"Some of the Pinjar units are due to retire in the mid-2030's, which means that this replacement is not really needed until then, which means in the meantime it is additional gas generation capacity."

The project will open to public consultation this week.

World.title: Hopes US and Iran will return to negotiating table after lull in hostilities
World.content:
Iran has passed another night without US air strikes, as Washington pauses a war nearing its fifth month and reports emerge that concerns over dwindling munitions were restraining plans for further escalation.

The lull has revived hopes of a return to negotiations after nearly two weeks of consecutive nightly US bombardments, although US media reported the pause could also reflect pressure on stockpiles of Patriot interceptors and other defensive weapons.

Houthis claim missile attacks on Saudi Arabia The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have claimed a missile attack on Saudia Arabia's cities of Jazan and Yanbu.

Fighting over the strategic Strait of Hormuz derailed diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran, but the conflict then expanded beyond the vital energy corridor to include attacks on US bases, regional shipping and Gulf allies.

However, US operations against Iran were "on a hold", CNN reported, quoting an unidentified Pentagon source, even as US President Donald Trump threatened a "much higher level" of strikes on Friday.

Plans to escalate the campaign have been shelved in part because of those shrinking supplies, The New York Times reported, citing two people briefed on the matter.

Mr Trump also faces the risk of a wider Middle East war, the estrangement of vulnerable Gulf allies and further shocks to the global economy, the newspaper said.

US Vice-President JD Vance and top general Dan Caine both raised concerns about escalation at a White House meeting on Friday, CNN reported.

General Caine told Mr Trump the military could carry out the options available to him successfully but warned of the possible implications, according to the network.

Trump undecided

Mr Trump said on Friday he had not decided whether to return to an all-out operation.

"We're talking to them right now. I think they're getting more and more serious," he said.

Mr Trump said Iran faced a choice between a deal and strikes at a "much higher level".

Donald Trump says he has not decided whether to return to an all-out operation against Iran. (AP: Rod Lamkey, Jr)

The war that Mr Trump once predicted would last four or five weeks is now nearing its fifth month, and is weighing on the Republicans' approval ratings ahead of crucial US midterm elections in November.

The Pentagon had presented Mr Trump with a plan for a 14th night of strikes but he declined to authorise it in favour of a push for talks, Axios reported.

Fighting spreads

Fighting has spread to a new front.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they struck Saudi Aramco sites in Jizan and Yanbu on Saturday, a day after Riyadh bombed Houthi targets.

A surface-to-air battery operated by Greek personnel in Saudi Arabia downed two ballistic missiles and a drone over Yanbu, the Greek air force media office said.

US and Iran trade strikes The strikes came after US President Donald Trump vowed "major military punishment" for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen over moves to block a second major international shipping route.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had stopped four ships attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz in 24 hours.

Tehran's effective blockade of the waterway remains the central flashpoint with Washington.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran could not be blamed for the escalation and offered to broker talks between the Houthis and Riyadh, saying "there is no military solution".

AFP

World.title: Millions of WA bees trucked across Nullarbor to save South Australian almonds
World.content:
Millions of West Australian bees are being trucked across the Nullarbor on a one-way mission to provide critical pollination for South Australia's almond industry.

Beekeepers are sending more than 7,500 healthy beehives to the neighbouring state where varroa mite has wreaked havoc on bee populations.

WA remains free of the bee parasite, but its beekeepers are nervous.

It is hoped thousands of WA beehives will boost the pollination of South Australian almonds. (Supplied: Steve Sannut)

Three prime movers humming with mite-free bees have crossed the South Australian border and another two trucks will make the journey in the coming days.

The bees were purchased by a commercial almond grower in a deal understood to be worth more than $2.3 million.

A dozen WA beekeepers delivered their bees to collection points in Donnybrook, Gingin and Esperance last week, fetching $350 per hive.

Trucks headed for the collection point were loaded with pallets of West Australian beehives. (Supplied: Steve Sannut)

In the nick of time

WA beekeeper Steve Sannut said the bees would be delivered right on time for the opening of the almond flowers, which is predicted to the precise day.

"It's two drivers, non-stop, all the way through to South Australia," he said.

"The hives travel with the entrances open because if it gets too hot the bees can come outside and sit on the front of the beehive.

Steve Sannut says millions of bees are on a one-way trip to varroa mite-ravaged South Australia. (Supplied: Steve Sannut)

"You definitely hear them on the outside [of the truck]."

Mr Sannut said the project had been in the making for several months after the same buyer initially purchased 600 hives this time last year.

He said the deal was "fruitful" for WA beekeepers who had enjoyed good conditions following last year's rain.

"Everyone's been able to achieve good results, as far as producing bees," he said.

Bees doomed by 'super mite'

Mr Sannut said while the delivered bees would boost almond pollination this season, they would eventually succumb to the deadly mite.

Bees are being decimated by the deadly varroa mite in Australia's eastern states. (Supplied: Phil Lester)

"This is the sad truth. These guys are going to get smashed," he said.

"We're just plugging a temporary hole.

" I put a blue dot on the queens ... they're in for a hard time. "

WA beekeepers remain nervous about the varroa mite reaching WA, as the most recent incursion continues to devastate eastern states colonies.

"We call it the super mite," Mr Sannut said.

"It's now carrying viruses, so beekeepers are getting whole apiaries wiped out."

Thousands of beehives bound for South Australia were dropped at collection points in WA. (Supplied: Steve Sannut)

The WA government spruiked the delivery of WA bees to South Australia as evidence of its biosecurity success, but this left a bitter taste in Mr Sannut's mouth.

"The government has done nothing extra," he said.

"If you talk to people in DPIRD [Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development] right now, they'd love a budget to be able to get more people out there inspecting stuff coming into our ports, our rail ports, and coming across the border."

A spokesperson for the WA government said DPIRD was delivering surveillance at ports and airports across the state, including 40 sentinel hives, catch boxes, floral sweeps and aerial pheromone monitoring at high-risk entry points.

"We continue to work closely with beekeepers and industry to strengthen our preparedness, including developing the state's varroa response strategy," they said.

West Australian beekeepers are supplying bees to South Australia to assist with almond pollination. (Supplied: WA Government)

Not enough healthy hives

Bee Industry Council of Western Australia (BICWA) chair Kate Byrne said the mite had killed most of the wild bees in the eastern states since it entered Australia in 2022 and was now decimating managed hives.

She said two different types of the mite were present, including a strain resistant to miticide.

"Because those hives have collapsed, there is now massive demand for managed honey-bee hives," she said.

Kate Byrne says bolstering biosecurity is the key to protecting local colonies from varroa mite. (Supplied: Kate Byrne)

"There's an estimated 290,000 hive shortfall for August pollination on the east coast this year.

" There just simply isn't enough hives over on the east coast to pollinate the crops. "

Ms Byrne said the situation was worsening and could impact food security.

"Decisions are having to be made around which crops will be provided with bees for pollination," she said.

Ms Byrne said BICWA's first priority was bolstering WA's biosecurity defences, and it was exploring options that included replacing sentinel hives with AI-capable detection units along the Nullarbor.

World.title: First H5 bird flu case confirmed on SA metro beach
World.content:
The CSIRO says two native birds found dead on separate beaches in South Australia have tested positive for the H5 strain of bird flu.

It is the first time a case has been confirmed on a SA metropolitan beach.

The two additional cases were flagged yesterday as suspected cases.

A greater crested tern was found near Robe on South Australia's Limestone Coast, while another greater crested tern was found at a beach ramp near the Semaphore Surf Life Saving Club, north-west of Adelaide.

Acting Australian chief veterinary officer Sam Hamilton said there have now been 20 confirmed or presumed positive detections of H5 bird flu in Australia.

"All of these have been individual wild seabirds found in coastal locations," Dr Hamilton said in a statement.

"There remains no evidence of any mass mortality events and there are no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system.

There are now seven confirmed H5 bird flu cases in SA. (ABC Goldfields & Esperance: Tara de Landgrafft)

"The risk to human health remains low."

SA Environment Minister Emily Bourke said on Saturday the bird found in Robe was located 4 kilometres from the location where the first Australian seabird confirmed to have the H5 strain of bird flu was found.

"Unfortunately, we are finding that these two cases are in our local [bird] species," Ms Bourke said.

Previous confirmed cases involved migratory birds from the sub-Antarctic region.

South Australia's first confirmed case was in a giant petrel found on the Fleurieu Peninsula on June 14.

As of today, there are seven confirmed cases in SA, 10 in WA, and two in NSW.

Queensland confirmed its first H5 bird flu case yesterday after a dead petrel was found on Moreton Island, east of Brisbane.

Before the two suspected cases were confirmed on Sunday, Premier Peter Malianauskas said the government's policy in response to the bird flu remains the same.

"We still don't have any evidence of it being anywhere near poultry facilities or the poultry industry, which of course is the biggest risk that we're keeping a close eye on," Mr Malinauskas said.

The premier said despite there being evidence of the bird flu in the native Australian bird population, he had received advice it cannot be "automatically assumed that means a spread throughout the population."

South Australia's chief veterinary officer Skye Fruean said it was too early to tell whether local transmission of H5 bird flu was occurring in Australia.

"We are still awaiting some further laboratory analysis from these two cases which would tell us exactly how related these strains are to other strains we've detected in Australia," Dr Fruean said.

"It also may just tell us that these are separate introductions like the other cases we've had to date.

"I'm expecting what we will find is that these are isolated introductions like all the other cases; until we have further evidence that it's spreading amongst local birds, we just don't know."

World.title: Body found after house fire in NSW coastal town
World.content:
Police are investigating a house fire at Kiama on the NSW south coast, after a person was found dead in the home on Saturday night.

Authorities were called to the property on Manning Street just before 9:30pm, finding a house engulfed in flames.

Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) responded with eight fire trucks and about 28 firefighters, and were assisted by the NSW Rural Fire Service and police.

NSW Police have confirmed the body of a person, who is yet to be formally identified, was located at the scene following the fire.

Investigators are still working to confirm the cause of the blaze but have told the ABC it is not being treated as suspicious.

The home in Kiama was destroyed by the blaze. (Supplied: Darin Sullivan)

FRNSW acting superintendent Peter Murray said crews worked to contain the fire to the property, which was located in a residential street in the coastal town, but the home was extensively damaged by the blaze.

"Fire crews worked to help make the site safe before handing the scene over to the NSW Police," Mr Murray said in a statement to the ABC.

Winter fire safety

Kiama state MP Katelin McInerney said the incident was "incredibly sad" and expressed her "deepest sympathies to [the deceased's] family and friends" in a statement posted to social media on Sunday morning.

"Thank you to the local first responders who acted so swiftly and worked to put out the blaze and responded with professionalism and compassion at a such a confronting scene," Ms McInerney said in the statement.

" With winter now truly upon us, please check all your smoke alarms are working, batteries are in, ensure heaters are plugged in correctly and used safely, and that you have fire blankets in the kitchen and bedroom. "

It comes a fortnight after another fatal Illawarra house fire, which claimed the life of a woman in Coniston, near Wollongong.

Investigations are ongoing into the blaze at Kiama and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Alan Joyce: Qantas survived COVID because of my decisions
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Alan Joyce: Qantas survived COVID because of my decisions Chris Zappone July 26, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Qantas CEO Alan Joyce has claimed responsibility for the airline’s survival, three years after a series of customer-service outages and operational failures infuriated the public. Joyce acknowledged the airline’s dismal post-COVID recovery experience, a chaotic period marked by skyrocketing fares and illegal sackings, in comments broadcast on 60 Minutes. Joyce stepped away from the role two months early in 2023 amid political and consumer backlash. Alan Joyce attempts to answer criticism about his leadership at Qantas in his memoir Riding the Jet Stream. 60 Minutes He said the hard decisions aided the company. “I think Qantas is in survival [mode] now because we got more things right than we got wrong,” he told 60 Minutes’ Tracy Grimshaw. “I recognise that when it comes down to it, the buck will always stop with the CEO on these things, and I accept that.” As COVID lock-downs ended in 2022, and the airline began restarting its flight schedule, passengers were left stranded amidst endless airport queues, backed-up call centres, and cancellations. Qantas’ performance was further imperilled by the decision in 2021 to fire 1820 ground crew and baggage handlers, which meant it struggled to process customer luggage.



60 Minutes is owned by Nine Entertainment, owner of this masthead. Joyce has been speaking to the media ahead of the release of his autobiography on Tuesday. Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared In some of his first extensive comments on his 15 years as Qantas boss, Joyce says that one of his biggest regrets is how the company handled its exit from COVID, a period that included the notorious “ghost flights”, the withholding of flight credits, and criticism of passengers for not being “match fit” for flying. “One of my biggest regrets is how we handled coming out of COVID because we got it badly wrong,” Joyce told The Australian this weekend. “COVID was not great. It was terrible.” Qantas fired 1800 ground crew in 2021, which was challenged in court by the Transport Workers Union, which ultimately prevailed. Qantas agreed to pay $120 million in compensation to the workers, and then was fined another $90 million by the court for not being sufficiently contrite. The events precipitated Joyce’s early departure as CEO in 2023.



Vanessa Hudson took over as CEO and has undertaken a rebuilding of trust and relationships both within the company and with the travelling public. Joyce said that the decision to fire the workers was that of then-CEO for Domestic and International Andrew David, according to The Australian. “This decision was Andrew David’s alone,” Joyce said, adding, however, that he takes responsibility for the airline’s actions during his time in charge. The 1820 affected workers are still awaiting compensation. In comments carried by The Australian, Joyce denied “suggestions that he ever personally upgraded” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to business or first class. In a reference to Joe Aston’s book The Chairman’s Lounge, Joyce said that “claims were aired that I’d personally upgraded the prime minister’s flights. My first thought was, ‘That’s news to me.’” Joyce also denied that he upgraded the prime minister’s son to the Chairman’s Lounge, an invitation-only club usually reserved for politicians, business leaders and top media editors.



Joyce referred questions about Albanese’s son to the PM. Editor's pick Updated

Aviation Qantas to pay $105m after class action over cancelled COVID flights Joyce, who earned global respect for his management of Qantas, was forced to front a Senate inquiry in 2023 in which he defended the company’s profits during a cost-of-living crisis. He was criticised for earning a combined $125 million over his tenure as CEO of 15 years, a time which saw clashes with unions, the successful launch of Jetstar, and forged a lasting alliance with Dubai-based Emirates. Joyce’s book, ‘Alan Joyce: Riding the Jet Stream’ will be released on Tuesday. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ‘Dead in the water’: Navy’s flagship ‘drone ship’ program in doubt
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalDefence ‘Dead in the water’: Navy’s flagship ‘drone ship’ program in doubt Matthew Knott July 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A centrepiece of the Albanese government’s push to modernise the navy – a fleet of large, heavily armed warships that can operate with or without sailors on board – has been thrown into doubt after the United States military dumped its plan to develop the vessels. The government insists it is committed to the vision outlined in its 2024 surface fleet review, but defence experts say they expect the plan will need to be abandoned or overhauled. The government announced with much fanfare two years ago that it would boost the firepower of the navy by acquiring six large optionally crewed surface vessels packed with missiles and based on a prototype being developed in the US. A US naval vessel, USV Ranger, on the Pacific Ocean during a training exercise in 2023. But the US navy last year scrapped that program and is instead pursuing a fleet of smaller drone ships that do not have the option of crew members.



Richard Dunley, a senior lecturer in maritime strategy at UNSW, said the US navy’s large unmanned surface vessel program “has been killed”, raising serious questions about the future of Australia’s plan. “The universal assumption was that Australia would piggyback off the US vessel,” he said. “I find it very difficult to see how Australia could do this on our own. “I keep expecting to hear that it’s dead, and I was surprised to see it feature in this year’s national defence strategy.” Former naval officer Jennifer Parker, an expert associate at the Australian National University’s national security college, agreed, saying: “I think we will end up abandoning the idea of large optionally crewed vessels and move to unmanned medium-sized surface vessels in line with the US.”



The vessels would also probably use containerised weapons rather than the vertical launch system envisaged under the government’s plan, she said. The government allocated up to $300 million for optionally crewed surface vessels in its 10-year defence spending plan released in April. But with the vessels estimated to cost around $US250 million ($360 million) each to build, the total cost of the program would ultimately be billions of dollars. Related Article Defence Why the navy is buying a ghost fleet of drone boats for ‘three D’ jobs: Dirty, dull or dangerous “The government is investing $52-$65 billion over the decade to deliver a larger, more lethal surface combatant fleet, through enhancements to strike, air defence and undersea warfare capabilities including six large optionally crewed surface vessels with up to 32 vertical launch system cells to increase the ADF’s maritime long-range strike capability,” a Defence spokesperson said. Greens defence spokesman David Shoebridge called for the government to admit it was proposing to buy a “ghost ship”, describing the affair as the “perfect example of what is wrong with Defence right now.



“The US had a thought-bubble about an experimental and boutique military asset and Labor and the Coalition was so desperate to show their loyalty to the US they immediately signed us up,” he said. “Then when the US spiked the program, without ever consulting Australia, we are left with $300 million attached to a project that is dead in the water. “It’s not just the embarrassment and the incompetence, there is also a huge opportunity cost here in terms of public money and defence resources.” Kamikaze drone boats have played a crucial role in the war in Iran, but these are far smaller and more expendable than the large arsenal ships Australia plans to acquire. Defence firm Austal in November unveiled designs for two new optionally crewed surface vessels – known as the Vantage-class – which it said could meet the Australian navy’s needs.



But military leaders have said they remain committed to developing the vessels with the US. “There is an opportunity for us to realise a really important capability that would take our fleet forwards in terms of its lethality and survivability, but that can’t happen if the US navy don’t commit to the program,” Defence Force vice chief Robert Chipman told Senate estimates hearings in June. “It was tied to the US navy, and there are currently no other options that we’re considering.” Chipman added: “We recognise that there are potential delays to the large optionally crewed vessel, so, yes, we are tracking what the US Navy is saying.” The surface fleet review said the navy would acquire the six vessels “through formal engagement with the United States Navy program as a fast follower”, with an expectation they would enter service in the 2030s and 2040s.



Defence Minister Richard Marles said at the time the vessels would be “exactly based on what has been developed in the United States”, describing the prototype as a “known quantity”. “They have the capacity to operate in an uncrewed fashion, but it is the intention of the Royal Australian Navy to crew these vessels,” he said. Dunley warned at the time that the government was gambling on unproven technology and that the vessels had critics within the US navy. Rear Admiral William Daly, the US navy’s surface warfare requirements director, said last year the large vessels had “walked the path towards exquisite, expensive [and] unpalatable”. The US Naval Institute reported last year that the US military was moving away from optionally crewed vessels because they are considered too costly and complicated.



Unmanned vessels do not require berthing space, galleys, toilets and other features needed to support sailors on board. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Five Liberal MPs supported a factional deal. Now it’s at the centre of a corruption probe
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny Five Liberal MPs supported a factional deal. Now it’s at the centre of a corruption probe Michael McGowan July 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Five current NSW Liberal MPs voted for a factional deal to replace sitting members of the Hills Shire Council while they were on the party’s powerful state executive – a decision likely to be central to an anti-corruption probe into fugitive property developer Jean Nassif’s links to Liberal powerbrokers. Ahead of the launch of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s Operation Rosny inquiry on Monday, the Herald has obtained documents from the October 2021 meeting of the Liberal state executive at which members voted to install new council candidates in The Hills. The eight-week ICAC inquiry into the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif’s links to Liberal powerbrokers will begin on Monday. Michael Howard The vote helped spark the ICAC’s probe, after Kellyville MP Ray Williams made an explosive speech to parliament in mid-2022 alleging Nassif had paid “significant funds” to Liberal Party apparatchik Christian Ellis and other senior party members to install new councillors in The Hills Shire Council who would support Nassif’s future development applications. Then-Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet referred Williams’ claims to the ICAC the following day.



Related Article Exclusive

Operation Rosny Revealed: First witnesses to front sensational corruption investigation The documents obtained by the Herald confirm for the first time the details of the decision to bypass a preselection and install new councillors. The motion, authored by then NSW Liberal president Philip Ruddock, states he had been advised of an “agreed position with respect to selecting and endorsing candidates for the 2021 local government elections in The Hills local government area”. Some of the candidates, the document noted, had not been vetted, while others “did not originally nominate for these positions”. Voting records for the meeting show while he is listed as the author of the motion, Ruddock himself abstained from voting. Asked why by the Herald, the former attorney-general said: “I have no recollection of those matters.”



But five current MPs who were on the state executive at the time supported it. The group includes four current members of Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane’s frontbench: Chris Rath, James Wallace, Jacqui Munro and Mark Coure. All four are from the dominant moderate faction. The fifth, upper house MP Aileen MacDonald, is from the right. NSW Liberal MP Chris Rath. Oscar Colman The five MPs either declined to comment or did not respond to questions by the Herald. There is no suggestion any of the five MPs were aware of the allegations surrounding the vote at the time. Instead, senior moderate sources said the vote was part of what had been a long-running agreement between the hard-right and moderate factions that emerged out of the agreement between senior NSW Liberals Matt Kean and Dominic Perrottet.



Related Article Exclusive

Operation Rosny The Liberals’ sliding doors moment that led to a blockbuster ICAC inquiry “As far as we were concerned, it was factional politics as usual in a part of the world that was always really brutal,” one senior moderate who asked to speak on the condition of anonymity to discuss an internal party matter said. However, many Liberal MPs are privately resigned to the likelihood that the eight-week ICAC inquiry will draw in multiple members of Sloane’s opposition. Although no MPs have been accused of any wrongdoing, the inquiry has the potential to be hugely damaging for the party even by dragging out a period of messy internal factionalism. At the same time, senior party members had long raised concerns about Ellis, and his links to Nassif, before the Hills vote.



The Herald has previously revealed senior party members had unsuccessfully sought to stop Ellis’s ascension to the party’s state executive as far back as 2019 because of his links to lobbying firm Beckington. Toplace, Nassif’s company, was registered as a client of Beckington’s from July 2020. Before his speech to parliament in 2022, Ray Williams, who is a member of the centre-right faction, also raised concerns with then-premier Gladys Berejiklian as early as November 2020. Ray Williams is the Liberal MP for Kellyville. Wolter Peeters In a series of text messages, first reported by the ABC and confirmed by the Herald, Williams wrote to Berejiklian urging her to help block attempts by the right faction to move three party branches into the Hills Shire in a bid to control council preselections there. “It’s completely uncalled for and just an attempt to put [councillors] into the Hills Council who support a particular developer,” Williams wrote at the time, referring to Nassif.



“Raymondo, I’ll call you first thing in the morning Darl,” Berejiklian replied. Berejiklian initially told Williams she and the then-police minister David Elliott, also a member of the centre-right, were “trying to calm the troops and delay”, but that “so far no one is budging”. After Williams sent a series of further entreaties, he texted the premier again on the day of the ballot asking whether her representative on the state executive would abstain from the vote. “I’m not getting involved in this Ray,” she wrote back. “I’m sick of everyone trying to embroil me in factional issues. I have too much on my plate.”



When Williams said it was “much bigger than factionalism” and involved “corruption by a few on state executive”, Berejiklian said: “You need to report it”. “I certainly am,” Williams replied. “Good!!” Berejiklian said. Ellis is one of 10 persons of interest before the ICAC as part of Operation Rosny, its wide-ranging probe into Nassif’s links to party powerbrokers, councils and the state’s Catholic schools. The first witness before the public inquiry on Monday will be Michael O’Hara, a publican, lawyer and developer who is a focus of the ICAC’s inquiry. Dylan Whitelaw, a one-time Liberal staffer who has previously been closely associated with many of the figures central to the inquiry, will appear on Tuesday. World.title: How about the 34-year-old who out-scored Essendon on Saturday
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 How about the 34-year-old who out-scored Essendon on Saturday Peter Ryan July 26, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points The AFL has 112 listed players in their 30s. A decade ago it was only 65.

Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has done it again in July.

‘F--- off’ should not be the phrase of choice between Suns teammates.

Carlton’s Lewis Young went back on his mark further than Michael Holding.

Jack Gunston’s seven-goal haul against Essendon helped the cause of veterans wanting to play on in 2027. He is 34, has kicked 100 goals in his past 30 matches, and kicked a matchwinning behind for the Hawks on Easter Monday against Geelong. He has now kicked five bags of five goals this season. According to @sirswampthing he became the third-oldest player to outscore the opposition with his 7.2 (44) topping the Bombers 5.9 (39) on Saturday. Hawthorn star Jack Gunston kicked his 600th goal during a brilliant third quarter. AFL Photos via Getty Images



His performance was a timely reminder of the increased presence and influence of older players in the competition in the same week he and 36-year-old Cat Patrick Dangerfield signed on for another season. Unusually, the trend has become the old-timer’s friend. It’s no longer unusual to have at least half a dozen players on a club list who are 30-something. In 2026, there were 112 listed players still getting dirty in their 30s. In 2016, there were only 65. In 2026, eight players of the top 20 highest rating players in the competition are 30-something. In 2016, the only player was then Suns’ champion Gary Ablett jr. Four of the top players in this year’s coaches’ votes are in their 30s right now. In 2016 there were zero.



The shift has not just occurred because the money is too good to pass up and sports science has improved player longevity. Games record holder and the oldest player in the game Scott Pendlebury makes a huge contribution to the Magpies AFL Photos Clubs now recognise how valuable it can be to have older players on their list as long as they fill a few preconditions. They need to lose the grumpy pills which are allocated to everyone in greater numbers after each year after they reach 30. That means accepting a different role which may mean playing out of the midfield, or less game time, or fewer games, or even playing VFL and accepting the importance and satisfaction of the often underappreciated teaching job.



The AFL’s oldest current players 38 Scott Pendlebury (Collingwood)

37 Dayne Zorko (Brisbane Lions)

36 Patrick Dangerfield (Geelong)*

36 Taylor Walker (Adelaide)

36 Dane Rampe (Sydney Swans)

36 Jeremy Howe (Collingwood)

35 Steele Sidebottom (Collingwood)

35 Rhys Stanley (Geelong)

35 Mason Cox (Fremantle)

34 Mark Blicavs (Geelong)

34 Jake Melksham (Melbourne)

34 Jack Gunston (Hawthorn)*

34 Max Gawn (Melbourne)*

34 Nick Haynes (Carlton)

34 Tom Liberatore (Western Bulldogs) Of the top 15 oldest players in the league, only Melbourne’s Max Gawn has played every match and remains at his peak every match. The rest have accepted something different. Even Gawn has pulled back a little to give Max Heath a taste when possible. Resisting the temptation to be grumpy means taking notice of players and people in the program, passing on wisdom and enjoying the achievements of those many years your junior. You can set some people straight or you can expand your own sense of what is possible and gain a new lease of life. Anyone who saw teammates celebrate the 600th career goal of the friendly curmudgeon that is Gunston by making him the centre of attention understood how great clubs are built on connections between generations. To play on, a player needs to maintain their weapons so they can be deployed in a role that suits the team’s needs – if not every match then often enough.



The skipper Patrick Dangerfield will play on in 2027 Getty Images Dangerfield’s power remains although it’s used to win or halve contests inside 50 rather than in the midfield where he would need to work too hard to stay in the game. Scott Pendlebury’s poise and ability to put teammates into space is a feature, Jeremy Howe’s leap and defensive know-how is strong, Dayne Zorko hasn’t lost his pace or capacity to kick darts. In an excellent piece of coaching, Gunston has had a role created for him inside 50 which suits his strengths. The disconnected forward leads hard and is an accurate set shot. It’s not easy but certainly his workload is less than others. Imagine what Ben King will learn from him next season? They are no longer their club’s best players – although they can be the best man on the ground in a quarter or half occasionally as Gunston was in the third quarter on Saturday – but the team is better for their presence.



Clubs have also decided a veteran who can play can add depth to their list and complement their team in a way a mediocre mid-20s player can’t. It’s why free agency has proved a bigger boon for strong teams than weaker ones (Good old Lachie Neale forever?). They can add quality players who increase competition for spots, add poise and experience and therefore valuable lessons to both AFL and VFL teams, and during the week when clubs undergo situational training their input is useful. It’s recognition of a point champion cricketer Greg Chappell made in his book Not Out - accepted wisdom among coaches without ego - that players learn better from their peers than coaches. There is also an in-built resilience in veterans as they navigate a long season under scrutiny with all sorts of ups and downs that helps younger players find perspective when challenges inevitably arise.



The extra man on the bench has also given an impetus to the clubs’ willingness to retain veterans as they can manage their time better and have more options when planning how they are going to cover roles. Going on might be good for Gunston and his peers, but this situation has not arisen because clubs have suddenly become generous. The times they are a-changin’ and the veterans’ importance will be on display in September when they challenge the relatively inexperienced premiership favourite Fremantle. Nasiah the messiah should get the three votes Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera defeated the Kangaroos to keep the Saints’ wildcard chances alive. He charged into the game like a fire truck scattering traffic when he kicked three goals and created another goal for Darcy Wilson after chasing down Finn O’Sullivan in the third quarter.



Not only did his sheer brilliance shift the contest, his presence lifted teammates and signalled a return to form after he lost his way against the close checking Cat in round 19. He became the first player to reach 30 disposals, gain 750 metres and kick three goals in the first three quarters. Then he kicked the Saints’ first goal of the final quarter with a steal from Caleb Daniel that ended with a running banana. View post on X The performance was a reprise of his memorable two-vote winning effort against Melbourne on July 27 last season (it was July 26 on Sunday) and a reminder of the reason the Saints paid such a large percentage of their salary cap this season to keep him. Does he get changed in a phone box before games at this time of the year? Thankfully, the umpires have the statistics on hand when voting for the Brownlow. Surely 46 touches (even allowing for kick-ins), four goals, and five clearances will earn him BOG honours.



For the Suns, it’s a season not to forget ‘F--- off’ should not be the phrase of choice between Suns’ teammates given the unfortunate pattern of players taking the direction literally. That teenager Leo Lombard chose to direct that response to animated feedback from a frustrated veteran Christian Petracca is not ideal but it can be easily addressed. It’s not uncommon for interactions between teammates to get off track midway through games. Leo Lombard looks on after a spray from Christian Petracca. Fox Footy



The problem for the Suns is that it reinforces the sense among other clubs that Suns’ players argue on field more than other teams in 2026 (officials at two clubs had mentioned this Suns’ characteristic to this column in the past few months). It also symbolises a season that has spun out of control since their win over Port Adelaide in round 10 in Darwin, when they sat fourth on the ladder and Ben King indicated he wanted to stay at the club. No doubt they have unravelled, but a more in-depth look at their performances indicates more lies behind the drop-off than suggestions of discord, of which there have been plenty, all denied by the Suns. In those first 10 matches, they beat an underdone Geelong, followed by wins over battlers West Coast, Richmond, Essendon, Giants, St Kilda and Port Adelaide. Since Darwin they ran out of legs against North Melbourne then have lost to Brisbane, Geelong, Hawthorn, Fremantle, Collingwood, Adelaide, Western Bulldogs and now Carlton.



That’s like a racehorse being found wanting when stepping up to the wrong grade. Add other elements and a clear picture emerges than the shadow the Suns are casting right now. Injury has ruined Matt Rowell’s year, Mac Andrew’s development has been slow, the ruck rules have pushed Jarrod Witts off the cliff, Bailey Humphrey became distracted by trade talk, and Ben Ainsworth, Sam Flanders, Brayden Fiorini, Connor Budarick and David Swallow all exited after playing in the winning final and were replaced with more talented but less ready players such as Lombard. The other - more existential issue - is that problems of retention have not been solved with Rowell the next contract discussion to be had. And their team needs to deal with frustration better and bounce back from disappointment. That is something they can’t stick their head in the Surfers Paradise sand and hide from.



Smart play young man Carlton’s Lewis Young consoles his Suns’ opponent Ned Moyle AFL Photos Carlton’s Lewis Young went back on his mark further than Michael Holding on his run-up when he had a set shot late in the game against Gold Coast. He not only used the 30 seconds available for players taking a set shot but by taking the Ben Brown run up was able to drain another 14 seconds off the clock during his run-up before kicking. The time remaining went from 3.48 to 3.04 minutes left in the game. It will be interesting if someone tries the same [long] approach in finals. Later that night, Richmond’s Luke Trainor kicked the ball out on the full from outside the boundary line after receiving a free kick for out on the full. However, because he had not returned into play the ball was brought back to where he kicked it for a boundary throw-in. It was a strange rule anomaly that requires consideration post-season. World.title: Which city is better, Sydney or Melbourne? I’m in a unique position to decide
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsCulture wars Opinion Which city is better, Sydney or Melbourne? I’m in a unique position to decide Damien Woolnough Fashion editor July 26, 2026 — 7:46pm

July 26, 2026 — 7:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After spending half my life in Sydney I have answered the footy siren call to return home to Melbourne. It’s fashion not football sending me down the Hume Highway to within sniffing distance of the Yarra River, but the AFL is Melbourne’s answer to Kevin Bacon, with six degrees of separation connecting anything within the city limits to the MCG. These are the final words I will type as fashion editor of The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald and they have nothing to do with Princess Catherine’s latest tiara, Taylor Swift’s wedding dress or the outrageous and well-deserved success of the Zimmermann sisters in conquering international fashion. Sydney v Melbourne … it’s about much more than the footy. Getty Before starting in my new role as the creative director of the Melbourne Fashion Festival, I would like to address the one question that has bombarded me since announcing my double defection: which city is better, Melbourne or Sydney? To do this, I would normally divide the question into categories, in the style of a Miss Universe pageant, without the swimsuit section, which is lucky for Melbourne.



Instead, I will don my custom Gucci sash and deliver my Miss Universe answer, which, like a desire for world peace, is 100 per cent truthful. Both cities are remarkable, and we are lucky to have two distinct capitals so close to each other in such a remote country. The differences between Melbourne and Sydney are all positive. Matt Davidson If Melbourne’s cultural creativity crossed the border, no one would be in bed by 10pm. Imagine having two Melbournes, two Sydneys or, grab your sunglasses, two Brisbanes. The differences between Melbourne and Sydney are all positive. One eye-wateringly beautiful harbour is enough for one country, and if Melbourne’s cultural creativity crossed the border, no one would be in bed by 10pm.



In my experience, most of the clichés we have created about the cities are as truthful as the Ava Gardner misquote that Melbourne was the perfect place to make a film about the end of the world, made up by a cadet journalist in 1959. Melbourne’s nightlife is a drawcard. The Age Sydney people are friendly; Melbourne people don’t always wear black; you can find great coffee and brilliant pasta joints (Pellegrino 2000 in Sydney and Il Solito Posto in Melbourne – fashion people do eat carbs) almost anywhere. Within seconds, without looking at your shoes, a Sydneysider will have you pegged socially, economically and sexually by your postcode. There are some things I will miss about Sydney. For most of my time here I have not owned an iron. Since the death of model Maggie Tabberer in 2024, there are few adherents to crisp collars that could cut prosciutto, with more people leaning towards a crushed lived-in appearance.



In a Sydney summer, crumpled linen shirts are as common as cabanas on the Port Philip Bay foreshore. Ironing a T-shirt in Kings Cross could be mistaken as trying too hard and putting an iron near some of the barely-there dresses at Bondi is a fire hazard. My first purchase in Melbourne will be an iron and a steamer for good measure. It’s not because the locals are more stylish, it’s just that they make more of an effort. Look beyond some of the fancy-dress outfits at the annual NGV Gala and there’s a commitment to a stylish look that disappeared in Sydney when people started turning up to the opening night of the opera in shorts. Dressing down and playing up in Sydney. Dominic Lorrimer Melbourne people like to dress up and Sydney people like to dress up to get down. The ability of Sydney people to introduce their home suburb in the first five minutes of conversation – even if it’s while debating whether J-Lo should have worn a ridiculously big hat to Wimbledon – will also be missed. Within seconds, without looking at your shoes, a Sydneysider will have you pegged socially, economically and sexually by your postcode.



The only way I will be able to cope is by realising that Melbourne people do the same thing by mentioning the school they attended, pigeonholing you with greater accuracy than the resident computer nerd on NCIS. Related Article Good Weekend Melbourne is poised to become our biggest, most liveable city. (Just don’t mention debt. Or crime) I won’t have to miss telling stories about fashion. Whether it’s the Logies, Brownlow, Met Gala or Melbourne Fashion Festival, all Australians have an opinion and appetite for style. Pauline Hanson at a Dolce & Gabbana show in Italy demonstrates the diversity of fashion’s appeal. The big difference is that now I will be telling those stories on the runway, and there just might be a few more people with crisp collars watching from the front row. Damien Woolnough is the departing fashion editor of The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. He is the new creative director of the Melbourne Fashion Festival. In need of some good news?

World.title: Toorak businessman charged with selling over 900 prohibited weapons
World.content:
A Toorak businessman accused of benefiting from the alleged deception of multiple landowners in Melbourne’s outer suburbs has been charged with selling hundreds of swords and other prohibited weapons, including one to a child. Digital marketing expert Kunal Atul Shah is accused of advertising, possessing and selling prohibited weapons, including more than 930 swords, without an exemption from Victoria Police. He is also charged with failing to keep records of the sales, failing to check the identity of his buyers, and selling a sword to a child. He is contesting some of those charges. Toorak businessman Kunal Atul Shah. Instagram Shah allegedly ran the weapons business online through his own website and third-party sellers. Some of the items on sale allegedly included knives, swords, sabres and other collectible fantasy items like toy swords. The businessman was charged after a woman discovered her teenage son had allegedly purchased a sword from Shah’s business on eBay, and contacted police.



Kunal Atul Shah (left) and Raine and Horne Land Victoria agent Kevin Paghdar holidaying in Bali. Shah is accused of benefiting from a contentious land “flipping” scheme allegedly being run by a syndicate of rogue agents within Raine and Horne Land Victoria, as revealed in an investigation by The Age this week. The scheme allegedly deceived the owners of valuable parcels of land in the city’s fringes by undervaluing their lots and selling them to friends and business associates without disclosing the relationship to the vendors. The agents – Rajwinder Singh, Jasdeep Singh, Kevin Paghdar, Amandeep Singh, and Atul Sama – have all denied any wrongdoing, and maintain they are the subject of a smear campaign by disgruntled former employees of the firm. The Age is not suggesting others within the firm are involved. An analysis of property records shows Shah is connected to the purchase of almost $30 million worth of real estate sold by the rogue syndicate since 2022, including in Stonehaven, Nar Nar Goon, Leopold and Werribee.



Images obtained by The Age show Shah is a close friend of Raine and Horne Land Victoria agent Kevin Paghdar and mortgage broker Hardik Shah, who has been involved in several property deals brokered by the syndicate. The pair feature heavily in Shah’s social media – attending lavish parties at his Toorak mansion and taking holidays overseas. Related Article Investigation

Victoria residential property Rogue real estate agents accused of deceiving landowners in scheme to sell to mates In one of the photographs, Shah and Paghdar can be seen standing in a Balinese pool bar surrounded by friends. A bottle of sparkling wine and several flutes sit on a table in the foreground. “If friendship came with an expiry date… ours forgot to show up – 16 years and counting,” a message above the image reads. The Age contacted Shah via phone, text and email, but he could not be reached for comment.



The outer-suburban properties targeted by Raine and Horne Land Victoria are often the subject of a precinct structure plan imposed by the state government to guide future residential development and infrastructure investment. The land can soar in value when rezoned by the government to allow residential subdivisions and boost the state’s housing supply. Shah is regularly featured on social media enjoying a luxurious lifestyle that includes travelling on private jets over the Swiss Alps, holidaying in exclusive resorts in Saudi Arabia, riding jet-skis in Dubai, buying luxury vehicles and hosting opulent parties. Shah next to a baby-blue Bentley. The businessman is often pictured online living a lavish lifestyle. Instagram In a video interview posted on Instagram, Shah can be seen standing next to a $400,000 baby-blue Bentley Continental as an influencer interviews him about his wealth. In the footage, Shah shows the car and a shiny $25,000 Rolex to the camera before offering what he believes is the secret to rebuilding wealth: “Work hard, put more hours in.” Last year, Shah and his wife unveiled The Shah Empire, a custom-made artwork for their Toorak home that represents a “visual chronicle of power, triumph and legacy”.



“The palette of classic gold and white is not accidental – gold represents grandeur, wealth, victory, and timeless glory, while white symbolises purity of purpose, unity, and the enduring spirit,” read the caption of an Instagram post about the artwork. “In essence, the painting is not just a tribute to legacy – a golden path etched in the purity of time, where milestones and hard work of an empire shines.” The Toorak-based businessman appeared in the Dandenong Magistrates’ Court over the weapons charges in May. The court heard submissions that despite having a “postcode locker” in place on his website to prevent orders from being placed within Victoria, a 15-year-old boy was able to order a sword from Shah’s business through eBay and arrange for the weapon to be delivered to his home in Pakenham. Machetes, swords and daggers are prohibited weapons that require a special exemption or approval from the chief commissioner of police in Victoria, regardless of whether the weapons are used for self-protection.



The package was intercepted by the boy’s mother, who then contacted Victoria Police. Investigators say they traced the delivery to a Dandenong South freight-forwarding business connected to Shah’s company, where they allegedly uncovered a stash of more than 900 swords. Raine and Horne agent Kevin Paghdar (front row) celebrating Diwali at a party organised by purchaser Kunal Atul Shah (back row right). Fellow purchaser Hardik Shah (middle row) is also in attendance. Shah’s lawyer told the court the businessman had a hands-off approach to the day-to-day operations of the online business, and the transaction had “slipped through” after his administration officer went on leave. “She was the last line of filtration,” the lawyer said.



He said Shah was aware he was not allowed to sell the weapons in Victoria and was advertising them outside the state. Editor's pick Victoria residential property The tree-change town where house prices have plunged $133,000 “The 15-year-old had faked the fact that he was 18 or over to get access to the site,” the lawyer said. “He deceived eBay, and he deceived my client.” Shah will return to court for a special mention in October. World.title: Alan Joyce: Qantas survived COVID because of my decisions
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Alan Joyce: Qantas survived COVID because of my decisions Chris Zappone July 26, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Qantas CEO Alan Joyce has claimed responsibility for the airline’s survival, three years after a series of customer-service outages and operational failures infuriated the public. Joyce acknowledged the airline’s dismal post-COVID recovery experience, a chaotic period marked by skyrocketing fares and illegal sackings, in comments broadcast on 60 Minutes. Joyce stepped away from the role two months early in 2023 amid political and consumer backlash. Alan Joyce attempts to answer criticism about his leadership at Qantas in his memoir Riding the Jet Stream. 60 Minutes He said the hard decisions aided the company. “I think Qantas is in survival [mode] now because we got more things right than we got wrong,” he told 60 Minutes’ Tracy Grimshaw. “I recognise that when it comes down to it, the buck will always stop with the CEO on these things, and I accept that.” As COVID lock-downs ended in 2022, and the airline began restarting its flight schedule, passengers were left stranded amidst endless airport queues, backed-up call centres, and cancellations. Qantas’ performance was further imperilled by the decision in 2021 to fire 1820 ground crew and baggage handlers, which meant it struggled to process customer luggage.



60 Minutes is owned by Nine Entertainment, owner of this masthead. Joyce has been speaking to the media ahead of the release of his autobiography on Tuesday. Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared In some of his first extensive comments on his 15 years as Qantas boss, Joyce says that one of his biggest regrets is how the company handled its exit from COVID, a period that included the notorious “ghost flights”, the withholding of flight credits, and criticism of passengers for not being “match fit” for flying. “One of my biggest regrets is how we handled coming out of COVID because we got it badly wrong,” Joyce told The Australian this weekend. “COVID was not great. It was terrible.” Qantas fired 1800 ground crew in 2021, which was challenged in court by the Transport Workers Union, which ultimately prevailed. Qantas agreed to pay $120 million in compensation to the workers, and then was fined another $90 million by the court for not being sufficiently contrite. The events precipitated Joyce’s early departure as CEO in 2023.



Vanessa Hudson took over as CEO and has undertaken a rebuilding of trust and relationships both within the company and with the travelling public. Joyce said that the decision to fire the workers was that of then-CEO for Domestic and International Andrew David, according to The Australian. “This decision was Andrew David’s alone,” Joyce said, adding, however, that he takes responsibility for the airline’s actions during his time in charge. The 1820 affected workers are still awaiting compensation. In comments carried by The Australian, Joyce denied “suggestions that he ever personally upgraded” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to business or first class. In a reference to Joe Aston’s book The Chairman’s Lounge, Joyce said that “claims were aired that I’d personally upgraded the prime minister’s flights. My first thought was, ‘That’s news to me.’” Joyce also denied that he upgraded the prime minister’s son to the Chairman’s Lounge, an invitation-only club usually reserved for politicians, business leaders and top media editors.



Joyce referred questions about Albanese’s son to the PM. Editor's pick Updated

Aviation Qantas to pay $105m after class action over cancelled COVID flights Joyce, who earned global respect for his management of Qantas, was forced to front a Senate inquiry in 2023 in which he defended the company’s profits during a cost-of-living crisis. He was criticised for earning a combined $125 million over his tenure as CEO of 15 years, a time which saw clashes with unions, the successful launch of Jetstar, and forged a lasting alliance with Dubai-based Emirates. Joyce’s book, ‘Alan Joyce: Riding the Jet Stream’ will be released on Tuesday. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
